$comment: Content for Raising Gender-Diverse Kids (node g66, Parent Layer, Chapter 8): NEW v2 build to GDD 66
(mechanic-embodying), a SENSITIVE Parent-Layer node handled with the care of Spectrum (g32): dignity-first,
never-out, child-safety-centred. The evidence is the spine: an affirming, accepting parent is the single biggest
protective factor in such a child's wellbeing & safety: family acceptance roughly HALVES (US research) the odds of a suicide attempt, not just suicidal
thoughts and attempts and raises self-esteem and health. 84 researched, India-grounded scenarios across
acceptance-is-protection → understand → if-they-come-out → protect-and-affirm → your-own-journey →
support-and-india, each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions (strike-rewrite / branch / role-play /
reflect / sort / match / spot): no binary "tap the right card". Lead: strike-rewrite (bust the myth), branch
(your move), role-play (say it). Six modes: acceptance is protection (busts 'accepting causes it' and
'disapproval steers them back'; lead with love before full understanding), understand (orientation, gender
identity & expression are three DIFFERENT things; busts phase/choice/illness/foreign-invention/bad-parenting
myths), if they come out (the first reaction matters most: lead with gratitude & unconditional love, process
your own shock later, NEVER out the child), protect and affirm (be the safe harbour & advocate, shield from
bullying, follow the child's lead with no pressure to label or mask, use their name & pronouns), your own
journey (meet your own fears & grief honestly and move toward acceptance without shame: take your struggle to a
supportive ADULT, not your child), support and the India context (affirming counsellors & helplines, NEVER
conversion 'cures', and the settled value that every child deserves a safe loving home: set against India's
constitutional dignity, the NALSA (2014) recognition of transgender persons (since the 2026 amendment a legal
certificate needs a medical board; the law is before the Supreme Court), and the
decriminalisation of consensual same-sex relations). Affirming and evidence-based, yet compassionate: it meets
parents wherever they start, without shaming them or their beliefs, while keeping the child's safety & dignity
NON-NEGOTIABLE; it never encourages outing a child, records no identity, and signposts Tele-MANAS 14416
& affirming counsellors; expert-reviewed. Builds on Spectrum (g32) and What Makes Me, Me (g07).
India: families navigate real cultural & legal complexity, so the node leads with the settled value and meets
fear with facts, not blame. gameId "raising-gender-diverse-kids".
title: Raising Gender-Diverse Kids
greet: Hey, it’s Lensy. If your child is LGBTQ+ or gender-diverse: US research found an accepting parent roughly halves the odds of a suicide attempt. Lead with love.

badge.title: Raising Gender-Diverse Kids 🏳️‍🌈
badge.blurb: An accepting parent is a child’s biggest protector (in US research, roughly halving suicide-attempt odds). You lead with love, never out them, reject ‘cures’. 🫶

helpLine: US research: an accepting parent halves an LGBTQ+ child’s odds of a suicide attempt. ‘Cures’ harm. Tele-MANAS 14416, crisis 112. India: NALSA dignity.
reassure: US research: an accepting parent roughly halves your child’s odds of a suicide attempt. Lead with love; ‘cures’ harm. Help: Tele-MANAS 14416. 🫶

scenarios.hook: "Accepting a gender-diverse child encourages or causes it."

myth.un: Accepting a gender-diverse child encourages or causes it.
myth.re: Acceptance doesn't cause anything; it's the single biggest protective factor in such a child's wellbeing and safety.
myth.why: Affirming a child protects them; it doesn't create who they are.

scenarios.relearn: Accepting a gender-diverse child doesn't cause it; an affirming parent is their biggest protective factor.

scenarios.hook: "Being strict or disapproving will steer my child back to 'normal'."

myth.un: Being strict or disapproving will steer my child back to 'normal'.
myth.re: Rejection doesn't change who a child is; it just raises their risk of depression, self-harm and worse.
myth.why: Disapproval harms; it doesn't redirect.

scenarios.relearn: Disapproval doesn't change a child's identity; it only raises their risk of depression and self-harm.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the research is clear, an affirming parent is the most powerful protection a gender-diverse child can have. Sit right?
scenarios.affirm: An affirming, accepting parent is the strongest protective factor for a gender-diverse child's safety and wellbeing.
scenarios.relearn: An affirming parent is the most powerful protection a gender-diverse child can have.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a parental response that protects a gender-diverse child, or one that raises their risk?

items.text: Warmth and acceptance
Shaming or punishing who they are
Standing up for them
Threatening to reject them
Welcoming their friends home
Going cold to show disapproval

scenarios.relearn: Warmth, acceptance and advocacy protect a child; shaming, punishing or threatening rejection raise their risk.

scenarios.hook: Match each affirming action to the protection it gives.

pairs.right: Far lower odds of a suicide attempt

pairs.left: Standing up for them with relatives
Saying 'I love you, no matter what'
pairs.right: A deep sense of being safe

scenarios.relearn: Supporting expression, talking respectfully, welcoming friends, defending them and unconditional love each protect a child.

scenarios.hook: Your son Neel wants to keep his long hair and nail polish, and your head is full of worries.

steps.prompt: He asks to go to his cousin's birthday like that. What do you do?

options.text: Say no this time, so nobody has a reason to tease him
options.then: Neel goes quiet and changes into plain clothes. He doesn't bring up parties for a while.

options.text: Say yes, but explain in detail how frightened you are for him
options.then: He says okay, then asks if he's in trouble. The party feels heavy before it starts.

options.text: Say yes, and plan together what he can say if anyone teases
options.then: Neel beams. You agree on a few words he can use, and a signal if he wants to leave.

options.text: Ask his aunt what she thinks before you decide
options.then: His aunt sighs and gives strong advice. Neel overhears some of it and goes to his room.

steps.why: Yes keeps him safe and included, and planning eases your worry without putting it on him.

steps.prompt: That week, the worries wake you again at 2 am. What do you do?

options.text: Ask Neel in the morning if he's really sure about his look
options.then: Neel stares at his cereal. He wonders if he did something wrong.

options.text: Decide the worries mean you should steer him back to plain clothes
options.then: Neel notices the new rules about his clothes. He starts hiding his nail polish in his bag.

options.text: Keep the worries to yourself and hope they fade
options.then: They don't fade. They leak out as sighs and tight questions all week.

options.text: Take them to a counsellor or friend who will keep it private
options.then: Saying them aloud helps you sleep. Neel still gets his usual morning hug.

steps.why: A trusted adult can hold your worries, so Neel gets your warmth and none of the weight.

steps.prompt: At the next parent meeting, Neel's teacher says some kids have been teasing him. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what the school will do, and tell Neel you're with him
options.then: The teacher agrees to speak to the class. Neel hears that you're on his side and relaxes.

options.text: Promise the teacher that Neel will wear plain clothes to school
options.then: The teasing eases a little. Neel comes home quieter and stops talking about his day.

options.text: Tell Neel that standing out is why they tease him
options.then: Neel nods and looks at the floor. He decides not to tell you next time.

options.text: Thank the teacher and say you'll keep an eye on it
options.then: Nothing changes at school. Neel keeps the teasing to himself for now.

steps.why: Asking the school to act and staying beside him protects Neel without asking him to shrink.

scenarios.debrief: Let your child's safety lead: accept first, work through your worries separately.
scenarios.relearn: Put your child's safety first; lead with acceptance while you process your worries.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you don't have to understand everything to love and protect your child today. Make sense?
scenarios.affirm: You can fully love and protect your child now, even while you're still learning and understanding.
scenarios.relearn: You don't have to understand everything to love and protect your child today.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two things that stop home from being a safe place for a gender-diverse child.

scene.text: Being loved and accepted as they are
Fearing rejection at home
Knowing a parent has their back
Walking on eggshells around a parent
Hearing 'you're safe with me'

scenarios.why: Fearing rejection and walking on eggshells stop home from being safe; a child needs love and a parent's backing instead.
scenarios.relearn: Home protects a gender-diverse child when they're loved as they are and know a parent has their back.

scenarios.hook: "My disapproval is harmless as long as I still feed and house my child."

myth.un: My disapproval is harmless as long as I still feed and house my child.
myth.re: Children feel rejection deeply; ongoing disapproval harms their mental health even when material needs are met.
myth.why: Felt rejection wounds, food or not.

scenarios.relearn: Disapproval isn't harmless even with needs met; children feel rejection deeply, and it harms their mental health.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'I love you, no matter what' may be the most protective sentence your child ever hears. Worth saying often?
scenarios.affirm: Hearing 'I love you no matter what', and feeling it, is profoundly protective for a gender-diverse child.
scenarios.relearn: 'I love you, no matter what' may be the most protective sentence your child ever hears.

scenarios.hook: "Being gender-diverse or LGBTQ+ is just a phase or a trend kids copy."

myth.un: Being gender-diverse or LGBTQ+ is just a phase or a trend kids copy.
myth.re: Identity isn't a trend or a passing phase to wait out; whether it shifts or not, your child deserves respect now.
myth.why: You respect a child as they are, today.

scenarios.relearn: Being LGBTQ+ or gender-diverse isn't a trend to wait out; respect your child as they are now.

scenarios.hook: "Someone chose to be this way, or was made this way by bad parenting."

myth.un: Someone chose to be this way, or was made this way by bad parenting.
myth.re: Sexual orientation and gender identity aren't a choice or caused by parenting; they're part of who a person is.
myth.why: It's not a choice and not your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Orientation and gender identity aren't chosen or caused by parenting; they're simply part of who a child is.

scenarios.hook: Sort: an accurate idea about gender and orientation, or a myth to drop?

items.text: Gender identity is an innate sense of self
It's an illness to be cured
Orientation and gender identity are different things
It's a foreign or modern invention
Expression is how a child shows who they are
It's something a child chose to do

scenarios.relearn: Identity as innate, orientation differing from identity, and expression are accurate; 'illness', 'foreign' and 'a choice' are myths.

scenarios.hook: Match each term to what it means.

pairs.right: Your own inner sense of your gender
How you show it, clothes, hair, style
Gender differs from the sex assigned at birth
Choosing to share who you are

scenarios.relearn: Orientation (attraction), gender identity (inner sense), expression (how you show it), transgender and coming out each mean something distinct.

scenarios.hook: "A boy who likes 'girl things' (or vice versa) must be confused or broken."

myth.un: A boy who likes 'girl things' (or vice versa) must be confused or broken.
myth.re: Children explore interests and expression freely; a boy in a dress or a girl who loves trucks is just a child being themselves.
myth.why: Interests have no gender; kids aren't broken for crossing them.

scenarios.relearn: A child crossing 'gendered' interests isn't confused or broken; they're just being themselves.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: replacing fear with accurate facts is the first gift you give a gender-diverse child. Resonate?
scenarios.affirm: Replacing fear and myth with accurate understanding is the foundation of affirming and protecting your child.
scenarios.relearn: Replacing fear with accurate facts is the first gift you give a gender-diverse child.

scenarios.hook: "Transgender means the same thing as gay."

myth.un: Transgender means the same thing as gay.
myth.re: They're different: being transgender is about gender identity, while gay is about orientation; a person can be either, both or neither.
myth.why: Identity and attraction are separate.

scenarios.relearn: Transgender (gender identity) and gay (orientation) are different things; they're not the same.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths about a gender-diverse child.

scene.text: They're being who they are
They're doing it to rebel or hurt you
Their identity is real and theirs
They're only doing it for attention
They deserve respect just as they are

scenarios.why: 'Doing it to hurt you' and 'only for attention' are hurtful myths; the child is simply being who they are.
scenarios.relearn: A gender-diverse child is being who they are; it isn't rebellion, an attack on you, or attention-seeking.

scenarios.hook: You don't fully understand your child's identity and feel out of your depth.

steps.prompt: Your child uses a word for how they feel that you've never heard. What do you do?

options.text: Read up on an affirming site, then ask them about it
options.then: Your child lights up when you use the word right. You still have lots to learn.

options.text: Nod along and read up on it privately later
options.then: You read for an hour. Your child could tell you weren't really listening.

options.text: Say it sounds like a fashion they'll grow out of
options.then: Your child stops mid-sentence and says "Never mind."

options.text: Ask them to explain everything, right now, in full
options.then: They try, then look tired. Teaching you feels like a job.

steps.why: Reading first, then asking, shows effort without making your child do all the teaching.

steps.prompt: Online you find two very different articles about children like yours. What do you do?

options.text: Trust affirming counsellors and parent groups
options.then: You find a parents' page with plain advice. Your shoulders loosen a little.

options.text: Read the scariest one so you're prepared for anything
options.then: You close it feeling alarmed and no clearer about your child.

options.text: Ask the neighbours and relatives what they've heard
options.then: Everyone has an opinion and nobody has facts. You feel more on edge.

options.text: Keep whichever one fits what you already believed
options.then: You feel calmer for an hour. The old worry is back by evening.

steps.why: Affirming, expert sources give facts you can build on. Fear and rumour don't.

steps.prompt: Weeks later your child quietly asks if this is still hard for you. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes, sometimes, and that you're learning and staying close
options.then: Your child smiles a little. "Thanks for telling me the truth."

options.text: Say it's all fine now, so they won't worry
options.then: Your child nods, but seems unsure whether to believe you.

options.text: Say you'll understand it fully when they're older
options.then: Your child goes quiet. Waiting years for you feels like a long time.

options.text: Say it's been hard because of what they've put you through
options.then: Your child's face falls. Now they're carrying your feelings too.

steps.why: Being honest that you are still learning, while staying close, builds trust.

scenarios.debrief: Meet what you don't understand with humble learning, not rejection.
scenarios.relearn: Learn with humility when out of your depth; rejecting what you don't grasp harms your child.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you can be a beginner at this and still be exactly the parent your child needs. Sit right?
scenarios.affirm: You don't need to be an expert; a willing, loving, learning parent is exactly what a gender-diverse child needs.
scenarios.relearn: You can be a beginner at this and still be exactly the parent your child needs.

scenarios.hook: "How I first react to my child coming out doesn't really matter."

myth.un: How I first react to my child coming out doesn't really matter.
myth.re: The first reaction matters enormously; a warm, loving response is something a child remembers and is protected by for life.
myth.why: That first moment can shape everything.

scenarios.relearn: Your first reaction to a child coming out matters enormously; warmth in that moment protects them for life.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Jia nervously tells you she thinks she may be LGBTQ+.
scenarios.setup: She sits very still, watching your face.

steps.prompt: Jia whispers: "Please say something. Anything."

options.text: "Are you sure? It's probably just a phase."
options.then: Jia's face closes. "It's not a phase."

options.text: "I'm not upset. I just don't know what to say."
options.then: Jia nods. "Okay." Her hands stay tight in her lap.

options.text: "Thank you for trusting me. I love you exactly as you are."
options.then: Jia's eyes fill. "I didn't know how you'd react."

options.text: "Where did you get this idea from?"
options.then: Jia flinches. "Nowhere. It's just me."

steps.why: Thanks and unconditional love, first, are the most protective words you can offer.

steps.prompt: Jia asks: "Does this change how you see me?"

options.text: "A little. I'll need time to see you differently."
options.then: Jia nods slowly. "Right. So you'll see me as someone else."

options.text: "Not if this turns out to be temporary."
options.then: Jia bristles. "It's not temporary. It's me."

options.text: "It changes nothing, so let's not talk about it."
options.then: Jia's face falls. She had hoped to talk.

options.text: "No. You're the same person I've always loved."
options.then: She lets out a long breath. "Okay. Good."

steps.why: A plain 'no' with your love in it answers the fear underneath her question.

steps.prompt: Jia says: "I don't want anyone else to know yet. Not even Papa."

options.text: "Understood. Who knows is up to you."
options.then: Jia breathes out. "Thank you. I'll tell you when I'm ready."

options.text: "I'll have to tell Papa. He's my husband."
options.then: Jia's eyes widen. "Please don't. I'm not ready."

options.text: "Okay, but I'll tell my sister. She'll keep it quiet."
options.then: Jia's face falls. "Then it isn't a secret at all."

options.text: "Not telling anyone will only make it harder."
options.then: Jia looks down. "I'll decide when," she says quietly.

steps.why: Who knows is her decision, so agreeing to her pace protects her trust.

scenarios.relearn: Leading with gratitude and unconditional love is the single most protective first response you can give.

scenarios.hook: Your son Ishaan has just come out to you. You feel shock, but you don't want to wound him.

steps.prompt: He's watching you, tense. What do you do?

options.text: React from the shock and say something harsh
options.then: Ishaan flinches. He says nothing, and walks to his room.

options.text: Say 'This is too much' and walk out of the room
options.then: Ishaan sits alone with the words he just said. He doesn't follow you.

options.text: Say 'We'll talk about it later' and go quiet
options.then: Ishaan nods. He spends the evening waiting for a later that doesn't come.

options.text: Say 'I love you and I'm glad you told me'
options.then: Ishaan's shoulders drop. "I was so afraid you'd be angry," he says.

steps.why: Love in the first moment is what he'll remember. Your shock can wait.

steps.prompt: That night, your shock keeps swirling as you lie awake. What do you do?

options.text: Take it to a counsellor or a friend who will keep it private
options.then: You arrange to talk to someone tomorrow and sleep a little. Ishaan gets a warm hello.

options.text: Wake Ishaan to talk your feelings through with him
options.then: Ishaan sits up, listening. By the end he's comforting you.

options.text: Decide it's only a phase and simply wait for it all to pass
options.then: You feel calmer for a day. The waiting starts to look like distance to Ishaan.

options.text: Push the feelings aside and act as if nothing happened
options.then: The feelings stay. They surface as sighs and flat answers all week.

steps.why: Your feelings deserve care, and a private counsellor or friend can give it without weighing on Ishaan.

steps.prompt: By the weekend, Ishaan seems to be avoiding you. What do you do?

options.text: Give him more space and wait for him to come to you when ready
options.then: Ishaan stays in his room. He decides you still need time.

options.text: Knock, and tell him you love him and are glad he told you
options.then: Ishaan looks up, guarded. "Really?" he asks, and stays.

options.text: Ask him to prove he's really sure before you talk any more
options.then: Ishaan stiffens. "It's not a test," he says.

options.text: Tell him he's being oversensitive and should come out of his room
options.then: Ishaan comes out, tight-lipped. He eats dinner and says little.

steps.why: Reaching out yourself shows him the door is open from your side, whatever you're still feeling.

scenarios.debrief: Lead with love the moment a child comes out; process your own shock later.
scenarios.relearn: Give love first when a child comes out; handle your shock later so you don't wound them.

scenarios.hook: Match each first-response instinct to the affirming version.
scenarios.relearn: Each doubting first instinct has an affirming version that protects the child instead of questioning them.

scenarios.hook: "If my child comes out, I should immediately tell relatives."

myth.un: If my child comes out, I should immediately tell relatives.
myth.re: It's the child's story to share or not; never out them, let them choose who knows and when.
myth.why: Their identity is theirs to disclose.

scenarios.relearn: Never out your child to relatives; whether and when to share their identity is the child's own choice.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'I love you and I'm so glad you told me' is a response your child will carry forever. Worth getting right?
scenarios.affirm: A warm 'I love you and I'm glad you told me' is a response a child carries, and is protected by, for life.
scenarios.relearn: 'I love you and I'm so glad you told me' is a response your child will carry forever.

scenarios.hook: Your child just came out. Spot the two responses that put them at risk.

scene.text: Warmth, love and 'thank you for telling me'
Shock, anger or denial
'I'm here, let's figure it out together'
'It's shameful, don't tell anyone'
Staying close and listening

scenarios.why: Shock or denial and 'it's shameful' both read as rejection and put a child at risk; warmth keeps them safe.
scenarios.relearn: Meet a coming-out with warmth and 'we'll figure it out together', not shock, denial or shame.

scenarios.hook: You said something harsh when your daughter Rhea first came out, and you regret it.

steps.prompt: Two days on, Rhea is polite but distant. What do you do?

options.text: Go to her, apologise and tell her you love her
options.then: Rhea's eyes fill. She doesn't say much, but she doesn't leave.

options.text: Let it stand, because the moment has passed
options.then: Rhea stays polite. The distance sits between you at every meal.

options.text: Bring her favourite sweet and say nothing about it
options.then: She thanks you and eats it slowly. No sorry has been said.

options.text: Explain that you were in shock and ask her to understand
options.then: Rhea listens and nods. She hears no sorry.

steps.why: A real apology and clear love repair what the moment broke.

steps.prompt: A week later, Rhea says she still remembers what you said. What do you do?

options.text: Say she's holding on to it for too long
options.then: Rhea nods and drops it. She looks like she feels dismissed.

options.text: Ask what she remembers, listen fully and say you're sorry
options.then: Rhea repeats the words. You listen. Her voice cracks, and so does yours.

options.text: Say it's in the past and you should both move on
options.then: She goes quiet. "Okay," she says, and leaves the room.

options.text: Explain that you were in shock at the time
options.then: Rhea listens patiently. She says "I know" and looks tired.

steps.why: Listening fully, and saying sorry, lets her hurt be seen instead of hurried past.

steps.prompt: Rhea's birthday is coming and she's unsure whether to expect a celebration. What do you do?

options.text: Plan a surprise party and invite all the relatives
options.then: Rhea walks in and freezes. She spends the evening on the edge of the room.

options.text: Skip the celebration this year to avoid tension
options.then: Rhea says okay. The day passes like any other.

options.text: Ask what kind of day she'd love and plan it with her
options.then: Rhea thinks, then names a small dinner with two friends. She smiles for the first time in days.

options.text: Give her a gift and don't talk about anything else
options.then: She thanks you and opens it. The gift is kind, but the silence stays.

steps.why: Asking what she'd love, and planning it with her, shows repair in action.

scenarios.debrief: If you reacted badly to a coming-out, go back, apologise and reaffirm love; repair is always possible.
scenarios.relearn: Repair a bad first reaction: go back, apologise, reaffirm love; it's never too late.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Aditi has come out to you, and she is watching whether anything has changed.
scenarios.setup: She stands at the door, holding her phone.

steps.prompt: Aditi asks: "Do you still love me? Be honest."

options.text: "Of course, but I wish things were different."
options.then: Aditi's smile falters. "Different how?"

options.text: "I love you completely. Nothing about this changes that."
options.then: Aditi's shoulders drop. "Okay," she whispers. "Say it again?"

options.text: "I love you. I just worry how hard your life will be."
options.then: Aditi nods. "I know," she says, as if she's heard it before.

options.text: "Yes. Now let's not talk about it any more."
options.then: Aditi pockets her phone. She had hoped for more.

steps.why: A clear, unconditional line leaves no room for the doubt that hurts most.

steps.prompt: Aditi says: "Sometimes I think you'd be happier if I were different."

options.text: "I want you happy. That's all I care about."
options.then: She nods. It's kind, but it doesn't answer her.

options.text: "Sometimes I wish it were easier for you."
options.then: Aditi stiffens. "So I make it hard for you?"

options.text: "No. You make me happy exactly as you are."
options.then: Aditi's eyes fill. "Really?"

options.text: "That's a silly thing to think."
options.then: Aditi's face closes. She never says it again.

steps.why: Saying she makes you happy as she is answers the real fear and takes the weight off her.

steps.prompt: Aditi asks: "What if Papa doesn't take it well?"

options.text: "Then you'll have to give him time to adjust."
options.then: Aditi frowns. "How much time? And what do I do meanwhile?"

options.text: "Then let me speak to him first, and you stay out of it."
options.then: Aditi bristles. "It's my news. I want to say it myself."

options.text: "Then it's probably best not to tell him."
options.then: Aditi's face falls. "So I hide from Papa forever?"

options.text: "Then I'll be beside you. You won't face him alone."
options.then: Aditi leans against you. "Okay. I feel less scared."

steps.why: Being beside her, without deciding for her, tells her she won't face it alone.

steps.prompt: Aditi asks: "Will you say it again tomorrow? That you love me?"

options.text: "Every day, if you like. You'll get tired of hearing it."
options.then: Aditi laughs, wet-eyed. "I won't."

options.text: "I shouldn't have to. You know it."
options.then: Aditi nods. She looks like she wants to be told.

options.text: "If you need it, just ask me."
options.then: Aditi shrugs. Asking is hard for her.

options.text: "Once should be enough."
options.then: Aditi's face falls. "Okay," she says quietly.

steps.why: Saying it again shows her it isn't a one-time reaction, but a steady fact.

scenarios.relearn: A clear, unconditional 'nothing changes my love' leaves no room for the doubt that endangers a child.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a child who comes out to you has handed you their trust; how you hold it shapes their life. Feel the weight?
scenarios.affirm: When a child comes out to you, they're handing you their trust; holding it with love shapes their whole life.
scenarios.relearn: A child coming out hands you their trust; how you hold it shapes their life.

scenarios.hook: "My job is to toughen my gender-diverse child up against a harsh world."

myth.un: My job is to toughen my gender-diverse child up against a harsh world.
myth.re: The world may be hard, but your job is to be their safe harbour and advocate, not another source of toughening or pressure.
myth.why: Be the shelter, not the storm.

scenarios.relearn: Your job isn't to toughen a gender-diverse child against the world, but to be their safe harbour and advocate.

scenarios.hook: Your child has been bullied at school for being different, and it has happened more than once.

steps.prompt: They come home with a torn notebook and say nothing. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with them, say it's not their fault, and listen
options.then: They cry a little, then tell you who was there and what was said.

options.text: Tell them to just fit in so it stops
options.then: They nod and look at the floor. The next day they wear plainer clothes.

options.text: Tell them to ignore it until it passes
options.then: They say okay, and then they stop mentioning school at all.

options.text: Phone the principal tonight and demand the bullies be punished
options.then: He coolly promises to look into it. Your child, overhearing, begs you to stop.

steps.why: Hearing it's not their fault, and being listened to, tells them you are their safe place.

steps.prompt: At the parent-teacher meeting, you raise the bullying, and the class teacher calls it "just kids being kids". What do you do?

options.text: Ask for a clear plan to stop it and a date to review
options.then: She agrees to watch the corridor and meet you in two weeks.

options.text: Accept it, since teachers know their classrooms best
options.then: You leave. The teasing goes on, and your child grows quieter about school.

options.text: Ask that your child be moved to another section
options.then: She says it may be possible. Your child looks shaken to be the one moving.

options.text: Post about the teacher in the parents' WhatsApp group
options.then: Other parents pile in. The principal calls you, and the teacher turns cold.

steps.why: A clear plan with a review date gives the school a job, and a day to report back.

steps.prompt: A week on, your child asks quietly if hiding who they are would make it stop. What do you say?

options.text: Say they never have to hide, and you'll watch it together
options.then: They straighten a little. "Okay. Can I tell you every time it happens?"

options.text: Say a little hiding at school is probably safest
options.then: They nod, and you watch them fold themselves smaller each morning.

options.text: Say it's their decision and you'll stay out of it
options.then: They shrug. "Fine." They are carrying it on their own again.

options.text: Say you'll ask the teacher to explain them to the class
options.then: Your child looks alarmed. "Please don't tell everyone about me."

steps.why: They shouldn't have to hide. Staying beside them and letting them lead keeps them safe.

scenarios.debrief: Protect a bullied gender-diverse child by stepping in and advocating, not by telling them to fit in.
scenarios.relearn: Advocate for a bullied child's safety; 'just fit in' abandons them to the harm.

scenarios.hook: Ahead of a big family function, relatives say your child must be "corrected" before people see them.

steps.prompt: Your uncle repeats it on the phone the night before. What do you say?

options.text: Say calmly that no one will shame your child
options.then: He goes quiet, then mutters that you are making a mistake.

options.text: Say you'll talk to your child about behaving
options.then: He sounds pleased. Your child overhears and goes silent.

options.text: Change the subject and hope it fades
options.then: He takes your silence as a yes and tells the others.

options.text: Ask your aunt to gently speak to your child instead
options.then: She says she'll "have a word". Your child hears and dreads the function.

steps.why: Saying it early and calmly protects your child before the function begins.

steps.prompt: At the function, a cousin whispers that people are staring at your child. What do you do?

options.text: Stay close to your child and keep them in the fun
options.then: Your child relaxes beside you and soon joins the cousins at the snack table.

options.text: Ask your child to stay near the kitchen, away from guests
options.then: They slip off to the kitchen and sit among the aunties' pots, alone.

options.text: Ask your child to tone things down for today
options.then: They freeze, then change into something plain. The light goes out of their face.

options.text: Plan to speak to the staring relatives after the function
options.then: You file it away for later. Your child drifts off to sit alone in a corner.

steps.why: Staying beside them shows they belong, and keeps the day from turning into a lesson.

steps.prompt: Over the meal, an older relative says loudly that your child must learn to behave. What do you do?

options.text: Say firmly that your child is fine as they are
options.then: The relative blinks. The table goes quiet, then someone asks for more rice.

options.text: Laugh it off with "Kids will be kids"
options.then: Some relatives laugh with you. Your child doesn't.

options.text: Whisper to your child to ignore it
options.then: Your child nods stiffly. The relative keeps going for another minute.

options.text: Explain your child's whole situation to the table
options.then: Everyone stares. Your child wants to disappear.

steps.why: A short, firm line shields them without a scene, and without sharing their story.

scenarios.debrief: Protect your child from relatives' pressure to shame them; their safety matters more than peace.
scenarios.relearn: Shield your child from relatives' shaming; don't join in to keep the peace. Home must stay safe.

scenarios.hook: At a family gathering, a neighbour mocks and misgenders your child right in front of you.
scenarios.setup: Your child stands right beside you.

steps.prompt: Mr Kapoor says with a laugh: "So what are we calling your kid this week?"

options.text: "This is my child. Please use their name and pronouns."
options.then: He raises his hands. "Arre, only a joke. Sorry, sorry."

options.text: "Haha, kids these days. Just ignore it, beta."
options.then: He laughs louder. Your child looks down at their shoes.

options.text: "Please don't say that here. Let's talk about it later."
options.then: He shrugs. "Later, sure." Your child still heard every word.

options.text: "You're a bigot, and I won't have you near my child at all."
options.then: His face darkens. "Who's a bigot? It was a joke!" Others turn to stare.

steps.why: A calm, clear correction in front of your child shows them you always have their back.

steps.prompt: Mr Kapoor goes on: "Kids today need thicker skin. We were all teased."

options.text: "Thick skin or not, it hurts them. Please stop."
options.then: He pauses, then mumbles: "Okay, fine. I'll be careful."

options.text: "You're right. I'm sorry. I'm just tired today."
options.then: He nods, smug. Your child looks at you, confused.

options.text: "Fine. Let's drop it and go eat something."
options.then: He shrugs and heads for the buffet, unchanged.

options.text: "People like you are the whole problem in this country."
options.then: The room goes cold. He storms off, and the family whispers about the scene.

steps.why: Saying it hurts, without insults, keeps the message clear and the room calm.

steps.prompt: Your child tugs your sleeve and says quietly: "Can we go home now?"

options.text: "Yes, let's go. Thanks for telling me. You did nothing wrong."
options.then: They squeeze your hand and walk out close beside you.

options.text: "Not yet. If we leave this early, people will start to talk."
options.then: They nod, tense, and hold your sleeve through the whole dinner.

options.text: "Just a bit longer. Try to enjoy yourself, beta."
options.then: They stand stiffly, and they stop asking.

options.text: "Don't let one silly comment ruin the evening."
options.then: They look down. "It's not silly," they murmur.

steps.why: Listening to their wish to leave shows them the comment mattered to you too.

scenarios.relearn: Calmly correcting and standing up for your child models advocacy and shows them you always have their back.

scenarios.hook: Your own beliefs and your child's identity feel like they're in tension.

steps.prompt: Your child asks you to use a new name at home. What do you do?

options.text: Use it, and work on your discomfort elsewhere
options.then: Their face lights up at the sound of it. Your unease is still there.

options.text: Say you need more time before you can use it
options.then: They nod but go quiet for days. Time passes without the name.

options.text: Use it only when nobody else is around
options.then: They notice. "So it's not really okay with you?"

options.text: Ask them to wait until they're a bit older
options.then: They nod slowly. They stop asking, and start hiding it.

steps.why: Using the name today keeps them safe and lets you do your own inner work in parallel.

steps.prompt: An elder you respect says your family's beliefs must come first. What do you do?

options.text: Say your child's safety comes first, politely
options.then: He frowns but lets it rest. Your child, listening, stands taller.

options.text: Say you'll follow his advice this time
options.then: He is pleased. Your child hears from the next room and goes quiet.

options.text: Argue with him about the belief itself
options.then: The debate lasts an hour, with raised voices your child can hear.

options.text: Nod, then quietly do what you think best
options.then: He believes he has persuaded you and returns next week with more advice.

steps.why: You can respect an elder and still hold your child's safety and dignity as fixed.

steps.prompt: The tension keeps you awake that night. Who do you talk to?

options.text: A supportive friend or an affirming counsellor
options.then: You feel lighter afterwards. Your child never has to carry it.

options.text: Your child, so they know how hard this is
options.then: Your child listens with wide eyes, then tries to comfort you.

options.text: A relative who shares your original beliefs
options.then: She agrees and adds her own worries. You feel more certain and more tense.

options.text: Nobody, because it is your own problem to bear
options.then: It leaks out as irritation at breakfast, and your child wonders why.

steps.why: Take your own struggle to a supportive adult so your child is not left to carry it.

steps.prompt: Your child asks for their chosen name to be used at school, and the school calls you in. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes, and ask them to use it from now on
options.then: The teacher smiles. Your child comes home noticeably lighter.

options.text: Ask them to wait until you feel ready
options.then: The school waits. Your child is called by a name that hurts every morning.

options.text: Say to use it only if other children ask
options.then: Your child spends each day waiting to be noticed.

options.text: Leave your child to sort it out with the teacher
options.then: Your child goes in nervous and comes out unsure whether it worked.

steps.why: Saying yes without delay keeps school safe for them while you keep learning.

scenarios.debrief: When beliefs and your child's identity feel in tension, hold their safety as non-negotiable.
scenarios.relearn: Make your child's safety non-negotiable as you work it through.

scenarios.affirm: Processing your own feelings privately, so they don't burden your child, is a real act of parental love.
scenarios.relearn: Doing the work on your own feelings, so they don't land on your child, is an act of love.

scenarios.hook: You're struggling with your child's identity and want to talk to someone supportive, not burden your child.
scenarios.setup: You call an old friend who has always listened.

steps.prompt: Your friend answers: "Hey, it's late. Is everything okay?"

options.text: "I love my child and I'm finding my feet. Can I talk?"
options.then: Her voice softens. "Of course. I'm here. Take your time."

options.text: "I just can't accept this, and I've told my child so."
options.then: Your friend goes quiet. "You told them that? How did they take it?"

options.text: "Everything's fine. I just wanted to hear your voice."
options.then: "At this hour? I know you," she says. "Is it about your child?"

options.text: "Can you talk to my child for me? They'll listen to you."
options.then: "Me? I'd rather not come between the two of you."

steps.why: Asking someone supportive to listen, and being honest about your own feelings, is what lets you process them.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "What frightens you most in all this?"

options.text: "I'm afraid for their future. And a bit ashamed."
options.then: She lets a moment pass. "That makes sense. You're allowed to be afraid."

options.text: "That someone is leading them astray somehow."
options.then: "Who do you mean?" You realise you don't know.

options.text: "I don't know. I just want it all to go away."
options.then: "I hear you. But wanting it gone won't help them," she says gently.

options.text: "I'd rather not say. Just tell me what to do."
options.then: "I can't tell you that. I can only listen," she says.

steps.why: Naming the fear, and the shame around it, is the first step to moving through it.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "What will you do the next time you feel this way?"

options.text: "Call you or a helpline before I speak to my child."
options.then: "Call me any time," she says. You feel a little steadier.

options.text: "Tell my child exactly how I feel. They should know."
options.then: "Maybe," she says carefully. "But they might end up carrying it for you."

options.text: "Keep it to myself. I don't want to bother anyone."
options.then: "You'd never be bothering me," she says. The offer hangs there.

options.text: "Write it all down in a long message to my child."
options.then: "That could hurt them," she says gently. "Maybe write it for yourself."

steps.why: Taking the fear to an adult first keeps your child from carrying it.

scenarios.relearn: Taking your struggle to a supportive adult, not your child, lets you process without making your child carry it.

scenarios.hook: You want help with parenting your child, but worry that reaching out could out them.

steps.prompt: You find a parents' support group online. The sign-up asks for your child's name and details. What do you do?

options.text: Find one that lets you join with just your own details
options.then: You find a group that asks only for your first name and email.

options.text: Fill in your child's full details so you're accepted quickly
options.then: The form is sent. You realise you don't know who reads it.

options.text: Skip support and manage on your own
options.then: The evening passes, and the online threads leave you more anxious.

options.text: Ask a relative to find a group for you
options.then: She finds one, and mentions it to two cousins before you can stop her.

steps.why: Support for you doesn't need your child's details, and their story stays theirs.

steps.prompt: You finally attend a parents' meeting, where someone asks everyone to introduce their children. What do you do?

options.text: Introduce yourself and share only what feels right
options.then: Others nod. Two parents share how they began, and you feel less alone.

options.text: Share your child's name, school and everything else
options.then: Afterwards someone asks which school. You feel a chill.

options.text: Say nothing and slip out quietly
options.then: You walk out with your questions unasked.

options.text: Describe your child's private struggles to get advice
options.then: You get advice, but feel you have said too much about a child who isn't there.

steps.why: You can share your own journey without telling your child's story for them.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting, a parent offers to introduce you to a counsellor she knows. What do you ask?

options.text: Ask how they treat gender-diverse children and privacy
options.then: She says the counsellor sees parents first and keeps notes private.

options.text: Ask if they can start with your child next week
options.then: She says the counsellor prefers to meet parents first. You feel rushed.

options.text: Ask if they can help your child feel more normal soon
options.then: She goes quiet, then says the counsellor doesn't work that way.

options.text: Book straight away, since she recommends them so warmly
options.then: On the first call you realise you don't know their approach.

steps.why: Asking about approach and privacy up front is how you find safe help.

steps.prompt: A relative sees the group's messages on your phone and asks what they are. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's a parents' group, and leave your child out
options.then: She shrugs. "Good, you need support." She doesn't ask more.

options.text: Show her the whole chat so she understands everything
options.then: She reads names and stories that aren't yours, and asks about your child.

options.text: Say it's nothing at all and quickly lock your phone
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. Your reaction makes her more curious.

options.text: Tell her your child's whole story so she can help you
options.then: She takes it all in, and asks what she should tell the others.

steps.why: Sharing that you have support, and not your child's story, protects their privacy.

scenarios.hook: Another parent of a gender-diverse child confides that they are scared and ashamed.
scenarios.setup: You are sitting together after a school event.

steps.prompt: The other parent says in a low voice: "I'm so ashamed. I don't know what to do."

options.text: "You're not alone. Loving your child through this matters most."
options.then: Their eyes fill. "Do you really think so?"

options.text: "Yeah, it's a disaster. I don't know how you'll cope."
options.then: They go pale. "Oh. So it's as bad as I thought."

options.text: "Don't be ashamed! There's nothing to be ashamed of, okay?"
options.then: They nod tightly. They don't feel any lighter.

options.text: "Have you tried asking a pandit or a doctor about it?"
options.then: They blink. "About what? I just wanted someone to hear me."

steps.why: Telling them they are not alone eases the shame before anything else can start.

steps.prompt: They say: "My family thinks it's my fault. Maybe it is."

options.text: "It isn't your fault, or anyone's. Your child is who they are."
options.then: They let out a breath they have been holding for weeks.

options.text: "Families always blame someone. Try not to listen."
options.then: They nod. Their shoulders stay tight.

options.text: "Maybe it's how they were raised. I wonder that too."
options.then: They fall silent. Now the blame has two voices.

options.text: "Don't tell your family anything more about it."
options.then: They nod, but it feels like being told to hide.

steps.why: It is never a parent's fault, and hearing that lifts the shame.

steps.prompt: They ask: "Where do I even start? I don't know anyone."

options.text: "There are groups and helplines. Let's find one together."
options.then: They take out their phone. "Okay. Let's look now."

options.text: "Start by reading everything you can find online."
options.then: They nod, but the first search leaves them more frightened.

options.text: "Ask your relatives. They'll know what to do."
options.then: They wince. "They're the ones I'm scared of."

options.text: "Wait a bit. Things often settle down by themselves."
options.then: They give a weak smile. The knot stays.

steps.why: Naming real support, and offering to look together, turns shame into a next step.

scenarios.relearn: Telling a frightened parent they're not alone and pointing to support, without judgement, helps them be their child's safe place.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: be the safe place, lead with love, protect fiercely, and reach for support. Your child is lucky to have you trying. Ready?
scenarios.affirm: Being the safe place, leading with love, protecting fiercely and reaching for support is how you raise a gender-diverse child well.
