scenarios.hook: Your child Riya has been quiet and watchful around you all week, as if testing something.
scenarios.setup: At bedtime she lingers in the doorway.

steps.prompt: Riya asks: "Would you still love me if I were different?"

options.text: "Nothing you could be would ever make me love you less."
options.then: Riya's eyes shine. "Really? Promise?"

options.text: "Different how? Tell me what you mean first."
options.then: Riya hesitates. "Never mind." She fiddles with her sleeve.

options.text: "I love you. I just hope you'll always be the child I know."
options.then: She nods slowly. "I'll try," she says, in a small voice.

options.text: "Of course I would. But not different in front of others."
options.then: She goes quiet. "Okay," she says, and looks at the floor.

steps.why: A plain, unconditional yes is the safety she's been checking for.

steps.prompt: Riya asks: "What if people say bad things about me? Will you be on my side?"

options.text: "Try not to give them reasons to talk."
options.then: Riya's shoulders tighten. "Okay," she says, and starts watching herself.

options.text: "Always. I'll be on your side, whatever anyone says."
options.then: She leans into you. "Even Dadi?"

options.text: "I'll listen to them as well, and then we'll see."
options.then: "Oh," says Riya. She looks unsure whose side that means.

options.text: "I'm on your side. Just don't make it hard for us."
options.then: She nods. "I won't," she says, and doesn't sound sure.

steps.why: Being plainly on her side, whatever others say, tells her she isn't facing anyone alone.

steps.prompt: Riya asks: "Can I still tell you things, even the scary ones?"

options.text: "Tell me only what won't upset me."
options.then: Riya thinks. "Okay," she says, and keeps the scary one for herself.

options.text: "Tell your aunt instead. She's better at this."
options.then: She looks disappointed. "Okay," she says, and goes to find her phone.

options.text: "Anything. I might not have answers, but I'll always listen."
options.then: Riya smiles. "There's something at school," she says, and begins.

options.text: "Yes, but think carefully before you say them."
options.then: "Okay," she says. She goes to think, and doesn't come back.

steps.why: Saying anything is welcome means she brings you the big things while they're small.

scenarios.relearn: An unconditional 'nothing makes me love you less' gives a child the safety that protects them most.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a parent behaviour shown to protect LGBTQ+ youth, or one shown to harm?

items.text: Supporting their identity openly
Blocking their friends and expression
Advocating when they're mistreated
Frequent criticism of who they are
Using their name and pronouns kindly
Pressuring them to mask who they are

scenarios.relearn: Open support, advocacy and respectful name use protect LGBTQ+ youth; blocking friends, criticism and forced masking harm them.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Isha has cut her hair short, and you feel a disapproval you're tempted to show.

steps.prompt: At dinner she chatters about her day, and your mood sinks. What do you do?

options.text: Go quiet and answer in one word so she gets the message
options.then: Isha's chatter fades. She asks softly if she did something wrong.

options.text: Skip her goodnight hug tonight and say you're tired
options.then: She notices the missing hug and lies awake, wondering why.

options.text: Stay warm, ask about her day and really listen
options.then: Isha talks on, her shoulders easing. The table feels lighter than it has all week.

options.text: Stay warm, but add that you hope this is just a phase
options.then: Isha's smile drops. She hears that your warmth comes with a wait.

steps.why: Steady warmth tells Isha she is loved, and that is what keeps her anchored.

steps.prompt: Later, your husband Sanjay says being warm will only encourage her. What do you say?

options.text: Agree to stay stern for a few weeks, for a united front
options.then: You both turn cool. Isha eats quickly and goes to her room early.

options.text: Say nothing, and be warm only when he isn't around
options.then: Isha learns which parent is safe, and when. Sanjay stays unaware and unmoved.

options.text: Tell him he's being cruel and stop talking to him
options.then: The house goes silent. Sanjay digs in, and Isha hears the fight through the wall.

options.text: Say your warmth keeps her steady, and invite him to learn with you
options.then: Sanjay frowns but takes the article you send. "I'll read it," he says.

steps.why: Sharing why warmth protects her, and inviting him to learn, keeps Isha safe and Sanjay on board.

steps.prompt: On Sunday, Isha wants to shop for clothes with you and has picked the boys' section. What do you do?

options.text: Go with her, help her choose what she likes and enjoy the trip
options.then: Isha models a shirt for you and laughs. It's the best afternoon you've had in weeks.

options.text: Go, but steer her toward the girls' section
options.then: She tries a few things politely. She stops asking your opinion after that.

options.text: Say you'll take her only if she picks something more suitable
options.then: Isha says she is still herself and stays home. The shopping trip never happens.

options.text: Say you're busy and hand her money to go with a friend
options.then: She goes, but the friend's mother ends up helping her choose. You hear about it later.

steps.why: Enjoying her day her way keeps your warmth steady, and that steadiness is her lifeline.

scenarios.debrief: Keep your warmth flowing even while you process; acceptance is your child's lifeline, not a reward.
scenarios.relearn: Don't withdraw warmth to show disapproval; that acceptance is your child's lifeline.

scenarios.hook: Match each fear to the protective fact that answers it.

pairs.right: Your support is what makes it easier
Rejection loses children; love keeps them
You can shield your child from them
A loving beginner is exactly enough

scenarios.relearn: Each parental fear has a protective fact: acceptance protects, your support eases their path, and love keeps your child close.

scenarios.hook: Your younger child has been watching their older sibling closely lately.
scenarios.setup: At bedtime, they turn to you with a question.

steps.prompt: Your younger child asks: "Why is my sibling not like the other kids?"

options.text: "Everyone is different. We love your sibling just as they are."
options.then: They think about it. "Okay. Can I still play with them?"

options.text: "Don't ask about that. It isn't normal, so leave it alone."
options.then: Their face falls. "Sorry." Now they stare at their sibling at dinner.

options.text: "Nothing is wrong, but don't ever bring it up with them."
options.then: "Okay." They nod, and now it feels like a secret.

options.text: "That's a question for Papa. Go and ask him about it."
options.then: They wander off. Papa looks up, confused. "Ask me what?"

steps.why: A simple, warm answer teaches acceptance, and leaves no room for shame.

steps.prompt: A day later, they say: "Kids at school called my sibling weird. Should I tell them to stop?"

options.text: "Say stop, and tell me. I'll talk to your teacher."
options.then: They look relieved. "So I don't have to fix it by myself?"

options.text: "Just ignore them. They'll get bored and stop soon enough."
options.then: "Okay." They shrug, but they look worried.

options.text: "Hit them back if they keep on after you've told them to stop."
options.then: Their eyes go wide. "Really? I'll get in trouble!"

options.text: "Say nothing, beta. It's better not to talk about it at all."
options.then: They nod slowly. Now they feel they must hide something.

steps.why: Speaking up helps, and a grown-up stepping in is what stops the bullying.

steps.prompt: They ask: "Can I tell my friends about my sibling?"

options.text: "That story is theirs. Ask what they're okay with."
options.then: "Okay!" They run to ask. Their sibling smiles. "Thanks for asking me."

options.text: "Yes, tell everyone you like. There's nothing to hide."
options.then: They tell the class the next day. Their sibling hears about it at school.

options.text: "No. Never mention your sibling to anyone at all."
options.then: They nod. It now feels like a shameful secret.

options.text: "Do what you like. It's your family too, after all."
options.then: They tell two friends. Their sibling finds out from someone else.

steps.why: A sibling's story is theirs to share, and asking first shows respect.

scenarios.relearn: A simple 'people come in lots of kinds, and we love them' teaches a sibling acceptance instead of shame.

scenarios.hook: Sort: an accurate statement, or a harmful myth, about gender-diverse kids?

items.text: A child can know their own gender
It can be 'caught' from friends
Expression and identity can differ
It's caused by too much screen time
It's simply part of who they are
Strict parenting could have prevented it

scenarios.relearn: Knowing one's gender, expression differing from identity, and 'simply who they are' are accurate; 'caught', 'screen time' and 'strict parenting' are myths.

scenarios.hook: You catch yourself reacting from an old myth you grew up believing.

steps.prompt: Your son asks for a doll, and you hear your mother's voice: "That makes boys weak." What do you do?

options.text: Pause, and ask him what he loves about it
options.then: He describes the doll's story with shining eyes. The old voice in your head goes quiet.

options.text: Say no and offer a cricket bat instead
options.then: He takes the bat politely. The doll is never mentioned again, but he glances at the shop.

options.text: Buy it, but tell him to keep it at home
options.then: He hugs the doll, then hides it under his bed. He has learned it is a secret.

options.text: Laugh it off and change the subject
options.then: He laughs along, unsure. The question is still sitting there.

steps.why: Curiosity about what he loves puts what is in front of you ahead of the old belief.

steps.prompt: At a family lunch, your sister repeats the old saying about boys and 'soft' toys. What do you say?

options.text: Say toys don't decide who a child becomes
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Hm. Never heard that." The table moves on.

options.text: Laugh and say you're just humouring him for now
options.then: Everyone relaxes. Your son, listening, hears himself called a joke.

options.text: Agree, and say you'll watch it very closely
options.then: She nods, satisfied. Your son picks at his food.

options.text: Stay silent and let her finish her point
options.then: She keeps going and others join in. Nobody speaks up for him.

steps.why: A simple fact answers the old saying without starting a fight.

steps.prompt: That night the old belief pulls at you again. What do you do?

options.text: Write the belief down with one fact that answers it
options.then: On paper, the belief looks smaller. You sleep a little easier.

options.text: Read forums until you find one that agrees with your fear
options.then: You find plenty. You go to bed more anxious than before.

options.text: Decide to watch him for signs before deciding anything
options.then: Watching him closely, you tense whenever he plays. He notices.

options.text: Push it away and hope it fades for good
options.then: It fades for an hour. The next comment brings it back.

steps.why: Naming the belief and pairing it with a fact loosens its grip on how you parent.

scenarios.debrief: When an old myth drives your reaction, update it with accurate information rather than acting on the fear.
scenarios.relearn: Replace inherited myths with facts; acting on a familiar myth just harms your child.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two harmful frames a parent might fall into.

scene.text: 'My child is showing me who they are'
'My child is sick and needs curing'
'My job is to understand and support'
'I have to fix this before anyone sees'
'I can learn as we go'

scenarios.why: 'Sick and needs curing' and 'fix this before anyone sees' are harmful frames; the accurate one is showing-and-supporting.
scenarios.relearn: The accurate frame is 'my child is showing me who they are, and my job is to support', not 'curing' or 'fixing' them.

scenarios.hook: Your son Neil came out days ago, and he is watching how you treat him.
scenarios.setup: He hovers in the kitchen doorway after school.

steps.prompt: Neil asks: "Are you still thinking about what I told you?"

options.text: "Yes. I'm proud you trusted me, and I'm here."
options.then: Neil smiles shyly. "Really? Proud?"

options.text: "Let's just not bring it up again, okay? It's easier."
options.then: Neil nods. He looks down at his shoes.

options.text: "Yes. It's a lot. Give me a bit more time."
options.then: Neil nods. "Okay," he says quietly. He starts to shrink.

options.text: "Not really. I've been busy with work all week."
options.then: Neil says "oh" and goes to his room.

steps.why: Telling him you're proud and present is the signal that says home is safe.

steps.prompt: The next evening, Neil says: "Some people at school have started guessing. I'm scared."

options.text: "Then ignore them and stay out of trouble at school."
options.then: Neil's shoulders sag. "That's not how it works."

options.text: "Scary, yes. Tell me more, and we'll decide together."
options.then: Neil sits down and tells you. You listen until he's done.

options.text: "Maybe you could act a bit less obvious for a while."
options.then: Neil stares. "You want me to hide?"

options.text: "I'll call the school tomorrow morning and sort it all out."
options.then: Neil looks alarmed. "Please don't. Not without asking me."

steps.why: Listening and deciding together keeps him in charge of his own story while you stand beside him.

steps.prompt: Neil asks: "Can you come to my school event on Saturday? Just you."

options.text: "I'll try, but I can't promise. Work is busy."
options.then: Neil nods, small. "Okay." He doesn't ask again.

options.text: "I'll come, but I'd rather sit at the back."
options.then: Neil's smile dims. "Okay," he says. "That's fine."

options.text: "Of course I'll come. I wouldn't miss it."
options.then: Neil grins. "Thanks. I'll save you a seat."

options.text: "Ask your father to go with you instead."
options.then: Neil looks stung. "I asked you."

steps.why: Showing up for him, in public, says you are with him and proud of him.

scenarios.relearn: Following up with pride and presence, rather than silence, tells a child the door is genuinely open and safe.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Kavya has come out to you, and you have many questions but fear saying the wrong thing.

steps.prompt: You're alone with her in the car. What do you do?

options.text: Fire off every question you've been saving up
options.then: Kavya answers two, then stares out the window and goes silent.

options.text: Ask if she's okay with a few questions, and say she can pass
options.then: Kavya thinks. "Sure. Ask, and I'll tell you if I don't want to answer."

options.text: Avoid it completely so you don't say something wrong
options.then: The silence stretches. Kavya wonders if you don't want to know her.

options.text: Ask only what the relatives will say and how to handle them
options.then: Kavya answers flatly. She doesn't say what she's feeling.

steps.why: Asking permission, at her pace, shows respect and lets you be imperfect.

steps.prompt: The next day, Kavya starts telling you more, then stops mid-sentence. What do you do?

options.text: Ask your next question anyway, since she brought it up
options.then: Kavya sighs and answers in one word. The openness fades.

options.text: Ask why she stopped and what she's hiding
options.then: She flinches. "I'm not hiding anything," she says.

options.text: Say 'That's enough for today. Thank you for telling me'
options.then: Kavya smiles, tired. "Thanks, Papa. We can do more later."

options.text: Say you'll pick it up again at dinner tonight
options.then: Kavya nods, but tenses as the evening approaches.

steps.why: Stopping when she stops shows her the pace is really hers.

steps.prompt: The next evening you think of a question you fear might sound clumsy. What do you do?

options.text: Ask it in the sharpest way, to get a straight answer
options.then: Kavya recoils at the tone, and gives the shortest answer she can.

options.text: Guess the answer from something online and never ask her
options.then: Kavya notices the questions have stopped and feels left out of her own story.

options.text: Never ask it, because it might upset her
options.then: The question stays in your head. Kavya can tell something is unsaid.

options.text: Ask it anyway and say 'Tell me if I word this badly'
options.then: Kavya laughs softly. "That was a bit off, but I get it," she says, and answers.

steps.why: Asking honestly, and admitting you might slip, is better than guessing or going silent.

steps.prompt: Kavya says she doesn't have answers to some of your questions yet. What do you do?

options.text: Say that's fine, and you can both keep learning
options.then: Kavya looks relieved. "I like that," she says. "Me too."

options.text: Press her with 'You must know by now'
options.then: Kavya's jaw tightens. "I don't. That's the point," she says.

options.text: Tell her to come back when she has answers
options.then: She nods, hurt. She takes her plate to her room.

options.text: Suggest an online quiz to help her work it out
options.then: She rolls her eyes. "A quiz can't decide that for me," she says.

steps.why: Not knowing yet is fine, and learning side by side is something you can offer.

scenarios.debrief: Ask gentle questions led by your child's comfort; you can be learning, not interrogating or avoiding.
scenarios.relearn: Ask gently and follow your child's comfort; you needn't get every word perfect.

scenarios.hook: Sort each line a parent might say: it affirms a coming-out, or it wounds?

items.text: 'Thank you for telling me'
'You're too young to know'
'I love you, tell me more'
'Don't tell anyone, it's shameful'
'I'm so glad you trusted me'
'What will the relatives think?'

scenarios.relearn: 'Thank you', 'tell me more' and 'I'm glad you trusted me' affirm; 'too young', 'shameful' and 'the relatives' wound.

scenarios.hook: Match each thing a child needs after coming out to how you give it.

pairs.right: Keep their confidence, don't out them

scenarios.relearn: After coming out a child needs to feel loved, safe, led, believed and sure the door stays open.

scenarios.hook: Your child has been quiet for days, and finds you alone in the kitchen.
scenarios.setup: Your child hovers by the counter, twisting a tea towel.

steps.prompt: Your child says: "Can you call me Kabir now, and say 'he'? It matters a lot."

options.text: "Of course, Kabir. I'll get it right. Remind me if I slip."
options.then: He stares at you. "Just like that? Thank you."

options.text: "That's too confusing. I'll call you what I always have."
options.then: His face falls. "Please, Ma. Will you at least think about it?"

options.text: "Let's wait until you're older before we decide anything."
options.then: "I'm not deciding," he says. "I'm asking."

options.text: "Fine, but only at home. Not in front of the relatives."
options.then: He nods, but the light in his face dims.

steps.why: Saying yes warmly, slips and all, tells him he is safe and seen.

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "Dadi comes on Sunday. I'm scared she'll find out."

options.text: "That's for you to decide. What would you like me to say?"
options.then: He thinks. "Use Kabir. I'll tell her the rest when I'm ready."

options.text: "I'll explain it to her for you. She'll surely understand."
options.then: "Please don't," he says quickly. "It's mine to tell."

options.text: "Let's not bring it up with her at all."
options.then: He looks relieved, then uneasy, as if it were something to hide.

options.text: "I'll use the old name when she's here, to be safe."
options.then: "Even in my own house?" His voice wobbles.

steps.why: It is his story to share, so let him decide who is told and when.

steps.prompt: At dinner you call him by the old name. Kabir says softly: "It's Kabir, Ma."

options.text: "Sorry, Kabir. I'm still learning. Thanks for telling me."
options.then: He smiles a little. "It's okay. You're trying."

options.text: "Ugh, sorry. It's just so hard for me to remember."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay," he says, and starts reassuring you instead.

options.text: "It was your name for years. Please give me some time."
options.then: He looks down. "How much time?"

options.text: "You know I didn't mean it. Don't make a fuss."
options.then: He pushes his rice around. He doesn't remind you again.

steps.why: A quick sorry and a thank-you repairs it without making him manage your guilt.

scenarios.relearn: Agreeing warmly to a child's name and pronouns, slips and all, is a powerful, daily act of affirmation.

scenarios.hook: A relative keeps telling your child to act like other kids "or else" there will be trouble.

steps.prompt: Your child repeats what the relative said, and looks scared. What do you do?

options.text: Tell them they don't have to change, and you'll handle it
options.then: Their shoulders loosen. "You're not angry with me?" they ask.

options.text: Tell them to just do as the relative says for now
options.then: They comply stiffly. At the next visit they stare at the floor.

options.text: Tell them the relative means well, so be patient
options.then: Your child nods, unconvinced, and starts dreading the next visit.

options.text: Call the relative tonight and end the conversation angrily
options.then: The relative shouts and the family group buzzes. Your child worries they caused it.

steps.why: Your child first needs to hear they don't have to change, and that you are with them.

steps.prompt: At the next festival, the relative says in front of you: "A little discipline and this will stop." What do you do?

options.text: Say calmly that your child is not a problem to fix
options.then: The relative frowns but stops. Your child's eyes find yours.

options.text: Say nothing to avoid a scene at the festival
options.then: The relative takes it as agreement. Your child watches you say nothing.

options.text: Say "We'll see" to keep things polite
options.then: The relative smiles, sure they have won. Your child's face falls.

options.text: Argue with the relative until the whole room is watching
options.then: Voices rise and the festival stalls. Your child slips out of the room.

steps.why: A calm, clear line in front of your child shows them you are on their side.

steps.prompt: Later, the relative corners your child alone and says to "act right". Your child comes to you shaken. What do you do?

options.text: Thank them, and say they won't be alone with that relative again
options.then: Their breathing slows. They lean against you and stay there.

options.text: Ask what they did to upset the relative first
options.then: They shrink. "Nothing," they say, and wish they hadn't spoken.

options.text: Tell them to keep out of that relative's way themselves
options.then: They nod. Staying safe is now their job, and they watch every door.

options.text: Tell them relatives don't mean it and to forget it
options.then: They nod, but they stop bringing anything to you after that.

steps.why: Thanking them, and keeping them away from that relative, keeps them safe and talking to you.

steps.prompt: The relative tells the family your child is "being difficult", and an aunt asks you to apologise. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, and say your child has done nothing wrong
options.then: The aunt purses her lips. Your child, listening from the door, stands taller.

options.text: Apologise for your child to end it quickly
options.then: The aunt smiles, satisfied. Your child, overhearing, feels like the problem.

options.text: Ask your child to say sorry so it ends
options.then: Your child says sorry with wet eyes. The relative nods, satisfied.

options.text: Agree to have a serious talk with your child later
options.then: The aunt is pleased. Your child spends the night dreading that talk.

steps.why: Your child has done nothing wrong, and should never apologise for who they are.

scenarios.debrief: Be the advocate who stands between your child and those pressuring them to conform.
scenarios.relearn: Protect your child from pressure to conform; don't side with the adult against them.

scenarios.hook: Sort: affirms and protects your child, or exposes them to harm?

items.text: Backing them up publicly
Mocking their expression at home
Keeping home a safe space
Letting others shame them unchecked
Welcoming their friends in
Telling them to 'toughen up' alone

scenarios.relearn: Backing them publicly, a safe home and welcoming friends protect; mocking, letting others shame them or 'toughen up' alone expose them to harm.

scenarios.hook: Match each pressure on your child to the protective response.

pairs.right: Advocate with the school, support at home
Shield your child, hold your line
Affirm that they can be themselves with you
Step between and end it kindly

pairs.left: A coach hinting at benching them
pairs.right: Ask to keep them included as they are

scenarios.relearn: Bullying, disapproval, masking pressure, a prying stranger and a benching coach each have a protective response.

scenarios.hook: You slipped and said something hurtful to your child out of your own fear.
scenarios.setup: You knock on your child's door that evening.

steps.prompt: Your child says without turning round: "What do you want?"

options.text: "That came from my fear, not the truth. I'm sorry."
options.then: They turn slowly. "It felt true." But they are listening.

options.text: "Nothing. I just wanted to check that you had eaten."
options.then: "I ate," they say. The door stays closed on the real thing.

options.text: "You'll understand when you're older why I said it."
options.then: They turn away. "That's what you always say."

options.text: "I was only saying what everyone else thinks."
options.then: They go still. "So everyone thinks that about me."

steps.why: Owning that it was your fear, not their fault, starts the repair.

steps.prompt: Your child says: "It hurt. I thought you were the one person who got me."

options.text: "I know. I love you, and I'm learning. I'll do better."
options.then: They turn to look at you. "Okay. I'd like that."

options.text: "Don't be so sensitive. It was only words."
options.then: Their eyes narrow. "Right. Only words."

options.text: "I was scared when I said it, so it's partly on you too."
options.then: They stare. "My fault, for being scary."

options.text: "Please don't tell the others what I said."
options.then: "I won't," they say slowly. Now they are holding your secret.

steps.why: Acknowledging the hurt and promising to learn tells them you take it seriously.

steps.prompt: Your child asks: "Do you still think that about me?"

options.text: "No. Nothing is wrong with you. I'm still learning."
options.then: Their shoulders drop a little. "Okay."

options.text: "I don't know yet. I'm still working it all out."
options.then: They nod slowly, but their face closes.

options.text: "Of course not. Let's not bring it up ever again."
options.then: They nod, but the question doesn't go away.

options.text: "Not the way I said it. It's complicated, really."
options.then: They wait for more. Nothing comes.

steps.why: Telling them plainly there is nothing wrong with them is what they most need to hear.

steps.prompt: Your child says: "What if you say something like that again?"

options.text: "Then I'll stop, say sorry and try again."
options.then: A small smile. "Deal." They lean their head against your arm.

options.text: "I won't. I promise I will never do it again."
options.then: They nod, but their eyes say they will believe it when they see it.

options.text: "Then just let it go, the way you did today."
options.then: They nod. Letting go of hurt has become their job.

options.text: "Then tell your aunt, and she'll handle it."
options.then: They nod. Their hurt now has to travel through someone else.

steps.why: Promising to repair, not to be perfect, is honest and gives them a way to speak up.

scenarios.relearn: Owning that a hurtful comment came from your fear, not the truth, repairs it and models growth for your child.

scenarios.hook: Your discomfort is tempting you to delay supporting your child 'until you're ready'.

steps.prompt: Your child asks you to meet a supportive counsellor with them. What do you do?

options.text: Go with them this week
options.then: The counsellor is kind to you both. You leave with your child's hand in yours.

options.text: Say you'll go once you feel ready
options.then: Your child nods. The appointment passes without you, and they go alone.

options.text: Suggest they go alone the first time
options.then: They go alone. They come back calm but wishing you had been there.

options.text: Say you'll read up first and decide later
options.then: You read for weeks. Your child keeps waiting for a yes.

steps.why: Showing up now tells your child they are not alone, even if you feel unsure.

steps.prompt: A week later your child uses their new name at dinner. What do you do?

options.text: Use it too, even if it still feels odd
options.then: They glow. Your voice wobbles on the second try, and they smile anyway.

options.text: Wait until it feels natural before using it
options.then: They wait too. The name hangs in the air at every meal.

options.text: Use it only when they are in the room
options.then: They notice. "Why not when I am not there?"

options.text: Say you will try it from next month
options.then: They nod and try to be patient. A month feels a long way off.

steps.why: Small, awkward steps now matter more than a perfect start later.

steps.prompt: Your child says quietly that they will wait until you are comfortable. What do you say?

options.text: Say they should not have to wait, and you are with them now
options.then: They exhale for the first time in weeks. "Okay."

options.text: Thank them for being so patient
options.then: They shrug. Patience is not what they were hoping for.

options.text: Say you appreciate it and will tell them when you are ready
options.then: They nod. Without a date, waiting has no end.

options.text: Say you are nearly there and to give it a little time
options.then: They smile politely. They stop asking for things.

steps.why: Your child should never have to wait for your comfort. Support them now and grow alongside.

scenarios.debrief: Support your child now and work on your own comfort in parallel; safety can't wait.
scenarios.relearn: Don't make your child wait for your comfort; support them now and keep growing alongside.

scenarios.hook: Sort: moves your own journey forward kindly, or stalls it?

items.text: Self-compassion for where you start
Drowning in guilt and freezing
Small, steady learning
Demanding instant perfection of yourself
Talking it through with a supportive adult
Comparing yourself harshly to other parents

scenarios.relearn: Self-compassion, steady learning and support move you forward; guilt-freezing, perfectionism and harsh comparison stall you.

scenarios.hook: Match each parent feeling to a healthy way through it.

pairs.right: Learn how support changes the odds
Feel it privately, embrace the real child
Own it, repair, and reaffirm love

scenarios.hook: Your co-parent is struggling to accept your child, and you want to bring them along gently.
scenarios.setup: Your co-parent sits on the edge of the bed, arms crossed.

steps.prompt: Your co-parent says: "I just can't see it your way. It's all too fast."

options.text: "This is hard. Our child needs us. Let's learn together."
options.then: Their arms uncross a little. "Learn how? I don't know where to start."

options.text: "You're a bigot, and you are ruining our child."
options.then: Their face hardens. "Then I have nothing more to say."

options.text: "Fine. I'll handle all of this on my own, then."
options.then: They shrug and leave the room. A door closes down the hall.

options.text: "It isn't fast. You just refused to see it earlier."
options.then: They flinch. "That isn't fair."

steps.why: Naming their difficulty and inviting them to learn keeps you on the same team.

steps.prompt: Later that night, your co-parent says: "What if we're wrong and this hurts them later?"

options.text: "Acceptance protects them. Let's read the evidence together."
options.then: They pause. "Show me. I'll read it."

options.text: "We can't be wrong. I know our child better than anyone."
options.then: They frown. "You can't be sure of that."

options.text: "Then let's ask the relatives what they think of it."
options.then: They agree quickly, and the relatives' opinions are not kind.

options.text: "Then we'll decide later. There's no need to hurry."
options.then: They relax. Meanwhile your child waits for both of you.

steps.why: Offering evidence to read together answers the fear with facts, not pressure.

steps.prompt: Your co-parent says: "I keep saying the wrong thing. I don't know how to fix it."

options.text: "Name it, say sorry and try again. Effort is enough."
options.then: They exhale. "Effort. I can do effort."

options.text: "Then say less, and let me do most of the talking."
options.then: They nod, relieved. Your child gets one parent's warmth and the other's silence.

options.text: "Stay out of their way until you've got it right."
options.then: They agree. Your child sees a parent who keeps a distance.

options.text: "Don't worry. Children forgive nearly everything."
options.then: They sigh. "I hope so." Nothing about the plan changes.

steps.why: Effort and repair matter more than perfect words, and they can start today.

steps.prompt: Your co-parent says: "Maybe we could go to a parents' group together. Not yet, though."

options.text: "Thank you. Let's pick a date when you're ready."
options.then: They nod slowly. "Okay. Soon, but let me choose the week."

options.text: "I'll go alone first and tell you everything."
options.then: They nod. Your co-parent hears about it second-hand.

options.text: "Let's go tomorrow. I'll pick the group."
options.then: They stiffen. "I said not yet."

options.text: "Forget it. You're never going to change."
options.then: They go silent, and the offer disappears.

steps.why: Following their pace, and choosing together, keeps them moving toward acceptance.

scenarios.relearn: Inviting a struggling co-parent to learn and support together moves them toward acceptance better than condemnation.

scenarios.hook: You want to find help but don't know where to start.
scenarios.setup: You have the number in front of you.

steps.prompt: A calm voice answers your call: "Hello. How can I help you today?"

options.text: "I'm a parent of a gender-diverse child. I want to support them well."
options.then: "Thank you for calling," the voice says. "Let's talk about that."

options.text: "Hi, can you tell me how to change my child back to normal?"
options.then: "I can't help with that," the voice says gently. "But I'm happy to talk."

options.text: "Sorry, I think I have the wrong number."
options.then: "That's all right," the voice says. "Are you sure?" You hesitate, and stay on the line.

options.text: "It's for a friend of mine. Can I ask on their behalf?"
options.then: "Of course," the voice says. "But I can help you directly too."

steps.why: A plain statement that you want to support your child opens the right kind of help.

steps.prompt: The voice asks: "What would you like to know first?"

options.text: "How do I show my child I accept them while I'm learning?"
options.then: "Just by saying so," the voice says. "Let's start there."

options.text: "Tell me how to make this stop."
options.then: The voice pauses. "Stop what? Let's talk about how you are feeling."

options.text: "Should I tell the relatives first, so it's out in the open?"
options.then: The voice pauses. "That is your child's story. Let's start with your child."

options.text: "Can you speak to my child and set them straight?"
options.then: "I'd rather help you support them," the voice says. "May I explain?"

steps.why: Asking how to show acceptance puts your child's need first, which is the right start.

steps.prompt: The voice offers: "Would you like the number of a parents' support group?"

options.text: "Yes please. Can I join without giving my child's details?"
options.then: "Yes. You share only what you choose," the voice says.

options.text: "Maybe later. I don't want to commit to anything."
options.then: "That's okay," the voice says. The number stays unwritten.

options.text: "Only if it's a group that helps me change things."
options.then: The voice says the group doesn't try to change children. You go quiet.

options.text: "Yes. I'll bring my whole family to the first meeting."
options.then: The voice says a first meeting may be easier alone. You hesitate.

steps.why: Asking to join on your own terms gets you support and keeps your child's story theirs.

scenarios.relearn: A simple 'I want to support them well' opens the right, affirming kind of help for you and your child.

scenarios.hook: A relative pushes you toward a "cure" or conversion practice for your child.

steps.prompt: Your aunt hands you a number for a "specialist" who can set your child right. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her, decline, and say you are finding affirming support
options.then: She looks disappointed, but pockets the slip of paper.

options.text: Call the number just to hear what they offer
options.then: The voice on the phone is confident and promises results in three months.

options.text: Say you'll think about it, to end the conversation
options.then: She nods, pleased, and asks a week later if you've called.

options.text: Tear up the number and tell her she is harming the family
options.then: She storms out. The family group fills with messages about you.

steps.why: A polite, clear no with a better plan closes the door without a fight.

steps.prompt: A week later, your aunt says the specialist has one slot left, and calls you selfish. What do you do?

options.text: Repeat calmly that you won't, and thank her for caring
options.then: She sighs. "You'll regret it," she says, but stops pressing.

options.text: Agree to visit the place once, just to keep the peace
options.then: She books it. You lie awake, wondering what you have promised.

options.text: Ask your spouse to deal with her, since you're tired
options.then: Your spouse agrees, but hesitates. It falls to you again next week.

options.text: Argue about the science until she finally gives in
options.then: An hour later she is angrier, and your child has heard the raised voices.

steps.why: Calm repetition is enough. You don't have to win the argument.

steps.prompt: Your child has overheard talk of the "specialist", and asks if something is wrong with them. What do you say?

options.text: Say nothing is wrong with them, and you'll keep them safe
options.then: They study your face, and believe you. "Thank you," they say softly.

options.text: Say it's just grown-up talk, nothing to worry about
options.then: They nod, but can tell it was about them.

options.text: Say your aunt only wants what's best for them
options.then: They wonder what the aunt thinks is best. They look worried.

options.text: Say you'll decide what's best and they needn't worry
options.then: They shrug, unconvinced, and start listening at doors.

steps.why: They need to hear directly that nothing is wrong with them, and that you will protect them.

steps.prompt: Your mother asks what you actually plan to do for your child. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're learning about affirming support
options.then: She listens. "Tell me if I can help," she says slowly.

options.text: Say you're waiting to see if it passes
options.then: She nods, relieved. Your child is now on a timer.

options.text: Say you'll try a gentler version of the cure
options.then: She relaxes. You wonder what "gentler" is supposed to mean.

options.text: Say it's none of her business
options.then: She goes quiet, hurt. The door to future help closes a little.

steps.why: Naming affirming support as your plan gives the family a way to help, not to change your child.

scenarios.hook: Your son Ayaan has just shared something about himself, and you don't fully understand it yet.

steps.prompt: He's watching your face and waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him you need to understand it all before you can respond
options.then: He nods and goes to his room, unsure whether he did something wrong.

options.text: Say 'Thanks for telling me. I'll read up and tell you how I feel'
options.then: He thanks you, then spends the evening wondering what your answer will be.

options.text: Hug him and say 'I love you. We'll figure it out together'
options.then: Ayaan's shoulders drop and he holds on tight. "Okay," he whispers.

options.text: Ask him to explain it again and again until it makes sense
options.then: Ayaan stumbles over the words each time and starts to look ashamed.

steps.why: Love now tells him home is safe. Understanding can grow later.

steps.prompt: Later that evening, Ayaan asks quietly if you've thought about it yet. What do you say?

options.text: Say you've read a lot and it's still hard for you to take in
options.then: He nods politely. You can see him deciding not to ask again soon.

options.text: Say you need more time before you can talk about it
options.then: Ayaan says fine and goes quiet. The evening ends with nothing settled.

options.text: Say you haven't thought about it and change the subject
options.then: He watches you talk about dinner, and doesn't mention it again tonight.

options.text: Say 'I love you just the same. I'm still learning'
options.then: Ayaan lets out a breath. "Okay. Me too," he says, and stays a while.

steps.why: You can say you're still learning and still love him. Both are true at once.

steps.prompt: A few weeks on, Ayaan asks you to watch a video with him that explains what he told you. What do you do?

options.text: Watch it with him and ask questions
options.then: Ayaan pauses the video to explain a part. You realise he's been ready to teach you.

options.text: Say you'd rather watch it alone later
options.then: Ayaan says okay, and you both know he won't ask again.

options.text: Say you don't need a video to understand your own son
options.then: He shrugs and puts his phone away, and the door closes a little.

options.text: Watch it with him, but keep scrolling your phone
options.then: Ayaan notices the scrolling and trims his explanations to one line.

steps.why: Learning beside him shows love now, while your understanding catches up.

scenarios.debrief: Lead with love first; understanding can grow later, without leaving your child alone.
scenarios.relearn: Lead with love before you understand; protecting your child today doesn't wait.

options.then: He answers in short words. The real reason stays hidden.

steps.why: Asking what is hard, warmly, helps his marks and his trust. Taking things away only adds a hurt.

scenarios.debrief: Keep warmth flowing as you work through feelings; acceptance is a lifeline, never leverage.
scenarios.relearn: Don't withdraw warmth to show disapproval; your acceptance is your child's lifeline.

scenarios.hook: At a family lunch, your uncle Mohan mocks your son Yash's clothes in front of everyone.

steps.prompt: Some cousins laugh and Yash goes red. What do you do?

options.text: Say calmly 'We don't talk about my child like that'
options.then: The table goes quiet. Mohan mutters, and Yash looks at you with relief.

options.text: Stay quiet to keep the peace with all the relatives at the table
options.then: The teasing carries on. Yash stares at his plate and stops eating.

options.text: Laugh along a little so that it sounds like a harmless joke
options.then: The cousins laugh louder. Yash looks at you as if you've switched sides.

options.text: Whisper to Yash to ignore it and keep eating
options.then: Yash nods stiffly. Mohan carries on, and Yash pushes his food around.

steps.why: A calm, clear line in public shows Yash he isn't on his own.

steps.prompt: After lunch, Mohan says it was only a joke, but Yash should dress like a boy. What do you say?

options.text: Apologise, and say Yash will dress normally next time
options.then: Mohan looks satisfied. Yash overhears and quietly folds his kurta away.

options.text: Say it wasn't a joke to Yash, and you won't allow it again
options.then: Mohan huffs and walks off. Yash sees from the doorway that you held your ground.

options.text: Shout at him in front of the whole family
options.then: Aunts rush in and the room erupts. Yash slips outside, wishing it would stop.

options.text: Say 'Let's not fight today' and walk away
options.then: Mohan takes it as a win. Yash wonders whether you'll say anything next time.

steps.why: Saying plainly that it isn't okay, without a scene, keeps the boundary and the calm.

steps.prompt: A week later, Mohan invites everyone to a festival and hints that Yash should dress properly. What do you do?

options.text: Ask Yash to dress plainly for just one day, to keep the peace
options.then: Yash does, and spends the festival tugging at his collar.

options.text: Go without Yash and say he isn't feeling well today
options.then: Yash stays home alone and knows exactly why. He scrolls through the photos later.

options.text: Say Yash is welcome as he is, and ask him if he wants to go
options.then: Yash thinks, then says yes if you sit next to him. Mohan says nothing more.

options.text: Accept for the family and hope Mohan behaves himself this time
options.then: At the festival, Mohan makes another remark. You're caught unprepared, and Yash notices.

steps.why: Welcoming Yash as he is, and asking what he wants, keeps him at the centre of the plan.

scenarios.debrief: Shield your child from a relative's shaming; their safety matters more than a fragile peace.
scenarios.relearn: Stand beside your child against a relative's shaming; don't allow it to 'keep the peace'.

scenarios.hook: You reacted badly when your daughter Anika opened up, and you can see it hurt her.

steps.prompt: That night she's quiet and avoids your eyes at dinner. What do you do?

options.text: Act as if nothing happened and pass her the rice
options.then: Anika takes the rice without looking up. The hurt stays where it was.

options.text: Go to her room and say 'I'm sorry. I love you. Tell me more'
options.then: Anika stays guarded, but she lets you sit on her bed. It's a start.

options.text: Wait for her to bring it up first
options.then: She waits too. The evening passes with both of you listening for the other.

options.text: Explain why you reacted that way and why it's understandable
options.then: Anika hears a long reason and no sorry. She says okay and turns to the wall.

steps.why: A plain sorry and an open door repair more than any explanation.

steps.prompt: At bedtime a few days later, Anika asks if you're still upset about what she told you. What do you say?

options.text: Say you were never upset, only very tired that day
options.then: Anika looks at you, unsure. She doesn't believe it, and doesn't say so.

options.text: Say she took you by surprise, and leave it there
options.then: She accepts it, but her eyes say she's still waiting for more.

options.text: Say it was your shock and fear, not anything in her
options.then: Anika nods slowly. "Okay," she says, and lets out a breath.

options.text: Say she should have picked a better moment to tell you
options.then: Anika pulls her blanket up. She decides to keep her next news to herself.

steps.why: Owning your shock as yours tells her the reaction was about you, not about her.

steps.prompt: A month on, Anika starts to tell you something about her day and stops, unsure. What do you do?

options.text: Say 'Hmm' and keep cooking
options.then: Anika waits a moment, then shrugs and says it's nothing.

options.text: Sigh and ask if it's about that thing again
options.then: Anika's face closes. "No," she says, and leaves the room.

options.text: Suggest she tell her father, since he's better at this
options.then: She looks confused. It's not what she wanted, and she says thanks and goes.

options.text: Put down what you're doing and say 'I'm listening. Take your time'
options.then: Anika tells you the whole story. Halfway through, she's laughing.

steps.why: Giving her your full attention shows repair is real, and keeps the door open for next time.

scenarios.debrief: A bad moment can always be repaired; go back, apologise, and reaffirm your love.
scenarios.relearn: A cold reaction can be repaired; go back, apologise and reaffirm love; it's never too late.

scenarios.hook: You have real fears about your son Dev's future, and tonight he is right there needing you.

steps.prompt: Dev climbs onto the sofa and asks why you look so worried. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him you're scared for his future and don't know what to do
options.then: Dev's face crumples. He asks if he should stop doing something.

options.text: Tell him it's because of how he's been lately
options.then: He goes still. He begins to watch himself around you.

options.text: Say it's grown-up stuff you'll sort out, and hug him tight
options.then: Dev relaxes into the hug and begins telling you about a drawing.

options.text: Say 'Nothing' and hug him stiffly
options.then: Dev feels the stiffness and says nothing. You both sit there, far apart.

steps.why: Warmth now, worries elsewhere: Dev gets a steady parent and you get the support you need.

steps.prompt: A week on, the fears are still heavy. Where do you take them?

options.text: To the family WhatsApp group, to see what everyone thinks
options.then: Twelve replies arrive by evening. Some are kind. Dev's business is now everyone's.

options.text: To Dev, a little at a time over the next few evenings
options.then: Dev starts asking how you're feeling before he tells you anything.

options.text: Nowhere. You tell yourself to be strong and carry on
options.then: The fears stay, and they show up as snapping at small things.

options.text: To a counsellor or trusted adult who will keep it private
options.then: She listens without judgement. You leave lighter and clearer.

steps.why: A trusted adult can carry the weight with you, without Dev or the family group learning anything.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Dev finds you crying in the kitchen and asks if it's his fault. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's never his fault, and your feelings are yours to sort out
options.then: Dev exhales. "Okay," he says, and helps you dry the plates.

options.text: Say you're just tired and send him to bed
options.then: Dev goes, unconvinced. He lies awake wondering what he did.

options.text: Say it's not his fault, then list everything that scares you
options.then: By the third worry, Dev is crying too.

options.text: Say 'I'm fine' sharply and turn back to the sink
options.then: Dev backs out of the kitchen. The question stays unanswered.

steps.why: Telling him it's never his fault, and that your feelings are yours to handle, frees him from them.

scenarios.debrief: Give your child love now; take your feelings to a supportive adult, not the child.
scenarios.relearn: Give love now; process your fears with a supportive adult, not your child.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Zoya asks if her close friend Mehr can come over, and you feel a flicker of hesitation.

steps.prompt: Zoya waits for your answer, hopeful. What do you do?

options.text: Find a reason to say no this time
options.then: Zoya says okay too quickly. She stops asking for a while.

options.text: Say yes, but plan to stay in the room the whole time
options.then: The girls whisper and keep an eye on you. Mehr leaves early.

options.text: Say 'Let me ask your father first' and leave her waiting
options.then: Zoya waits all evening for an answer. The invitation goes cold.

options.text: Say 'Of course she's welcome' and ask what Mehr likes to eat
options.then: Zoya's face lights up. She texts Mehr before you've finished the sentence.

steps.why: A warm yes tells Zoya her world is welcome, and that is real protection.

steps.prompt: Another day, Mehr turns up at the door looking nervous. What do you do?

options.text: Greet her warmly by name and offer her tea and a snack
options.then: Mehr smiles and relaxes. Zoya beams from behind her.

options.text: Nod and point her to Zoya's room, then keep away
options.then: The girls go in quietly. They seem to be waiting for you to come in.

options.text: Ask Mehr lots of questions about her family and plans
options.then: Mehr answers politely. She keeps glancing at the door.

options.text: Tell Mehr she's welcome, but ask her not to influence Zoya
options.then: Mehr goes red. Zoya leaves with her, mortified.

steps.why: Greeting her by name and feeding her makes Mehr welcome, and shows Zoya how you treat her friends.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Mehr is visiting again when Zoya's aunt drops by and raises an eyebrow. What do you do?

options.text: Send the girls to another room and explain to Aunt later
options.then: The girls go, and Zoya wonders why they had to hide.

options.text: Introduce Mehr warmly as Zoya's friend, and keep the visit light
options.then: Aunt says a stiff hello and drinks her tea. The girls exchange a small smile.

options.text: Tell Aunt privately that you'll sort it out
options.then: Aunt nods, satisfied. Zoya overhears the words 'sort it out' from the hall.

options.text: Ask Mehr to head home early to avoid a scene
options.then: Mehr collects her bag politely. Zoya walks her to the door without a word.

steps.why: Introducing Mehr warmly shows Zoya you stand with her friends, in front of family too.

scenarios.debrief: Welcoming your child's friends is a concrete act of acceptance that lowers their risk.
scenarios.relearn: Welcoming your child's friends is a protective act of acceptance; don't shut them out.

scenarios.hook: Your son Kabir says he has something to tell you and looks nervous, while your heart races.

steps.prompt: He tells you something about himself you never expected. What do you do?

options.text: Say 'Thank you for trusting me. I love you'
options.then: Kabir's eyes fill. "Really?" he says, and leans against you.

options.text: Let the panic out and demand that he explain himself right now
options.then: Kabir stiffens and says he's sorry he said anything.

options.text: Say 'I need to think' and leave the room for a while
options.then: Kabir hears the door close. He waits a long time for you to come back.

options.text: Ask if he's sure, and if a friend put the idea in his head
options.then: Kabir's face closes. "Forget it," he says, and looks away.

steps.why: A warm first response is what he'll remember and lean on for life.

steps.prompt: The next morning Kabir comes to breakfast, quiet, watching you. What do you do?

options.text: Talk about the weather and school so things feel normal again
options.then: He follows the small talk. You both wonder what the other is thinking.

options.text: Squeeze his shoulder and say 'Good morning. Glad you told me'
options.then: Kabir gives a small, shy smile and eats properly for the first time in days.

options.text: Ask whether he's had a night to think and reconsider it
options.then: Kabir pushes his plate away. "I haven't changed my mind," he says quietly.

options.text: Say you need a few days before you can talk about it
options.then: Kabir nods and goes to school. He checks his phone for a message from you all day.

steps.why: A small, clear sign that nothing has changed keeps the door open after the big moment.

steps.prompt: A week on, your husband Ashok asks if something is going on with Kabir lately. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him everything so you can decide together how to handle it
options.then: Ashok is stunned, and Kabir finds out you told. He stops confiding in you.

options.text: Tell him, but ask him to promise not to react
options.then: Ashok promises, then reacts anyway. Kabir sees both his parents watching him.

options.text: Say Kabir has things on his mind, and anything more is his to share
options.then: Ashok raises an eyebrow but lets it go. Kabir's news stays his to tell.

options.text: Say he's just growing up and change the subject
options.then: Ashok shrugs. The question stays, and so does the distance between you and Ashok.

steps.why: Whether and when anyone learns is Kabir's to decide, even inside the family.

scenarios.debrief: Lead the first moment with gratitude and love; that warm response protects your child for life.
scenarios.relearn: A warm first response is remembered and protective for life; lead with love.

scenarios.hook: Your son Arjun is teased at school, and you wonder if a stern home would toughen him.

steps.prompt: He comes home upset after another day of teasing. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him to stop crying because the world is tougher than this
options.then: Arjun wipes his face fast and goes silent. He hides his tears from now on.

options.text: Sit with him, hear it out and tell him home is safe
options.then: Arjun crumples against you and cries. Later he eats a full dinner.

options.text: Tell him to toughen up and hit back next time
options.then: Arjun looks frightened at the idea. He stops telling you about school.

options.text: Storm to school next morning without asking him first
options.then: The teacher is startled, and Arjun is mortified that you went without asking.

steps.why: A safe home is where a hurt child recovers, and recovery is what builds strength.

steps.prompt: Your father-in-law says Arjun needs a firm hand, not coddling, to survive school. What do you say?

options.text: Nod, and tell Arjun to man up whenever visitors are around
options.then: Arjun hears the words and begins to hide his feelings even from you.

options.text: Say he may be right and make the house rules stricter
options.then: The house gets tighter. Arjun eats in silence and asks fewer questions.

options.text: Say safety at home makes children strong, and he'll have it
options.then: Grandfather grumbles but goes quiet. Arjun, on the stairs, lets out a breath.

options.text: Change the subject and tell yourself he's just old-fashioned
options.then: Grandfather keeps talking. Arjun sees you say nothing.

steps.why: Saying a safe home makes children strong protects Arjun from being handed to the hard way.

steps.prompt: One morning, Arjun says his stomach hurts and begs to stay home from school. What do you do?

options.text: Say no because he has to face it and get tougher
options.then: Arjun goes, silent and pale. He walks in dreading it more.

options.text: Say yes, and let him stay home for as long as he likes
options.then: By the third day, school feels even scarier. Nothing at school has changed.

options.text: Tell him teasing is part of life and everyone goes through it
options.then: Arjun says okay. The stomach aches keep coming, and so does the dread.

options.text: Ask what's worrying him, and plan with him and the school
options.then: Arjun names a corridor and a recess. The teacher agrees to be nearby.

steps.why: Listening and planning with him and the school makes home a base to face things from.

scenarios.debrief: Your job isn't to toughen your child against the world; be the safe harbour.
scenarios.relearn: Don't toughen a child with a hard home; be the safe harbour; that builds resilience.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that would push a gender-diverse child away.

scene.text: "I love you exactly as you are"
"You're a shame on this family"
"I'm so glad you told me"
"Act normal or you're not my child"
"Whatever happens, I'm with you"

scenarios.why: Shaming a child and threatening to disown them are the rejecting lines that raise their risk and push them away.
scenarios.relearn: Shaming and threatening to disown a child are rejection; they raise risk and never change who the child is.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two parent moves that withdraw the warmth a child needs.

scene.text: Hugging her after a rough day
Going silent and cold for a week
Asking warmly how she's doing
Refusing to look at or speak to her
Sitting with her when she's upset

scenarios.why: Days of cold silence and refusing to speak to a child withdraw the warmth that is her lifeline.
scenarios.relearn: Cold silence and refusing to speak withdraw a child's lifeline; steady warmth is what protects her.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths hiding among these statements about acceptance.

scene.text: Acceptance keeps a child safer
Strictness will change who they are
Rejection only raises a child's risk
Disapproval steers a child back to 'normal'
Your love makes their path easier

scenarios.why: 'Strictness changes them' and 'disapproval steers them back' are myths; rejection never changes a child, it only raises risk.
scenarios.relearn: Strictness and disapproval don't change a child; that's myth. Acceptance protects; rejection only raises risk.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that make a child earn your love.

scene.text: "I love you, no matter what"
"I'll love you again once you change"
"You're always welcome here"
"Be normal and then I'll be proud"
"Nothing could lose my love"

scenarios.why: Lines that promise love only after a child changes make warmth a thing to earn; that conditional love wounds.
scenarios.relearn: Love a child must earn by changing wounds them; unconditional warmth is the acceptance that protects.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two moments where a parent leaves their child unprotected.

scene.text: Standing beside her when a relative jabs
Staying silent while she's mocked at lunch
Welcoming her friend home for dinner
Telling her to 'just fit in' to avoid trouble
Defending her to a shaming aunt

scenarios.why: Staying silent while she's mocked and telling her to 'just fit in' abandon a child to harm instead of shielding her.
scenarios.relearn: Staying silent and telling a child to 'just fit in' abandon them to harm; your job is to shield them.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two 'solutions' that would harm a child rather than help.

scene.text: Finding an affirming counsellor together
Booking a 'cure' to change them
Joining a parent support group
Pressuring them to mask who they are
Reaching out to a helpline for guidance

scenarios.why: 'Cures' and pressuring a child to mask are discredited and harmful; only affirming support genuinely helps.
scenarios.relearn: 'Cures' and forced masking are discredited and harmful; only affirming support genuinely helps a child.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two things that would make a child feel rejected at home.

scene.text: Feeling loved exactly as they are
Bracing for a cutting comment daily
Knowing a parent has their back
Hiding who they are to keep the peace
Hearing 'this is your safe place'

scenarios.why: Bracing for cutting comments and hiding to keep peace are felt rejection; children feel that deeply even when fed and housed.
scenarios.relearn: Bracing for cutting comments and hiding to keep peace are felt rejection; children feel it deeply.

scenarios.hook: Your teenage son has told you something big about himself and has avoided you since.
scenarios.setup: Tonight he stands in your doorway.

steps.prompt: Your son asks: "Are we okay? Do you still love me, now that you know?"

options.text: "We'll see how things go, I suppose."
options.then: He nods and looks at the floor. "Right," he says.

options.text: "There is nothing about you that could ever make me love you less."
options.then: His shoulders drop. "Okay," he says, and sits down beside you.

options.text: "Of course I love you. I just need time before I say more."
options.then: "Okay," he says. He hovers, then goes to his room.

options.text: "Let's not talk about this tonight. I'm tired."
options.then: He says fine and goes. You hear his door click shut.

steps.why: A plain 'nothing could' answers the fear underneath his question, with no conditions.

steps.prompt: Some days later he asks: "Are you going to tell Dadi and the rest of the family?"

options.text: "They'll find out anyway, so it's better it comes from us."
options.then: He goes pale. "Please don't," he says.

options.text: "I think I should, so they're prepared."
options.then: He stares at you. "I thought this was mine to decide," he says.

options.text: "No. Who knows is your call, and I'll follow your lead."
options.then: He nods, and the tension in his face leaves. "Thanks," he says.

options.text: "Not yet. Let me think about who needs to know."
options.then: "Right," he says, and looks unsure. He starts guarding what he says.

steps.why: Who knows, and when, is his decision, so promising to follow his lead is the caring answer.

steps.prompt: A month on he asks: "Is it easier for you if I don't talk about it?"

options.text: "A little. But I'll manage."
options.then: He nods. He starts to manage it for you.

options.text: "It's easier if you don't talk about it outside the house."
options.then: "Okay," he says. It feels like a rule about who he is.

options.text: "Let's just not make it a big deal."
options.then: He shrugs. "Fine," he says, and doesn't raise it again.

options.text: "No. I want you to talk about it whenever you like."
options.then: He gives a shy smile. "Okay. Actually, there's something I wanted to ask."

steps.why: Inviting him to talk whenever he likes shows the door is genuinely open.

scenarios.relearn: An unconditional 'nothing could make me love you less' gives the safety that protects a child most.

scenarios.hook: Your son Vihaan has just told you something big about himself and is watching your face.
scenarios.setup: The kitchen goes very still.

steps.prompt: Vihaan asks: "Are you angry? Say something, please."

options.text: "Why are you telling me this now?"
options.then: He flinches. "I don't know. I thought it was time."

options.text: "I'm not angry. I just need a minute to take it in."
options.then: He nods, looking at his hands. "Okay. I'll wait."

options.text: "Thank you for trusting me with this. I love you."
options.then: He lets out a shaky breath. "I was so scared you'd hate me."

options.text: "Who else knows about this?"
options.then: "Just Ishaan," he says, sounding uneasy. "Why does it matter?"

steps.why: Thanks and love first answer what he is really asking, before anything else is said.

steps.prompt: Vihaan asks: "Do I have to tell everyone now?"

options.text: "It's better to tell Papa soon, so it isn't a secret."
options.then: He tenses. "Please don't do it for me."

options.text: "Better not to tell anyone, ever. It's safer."
options.then: He looks at you. "So I should hide it forever?"

options.text: "Let's tell everyone together at Diwali. Then it's done."
options.then: "No," he says, alarmed. "I'm not ready for that."

options.text: "Not at all. You decide who to tell, and when."
options.then: His shoulders loosen. "Okay. Thanks. I need to think about it."

steps.why: The story is his, so he decides who hears it and when.

steps.prompt: Vihaan says: "I don't know what to call it yet. Is that okay?"

options.text: "Of course. You don't need a label. We'll go at your pace."
options.then: He smiles, relieved. "Thanks. I like that I don't have to figure it out today."

options.text: "You should find a word soon, so people understand."
options.then: He sinks a little. "Okay. I'll look for one."

options.text: "Then maybe it's nothing yet. Let's wait and see."
options.then: He looks confused. "It's not nothing."

options.text: "Ask your friends what to call it, and tell me."
options.then: He shrugs. "I guess. I wanted to ask you, though."

steps.why: He can learn about himself at his own pace, without a label he has to hurry to find.

scenarios.relearn: Leading with thanks and love makes the first reaction the protection your child remembers for life.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Diya seems afraid that home might turn against her.
scenarios.setup: She sits on the stairs, hugging her knees.

steps.prompt: Diya asks: "Is home always going to be okay for me?"

options.text: "As long as you don't cause trouble, it's fine."
options.then: Diya nods, small. "What counts as trouble?" she asks.

options.text: "Of course it is. Why would you even ask that?"
options.then: She shrugs and looks down. "No reason," she says.

options.text: "It is, but be careful what you say around Dadaji."
options.then: She nods and pulls her knees closer. "Okay. I'll be careful."

options.text: "This home is your safe place, today and always."
options.then: Diya's shoulders drop. "Even if I mess up?"

steps.why: A plain, unconditional yes tells her home is where she is safest.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Diya says: "I heard you and Papa arguing about me last night."

options.text: "We did disagree. That's ours to sort out, never your fault."
options.then: Diya searches your face, then lets out a breath. "Okay."

options.text: "You shouldn't be listening at doors late at night."
options.then: Diya's face closes. "Sorry," she says, and leaves it.

options.text: "Grown-ups argue sometimes. It had nothing to do with you."
options.then: She frowns. "But you said my name," she says.

options.text: "Papa needs more time. Please try to be patient with him."
options.then: "Okay," she says. She looks like she's already begun waiting.

steps.why: Admitting the disagreement, and saying it's never her fault, lifts a weight she shouldn't carry.

steps.prompt: Diya asks: "If someone at school is mean to me, can I tell you?"

options.text: "Try to handle it yourself first."
options.then: "Okay," she says. "I'll try." She doesn't sound sure.

options.text: "Always. Tell me straight away. I'm on your side."
options.then: She nods slowly. "There's a boy who says things," she begins.

options.text: "Tell me, but don't mention it to Papa."
options.then: "Why not?" she asks. "Is he angry at me?"

options.text: "Tell your teacher. It isn't really for us to fix."
options.then: She goes quiet. "Okay," she says, and doesn't ask again.

steps.why: Saying yes plainly, and that you're on her side, is what makes her bring it to you.

steps.prompt: A week later, Diya asks: "What if Dadaji doesn't want me at his birthday lunch?"

options.text: "Then we'll go without you, just this once, to keep it calm."
options.then: She goes silent. "Okay," she says. She looks like she's already left.

options.text: "Then be extra polite and quiet, so that he won't mind."
options.then: Diya nods. "I'll be so polite," she says, and starts practising.

options.text: "Then I'll talk to him. You tell me what feels right."
options.then: Diya thinks. "Okay. Will you sit next to me?"

options.text: "Let's not worry about it until it actually happens."
options.then: "Okay." She goes to her room. The worry goes with her.

steps.why: Speaking to Dadaji, and letting her say what feels right, keeps her included and protected.

scenarios.relearn: Telling a child home is their safe place, with no conditions, gives them protection they carry everywhere.

scenarios.hook: At Diwali, your aunt Sushma makes a sharp remark about your daughter Tanvi while she stands right there.
scenarios.setup: The room goes quiet.

steps.prompt: Aunt Sushma says: "She looks like a boy. Can't you make her dress properly?"

options.text: "Please don't speak about my child that way."
options.then: Sushma blinks. "I only meant..." Tanvi steps closer to you.

options.text: "Sorry, you know how kids are these days."
options.then: Sushma smiles, satisfied. Tanvi looks at the floor.

options.text: "She's just going through something. It will pass."
options.then: Sushma raises her eyebrows. "Then you must correct it soon."

options.text: "Tanvi, go inside. Let the adults talk."
options.then: Tanvi leaves quickly. Sushma carries on as if she was right.

steps.why: A short, clear line in front of Tanvi shows her she is protected.

steps.prompt: Aunt Sushma adds: "I'm only saying what everyone thinks. You're too soft."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I'll think about it."
options.then: Sushma nods, pleased. Tanvi, at the door, hears every word.

options.text: "You can have your view. Not about her, not in front of her."
options.then: Sushma purses her lips and goes to help with the sweets.

options.text: "Then you can tell Tanvi how wrong she is yourself, can't you?"
options.then: The room gasps. Tanvi flushes and the whole family stares.

options.text: "Let's not fight at a festival."
options.then: Sushma takes it as a win. She says one more thing about Tanvi's clothes.

steps.why: Naming the line without a fight protects Tanvi and keeps the room calm.

steps.prompt: After the party, Tanvi asks quietly: "Was Aunty right? Is something wrong with me?"

options.text: "Aunty means well. Just ignore her."
options.then: Tanvi nods, but her eyes stay on the floor.

options.text: "Some people always talk. It's best to blend in."
options.then: Tanvi's face falls. "So I should hide?" she asks.

options.text: "No. Nothing is wrong with you. I'm sorry she said it."
options.then: Tanvi exhales. "Okay," she says, and leans against your shoulder.

options.text: "Don't think about it. Go to sleep."
options.then: She goes, but the question follows her to bed.

steps.why: A plain 'nothing is wrong with you' undoes the sting, and owns that it should not have been said.

scenarios.relearn: Standing up for your child in front of a relative shows them they are protected, not on their own.

scenarios.hook: Your son Nikhil has just shared something about himself, and you honestly don't know what to say yet.
scenarios.setup: He waits, arms wrapped around a cushion.

steps.prompt: Nikhil asks: "So... what do you think?"

options.text: "Let's not talk about this until I understand it."
options.then: He nods slowly and puts the cushion down. "Okay."

options.text: "I don't have all the answers, but I love you and I'm here."
options.then: He half-laughs. "That's enough for me right now."

options.text: "I think you should see a doctor first."
options.then: He stares. "I'm not sick, Mama."

options.text: "Give me a week and I'll tell you what I think."
options.then: He nods. "A week," he repeats, as if counting.

steps.why: You can say you have no answers and still say the one thing he needs: you love him.

steps.prompt: Nikhil asks: "Are you going to look it up?"

options.text: "I already have a feeling. I don't need to look anything up."
options.then: His face closes. "Right," he says, and stops explaining.

options.text: "I'll read a lot, then tell you where you're wrong."
options.then: He winces. "I thought you wanted to understand."

options.text: "Yes, I'd like to learn. Will you tell me what feels true to you?"
options.then: He brightens. "Okay. There's a page I like. I'll send it."

options.text: "You do the reading, and just tell me what to do."
options.then: He shrugs. "I don't know what to tell you," he admits.

steps.why: Learning with him, and asking what feels true to him, makes you a partner instead of a judge.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Nikhil says: "Please don't tell anyone yet."

options.text: "I'll only tell Papa. He's your father."
options.then: He goes stiff. "I wanted to be the one to tell him."

options.text: "I can keep it quiet, but I'll have to tell my sister."
options.then: "Then it's not private," he says quietly.

options.text: "Okay, but you'll have to tell people someday."
options.then: "Maybe," he says. He looks pressured about it now.

options.text: "I won't. It's yours to share, whenever you're ready."
options.then: His face softens. "Thank you. I'll tell you who, when I know."

steps.why: Keeping his story private, and letting him share when he chooses, protects his trust in you.

steps.prompt: Nikhil asks: "Are you still worried about me?"

options.text: "Sometimes, about the world. That's mine to handle, not yours."
options.then: He nods. "Thanks for telling me the truth," he says.

options.text: "No, I'm perfectly fine with everything."
options.then: He gives you a look. He doesn't quite believe it.

options.text: "Yes, a lot. I can't sleep or eat."
options.then: His face crumples. "I'm sorry," he says. "I didn't want that."

options.text: "That depends on how you behave."
options.then: He goes pale. "So it's conditional?"

steps.why: Naming your worry as yours, and separate from who he is, lets him feel loved and free.

scenarios.relearn: You can lead with love before you have any answers; the warmth protects your child while you learn.

scenarios.hook: Your son Aryan and his best friend Sameer are inseparable, and Aryan seems unsure how you see it.
scenarios.setup: He hovers by the kitchen door.

steps.prompt: Aryan asks, nervously: "Can Sameer stay for dinner tonight?"

options.text: "Maybe another time. We're a bit busy."
options.then: Aryan's smile fades. "Okay. I'll tell him."

options.text: "Yes, but keep it short. Your father won't like it."
options.then: He hesitates. "I'll ask him, but it'll be quick."

options.text: "Of course, your friends are always welcome here."
options.then: Aryan grins. "Yes! I'll tell him!"

options.text: "Who is he to you, exactly?"
options.then: Aryan goes red. "He's my friend, Mama."

steps.why: A warm yes with no strings tells Aryan his friends and his world are welcome.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Aryan asks: "Can Sameer and I eat in my room tonight? Just us two."

options.text: "No. From now on the door stays open when Sameer is over."
options.then: Aryan stares. "Why only Sameer? We're just eating."

options.text: "Only when Sameer's here, and only if your sister sits with you."
options.then: He frowns. "Fine. She'll just listen in."

options.text: "Eat with us. I want to keep an eye on you both."
options.then: "Okay," he says. They eat in near silence.

options.text: "Yes, of course. I'll bring your plates in a bit."
options.then: Aryan beams. "Thanks, Mama. You're the best."

steps.why: Trusting their time together, as you would with any friend, tells him his friendship is welcome.

steps.prompt: Aryan asks: "Are you okay with Sameer being my best friend?"

options.text: "Very okay. He's welcome any day, and so is everyone you like."
options.then: Aryan lets out a breath. "Thanks. I wasn't sure."

options.text: "As long as he stays just a friend."
options.then: Aryan looks at you. "What does that mean?"

options.text: "I'm okay, but let's not mention him to Chacha."
options.then: "Why not?" asks Aryan. "Is there something wrong with him?"

options.text: "Why would you ask that? You ask too many questions."
options.then: Aryan shrugs. "Sorry," he says, and drops it.

steps.why: Saying yes and welcoming him plainly tells Aryan his world has room for his people.

scenarios.relearn: Warmly welcoming a child's friends is a concrete act of acceptance that lowers their risk.

scenarios.hook: Earlier this week your daughter Pari told you something personal, and you reacted coldly. She has gone quiet since.
scenarios.setup: You find her doing homework alone.

steps.prompt: Pari says without looking up: "It's fine. I'm just busy."

options.text: "Let's just forget that happened, okay?"
options.then: She nods. "Okay." The pen starts again, harder.

options.text: "I know you're upset, but I was surprised too."
options.then: She says "I know" flatly. "You didn't have to say that."

options.text: "Tell me what I did wrong and I'll fix it."
options.then: She sighs. "I don't want to say it all again."

options.text: "I'm sorry for how I reacted. I love you, and I'm glad you told me."
