Pretending it never happened
Reaffirming 'I love you' clearly
Blaming them for shocking you
Asking to understand them better
Going silent and hoping it fades

scenarios.relearn: Apologising, reaffirming love and seeking to understand repair; erasing, blaming or going silent don't.

scenarios.hook: Sort each statement about a child coming out: true, or a myth that holds parents back?

items.text: The first reaction matters enormously
How I react doesn't really matter
A bad first reaction can be repaired
Once said wrong, the damage is permanent
Love can come before full understanding
I must understand it all before I respond

scenarios.relearn: The first reaction matters and is repairable, and love can come first; the opposites are myths that stall parents.

scenarios.hook: In the days after a coming-out, sort each signal: it opens the door, or quietly shuts it?

items.text: Checking in with warmth
Never bringing it up again
Saying 'I'm proud of you'
Acting strangely formal and distant
Welcoming their friends warmly
Changing the subject every time

scenarios.relearn: Warm check-ins, spoken pride and welcoming friends open the door; silence, distance and dodging shut it.

scenarios.hook: Your child just came out and you feel a wave of emotion. Sort each: hold it for now, or go find support for it?

items.text: Your love for your child
Your fear of what relatives will say
Your gladness they trusted you
Your grief for an imagined future
Your reassurance that you're staying
Your confusion and unanswered questions

scenarios.relearn: Show love, gladness and reassurance to your child; take fear, grief and confusion to a supportive adult.

scenarios.hook: Match each doubting first instinct to the affirming version that protects your child.
scenarios.relearn: Every doubting instinct has an affirming twin that protects the child instead of questioning them.

scenarios.hook: Match each thing your child fears as they come out to the reassurance that answers it.
scenarios.relearn: Each fear a child carries into coming out has a clear reassurance that meets it and keeps them safe.

scenarios.hook: Match each first feeling a parent has to where that feeling should go.

pairs.right: Say it to them, right away
Sit with it, then share later
Take it to a supportive adult

scenarios.relearn: Warm feelings go straight to your child; shock, fear and grief go to another adult, not onto the child.

scenarios.hook: Match each repair step to what it restores for a child after a rough first reaction.
scenarios.relearn: Each part of a genuine repair restores something: the sting, the cause, their safety, the talk, your presence.

scenarios.hook: Match each way a child might come out to the warm response that fits it.

pairs.right: Reply warmly, no rush to meet
Pause the fight, lead with love
Honour that they chose their pace

scenarios.relearn: However a child comes out, a warm response fits it; meet them where they are, not how you'd have chosen.

scenarios.hook: Match each protective thing to do after a coming-out to why it matters.
scenarios.relearn: Each follow-up act protects: warmth, confidence, welcome, spoken pride and refusing 'cures' all keep a child safe.

scenarios.hook: Match each unhelpful first reaction to the harm it does, so you can choose differently.

pairs.right: Reads to a child as rejection
Doubts who they say they are

scenarios.relearn: Naming the harm of each cold reaction makes the warm choice clearer: lead with love, privacy and belief.

scenarios.hook: Match each gentle question to the moment it belongs in after your child comes out.
scenarios.relearn: Love leads, deeper questions follow at the child's pace, and 'I'm here' gets repeated in the days after.

scenarios.hook: "If I let bullies have their way, my child will learn to cope. Toughening is kindness."

myth.un: Letting bullies have their way teaches my child to cope; toughening is kindness.
myth.re: A bullied child needs an advocate, not abandonment; stepping in teaches them they are worth defending.
myth.why: Backing them up is the real strength.

scenarios.relearn: A bullied gender-diverse child needs you to advocate, not to leave them to 'toughen up' alone.

scenarios.hook: "Home has to push my child harder than the world will, or they'll be soft."

myth.un: Home must push my child harder than the world will, or they'll be soft.
myth.re: Home is the one place a gender-diverse child should be able to rest from pressure, not face more of it.
myth.why: Make home the harbour, not another storm.

scenarios.relearn: Home should be the safe rest from pressure, not where a gender-diverse child is pushed hardest.

scenarios.hook: "Using their new name at home but the old one outside protects them. That's just being practical."

myth.un: Using their new name at home but the old one outside is just being practical and protects them.
myth.re: Following the child's lead on where and when feels safe is fine; deciding it for them isn't affirming.
myth.why: Follow the child's pace, don't override it.

scenarios.relearn: Let the child set where their name feels safe; don't decide it for them in the name of being practical.

scenarios.hook: "My slips with their pronouns prove I'm failing them, so why even try."

myth.un: My slips with their pronouns prove I'm failing them, so why even try.
myth.re: Slipping and correcting yourself shows your child you're trying for them; the effort itself is affirming.
myth.why: Trying out loud is what they remember.

scenarios.relearn: Slipping then correcting yourself is still affirming; the visible effort is what protects, not perfection.

scenarios.hook: "I should keep the peace with relatives; my child can handle a few harsh words."

myth.un: I should keep the peace with relatives; my child can handle a few harsh words.
myth.re: Keeping the peace by letting relatives shame your child tells them home isn't on their side.
myth.why: Peace bought with their dignity costs too much.

scenarios.relearn: Don't buy family peace by letting relatives shame your child; stand between them and the harm.

scenarios.hook: "If my child just blended in, the teasing would stop. So I should help them blend in."

myth.un: If my child just blended in the teasing would stop, so I should help them blend in.
myth.re: Asking a child to hide who they are to dodge teasing makes them the problem; the teasing is.
myth.why: Affirm the child, name the teasing as the issue.

scenarios.relearn: Don't ask your child to hide to avoid teasing; the teasing is the problem, not who they are.

scenarios.hook: "Once they pick a label, they have to stick to it, or I'll look foolish for going along."

myth.un: Once they pick a label they must stick to it, or I'll look foolish for going along.
myth.re: A child is allowed to explore and change; following them as it shifts is the affirming thing, not a failure.
myth.why: Follow the child, not a fixed label.

scenarios.relearn: Following a child as their sense of self shifts is affirming; you don't lock them to one label.

scenarios.hook: "Defending my child in public will only draw more attention and make it worse for them."

myth.un: Defending my child in public only draws attention and makes it worse for them.
myth.re: A calm, public 'we use their name, please respect that' shows your child you'll stand up wherever they are.
myth.why: Your steady defence is their shield, not a spotlight.

scenarios.relearn: Calmly defending your child in public shows them you'll stand up anywhere; it shields, it doesn't expose.

scenarios.hook: At a wedding, an uncle loudly tells your son to "stop the girly stuff and act like a boy".

steps.prompt: Guests turn to look, and your son freezes. What do you do?

options.text: Step in warmly: "He's wonderful as he is. Leave him be."
options.then: The uncle huffs and turns away. Your son moves closer to you.

options.text: Say nothing and hope the uncle drops it
options.then: The uncle moves on to the buffet. Your son looks at you, then away.

options.text: Laugh and say your son is just going through a phase
options.then: A few guests chuckle. Your son goes very still.

options.text: Take your son aside and tell him to be more careful
options.then: He nods and stays glued to your side, watching how he moves.

steps.why: Stepping in gently shows him you have his back, even in a crowd.

steps.prompt: The uncle mutters that you are spoiling him, and your son asks to go home. What do you do?

options.text: Ask if he wants to leave or stay, and follow what he says
options.then: He whispers that he'd like to stay if you sit with him. You do.

options.text: Insist you stay so the family doesn't talk
options.then: He sits stiffly through dinner and barely eats.

options.text: Take him home right away and skip the rest of the wedding
options.then: In the car he asks quietly if the wedding is ruined because of him.

options.text: Ask the uncle to apologise to your son in front of everyone
options.then: The uncle blusters. Your son squeezes your hand and begs you to drop it.

steps.why: Asking what he wants lets him lead, and tells him he isn't the problem.

steps.prompt: The next day, your mother says the uncle only meant to help, and asks you to let it go. What do you say?

options.text: Say his words hurt your son, and you'll step in again
options.then: She sighs and says nothing more, though she is not convinced.

options.text: Say he meant well and you'll let it go
options.then: Your mother is relieved. Your son, listening, learns not to mention it again.

options.text: Say you'll ask your son to be careful around him
options.then: She agrees, glad. Your son is now the one who has to adjust.

options.text: Say nothing, since you don't want a fight with her
options.then: The call ends politely. She takes your silence as agreement.

steps.why: Naming the harm calmly keeps your son protected at the next family event.

scenarios.debrief: When a relative shames your child in front of others, step between them gently.
scenarios.relearn: Shield your child from a relative's shaming; silence reads to the child as agreement.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter's school says she must wear the "boys" uniform on the register, and she is distressed.

steps.prompt: She comes home in tears about the uniform. What do you do?

options.text: Listen first, then say you'll take it up with the school
options.then: She wipes her face. "Will you really? Can I come to the meeting?"

options.text: Tell her rules are rules and she will simply have to manage it
options.then: She nods and goes to her room. The uniform hangs unworn on the door.

options.text: Tell her to wear it just until the term ends
options.then: She agrees, but crosses off the days on her calendar every night.

options.text: Write an angry email to the principal tonight
options.then: The principal replies coldly. Your daughter wishes you had asked her first.

steps.why: Hearing her first, then taking it to the school, tells her she's worth speaking up for.

steps.prompt: The school office asks you to come in and discuss it. What do you do?

options.text: Go calmly, and ask for an option that fits how she lives
options.then: The vice-principal listens and says she will check what is allowed.

options.text: Go, and agree to whatever the office decides
options.then: You leave with a note that changes nothing.

options.text: Go, and explain her whole story in detail so they understand
options.then: The staff learn far more about your daughter than she wanted them to.

options.text: Send a relative in your place to keep things calm
options.then: The relative repeats the school's rules back to you, and nothing more.

steps.why: A calm, specific request gets a real answer and keeps her details private.

steps.prompt: The school says other families may complain if her uniform changes. What do you do?

options.text: Ask them to keep her name out and put the change in writing
options.then: The vice-principal nods, and promises a letter by Friday.

options.text: Let it go, since other families might complain
options.then: You leave it. She wears the register uniform, and goes quiet at dinner.

options.text: Suggest she change in a separate room from the others
options.then: She sits alone in the office each morning and asks why she must hide.

options.text: Tell the other families yourself, to head off any complaints
options.then: Word spreads through the class WhatsApp group. Your daughter dreads school.

steps.why: Keeping her details private, and getting it in writing, protects her at school.

steps.prompt: One evening, your daughter asks if you think she's making trouble. What do you say?

options.text: Say she is not trouble, and you're proud of her
options.then: She lets out a shaky laugh and leans into your shoulder.

options.text: Say it's a small thing and nothing to fuss over
options.then: She nods, though she still looks unsure how she feels.

options.text: Say she should try not to upset the teachers
options.then: She goes quiet, as if her feelings were the problem.

options.text: Say you'll handle it, so she needn't think about it
options.then: She shrugs. The worry doesn't go away.

steps.why: She needs to hear plainly that asking for respect is not making trouble.

scenarios.debrief: When school policy clashes with who your child is, advocate with the adults.
scenarios.relearn: Advocate with the school for your child; don't leave her to cope alone.

scenarios.hook: Your son wants to wear his bangles to his cousin's birthday, but he is nervous about what people will say.

steps.prompt: He holds up the bangles and looks at you. What do you say?

options.text: "Wear them if you like. I'll be right there with you."
options.then: His face lights up. He slides them on and checks himself in the mirror.

options.text: "Better leave them home so nobody talks."
options.then: He puts the bangles back in the drawer and closes it slowly.

options.text: "Wear them, but be ready for comments and handle them."
options.then: He wears them, then hides his wrist behind his back at the party.

options.text: "Let's ask your aunt whether it's alright at her party."
options.then: Your aunt hesitates. He sees it and starts taking the bangles off.

steps.why: Saying yes and staying beside him lets him be himself and be safe.

steps.prompt: At the next family gathering, an aunt hears about the bangles and says in front of him: "Boys don't wear bangles." What do you do?

options.text: Say lightly and clearly that he wears what he likes
options.then: The aunt raises her eyebrows but lets it go. He leans against your arm.

options.text: Smile and say nothing to keep the aunt happy
options.then: The aunt carries on. He tugs his sleeve over his wrist.

options.text: Tell him quietly to cover them until the aunt leaves
options.then: He covers them and stays near the wall until the aunt has gone.

options.text: Argue with the aunt about how old-fashioned she is
options.then: The aunt is offended. Your son wishes he had never worn them.

steps.why: A light, clear line shows him he can be himself, without a fight.

steps.prompt: Your son asks if he should stop wearing them to school too. What do you say?

options.text: Ask what he wants, and say you'll help if there's trouble
options.then: He thinks, then says he'd like to keep wearing them on weekends and see.

options.text: Suggest he wear them only at home
options.then: He nods, and slides the bangles into his drawer after dinner.

options.text: Say it's up to him, and you'd rather not get involved
options.then: He shrugs, but looks as if he wanted your answer.

options.text: Tell him to wear them and not care what anyone thinks
options.then: He tries to look brave the next morning. His hands tremble a little.

steps.why: He decides, and knows you'll help with any trouble. That is what keeps him safe.

scenarios.debrief: Let your child express himself with you beside him; don't ask him to hide for others.
scenarios.relearn: Back your child's self-expression and stay beside him; don't ask him to shrink for others.

scenarios.hook: A neighbour "jokes" about your child in the lift while your child stands right there.

steps.prompt: Your child's smile freezes as the neighbour chuckles. What do you do?

options.text: Say lightly but clearly that you don't joke about your kid
options.then: The neighbour blinks. "Arre, only fun," he says, and stops. Your child looks up at you.

options.text: Laugh along so it doesn't get awkward
options.then: The neighbour beams. Your child studies the lift floor.

options.text: Say nothing and press the button for your floor
options.then: The doors open. The neighbour waves. Your child walks out in silence.

options.text: Whisper to your child that it's only a joke
options.then: Your child nods and swallows. The neighbour chuckles again.

steps.why: A calm, clear line shows your child whose side you are on, right then.

steps.prompt: In the lobby, your child asks quietly why he said that about them. What do you say?

options.text: Say he was wrong to, and nothing is wrong with them
options.then: They breathe out. "Okay. It felt like it was me."

options.text: Say he was only joking, so don't take it hard
options.then: They nod, but the hurt stays on their face.

options.text: Say maybe they can try to stand out a little less
options.then: They go quiet, and start checking themselves in shop windows.

options.text: Say you'll go back and shout at the neighbour
options.then: They grab your sleeve. "No, please, everyone will hear."

steps.why: Telling them plainly that nothing is wrong with them undoes the hurt.

steps.prompt: The next week, the neighbour jokes again at the mailboxes. What do you do?

options.text: Say calmly it must stop, then walk on with your child
options.then: The neighbour mumbles a reply. Your child walks a little taller.

options.text: Ignore it this time, to avoid a scene
options.then: The neighbour grins, thinking it is fine. Your child studies the mailboxes.

options.text: Ask your child to tell the neighbour to stop
options.then: Your child's voice shakes. The neighbour laughs at how small it sounds.

options.text: Complain about the neighbour in the building group chat
options.then: The group erupts, and your child's name is now in the messages.

steps.why: A calm, firm line every time shows you'll keep protecting them, without a public fuss.

scenarios.debrief: Draw a calm, clear line when someone mocks your child; they watch whose side you take.
scenarios.relearn: Draw a calm line when your child is mocked; don't laugh along with it.

scenarios.hook: Your child wants to invite a close friend home for the weekend. The friend is also gender-diverse.

steps.prompt: Your child asks nervously if the friend can come and stay. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes warmly, and ask how to make it easy for both
options.then: Your child beams. "Really? I'll tell them tonight."

options.text: Say no, and suggest they keep that friendship outside
options.then: Your child nods, crushed. The friend still turns up at the door, unsure of the welcome.

options.text: Say yes, and talk to the friend's parents about their identity
options.then: Your child goes pale. The friend hasn't told their parents everything.

options.text: Say yes, but ask them to keep it quiet from relatives
options.then: Your child agrees, but the visit now begins with a rule about hiding.

steps.why: A warm yes, and asking what would help, tells them their friendships are welcome.

steps.prompt: The friend is at the door, polite but tense, glancing at you. What do you do?

options.text: Greet them by name, offer tea, and let them settle
options.then: The friend's shoulders drop a little. They smile at your child.

options.text: Ask if their family knows about them
options.then: The friend goes stiff. "They know enough," they say.

options.text: Explain the house rules straight away, with a stern look
options.then: The friend nods too quickly, and your child looks embarrassed.

options.text: Stay out of the way and let the kids sort themselves
options.then: The friend hovers by the door, unsure if they are welcome.

steps.why: A warm greeting by name tells a wary guest they are safe here.

steps.prompt: A relative drops in and asks who the friend is. What do you do?

options.text: Introduce them by name as your child's friend, nothing more
options.then: The relative nods and asks nothing more. The friend eases.

options.text: Explain to the relative everything about the friend
options.then: The relative stares at the friend. The friend leaves the room.

options.text: Say they are just a classmate and change the subject
options.then: The friend hears it and looks down. Your child stiffens.

options.text: Send the friend to the other room while the relative visits
options.then: The friend spends an hour alone on the bed, hearing the voices.

steps.why: Introducing them simply keeps them safe, and never shares what isn't yours to tell.

steps.prompt: As the friend leaves, they thank you quietly, and your child asks if they can come again. What do you say?

options.text: Say they are always welcome, and mean it
options.then: The friend smiles properly for the first time all weekend.

options.text: Say of course, but not too often
options.then: The friend nods politely. Your child does the sums in their head.

options.text: Say maybe, once you've thought about it
options.then: "Okay," the friend says, with a small nod. Your child looks away.

options.text: Say yes, but only when relatives aren't visiting
options.then: Your child nods. The friendship now has rules about who may see it.

steps.why: A clear, open invitation tells them your home is a place they belong.

scenarios.debrief: Welcoming your child's friends is a concrete affirming act, not just hospitality.
scenarios.relearn: Welcome your child's friends warmly; it's a real protective act.

scenarios.hook: Your spouse wants you both to "discipline the softness out" of your son before he is older.

steps.prompt: Your spouse says this over dinner, with your son in the next room. What do you do?

options.text: Hold the line: "We protect him. We don't toughen him."
options.then: Your spouse stares at you. "That's not what I meant," they say, less sure.

options.text: Go along quietly to avoid a fight at home
options.then: Your spouse takes it as a yes and starts planning the talk.

options.text: Say you'll think about it and change the subject
options.then: Your spouse says the talk is still on. The tension stays in the house.

options.text: Say they are a terrible parent for even suggesting it
options.then: Your spouse slams a cupboard. Your son turns the TV up in the next room.

steps.why: Holding the line calmly keeps your son's home safe, without turning it into a war.

steps.prompt: The next night, your spouse admits: "I'm scared for him." What do you do?

options.text: Say you're scared too, and ask what worries them most
options.then: Your spouse sits down. "The boys at his school," they say quietly.

options.text: Say fear is no excuse for what they said
options.then: They go rigid. "So I'm the bad one now?"

options.text: Tell them not to worry, since everything will be fine
options.then: They nod, unconvinced. The fear stays in the room.

options.text: Suggest they tell your son how scared they are
options.then: Your spouse pictures it, and looks even more worried.

steps.why: Naming the fear you share opens a door, and blame would shut it.

steps.prompt: Your spouse asks what you can do instead to keep him safe. What do you suggest?

options.text: Learn together, and back him at home and at school
options.then: Your spouse agrees to try, and asks where to start.

options.text: Each handle it your own way, for now
options.then: Your spouse nods. Your son ends up with two very different parents.

options.text: Wait until he is older and then see
options.then: You both nod. Nothing changes, and your son notices.

options.text: Ask your spouse to stay away from him for a while
options.then: Your spouse looks stung. Your son wonders why they are avoiding him.

steps.why: Backing him together makes home a place he can always count on.

scenarios.debrief: Don't side with a co-parent against your child to keep the peace.
scenarios.relearn: Don't side with a partner against your child; protecting him at home is non-negotiable.

scenarios.hook: Your child slips you a note saying kids called them names today, and they told no teacher.

steps.prompt: They watch your face as you read it. What do you do?

options.text: Thank them, say it's not their fault, and ask how to help
options.then: Their face softens. "I didn't know if I should tell you," they say.

options.text: Tell them to ignore it, and it will stop
options.then: They nod. There is no note the next day, and no word either.

options.text: Go straight to the class teacher tomorrow without telling them
options.then: The teacher pulls them aside the next day. Your child feels exposed.

options.text: Ask exactly what was said, word for word
options.then: They recite it in a flat voice, and look smaller for it.

steps.why: Thanking them and saying it's not their fault teaches them that telling you brings support.

steps.prompt: A few days later the names haven't stopped, but your child dreads anything being done at school. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what worries them, and agree on one small step
options.then: They say they fear it will get worse. You settle on something small.

options.text: Say you will act anyway, without asking them first
options.then: They fall silent. Next time they won't leave you a note.

options.text: Drop it entirely, since they'd rather nothing happened
options.then: You let it go. The names are still there the next morning.

options.text: Wait a few days and see if it stops by itself
options.then: It doesn't. By the fourth day your child stops sitting with others at lunch.

steps.why: Working out a step together keeps their trust, and still moves things forward.

steps.prompt: Now the names spread to the class group chat as well. What do you do?

options.text: With their okay, save screenshots and go to the school together
options.then: The school takes it seriously, and your child feels heard.

options.text: Tell your child to leave the group and forget all about it
options.then: They leave. The messages carry on elsewhere, where they can't see them.

options.text: Message the other children's parents angrily
options.then: Two parents reply defensively, and it turns into a fight among adults.

options.text: Reply in the group yourself to shame the children
options.then: The group goes silent, then a screenshot of your message spreads.

steps.why: Evidence, with your child agreeing and beside you, gives the school what it needs to act.

scenarios.debrief: When your child reports bullying, thank them and follow their lead.
scenarios.relearn: Thank your child for reporting bullying and follow their lead; don't dismiss it.

scenarios.hook: At a function, a relative corners you about your son.

steps.prompt: She says people will keep talking until he changes. What do you say?

options.text: Say you hear her, but your job is to keep your son safe
options.then: She presses her lips together. "Hmm," she says, and lets you go.

options.text: Promise to work on him, just so she leaves you alone
options.then: She smiles, satisfied. Now you owe her a change that will never come.

options.text: Say people should mind their own business
options.then: She bristles. By evening the whole family knows you snapped.

options.text: Say you'll think about it and step away
options.then: She takes that as a yes, and mentions it to your mother.

steps.why: A calm, firm line hears her worry, and still keeps your son safe.

steps.prompt: Your mother calls the next day and says the family is worried for his future. What do you do?

options.text: Say you want his future safe too, and that means backing him
options.then: She is quiet, then says: "I only want him happy."

options.text: Agree to take him for counselling to change him
options.then: She sounds relieved and asks about clinics. Trying to change a child only harms him, and you feel cold.

options.text: Say you'll handle your family, and end the call
options.then: She hangs up hurt. The next call comes from an uncle.

options.text: Ask her to explain it to the other relatives for you
options.then: She agrees, and explains it in her own words, which are not yours.

steps.why: Sharing her goal and holding your ground brings her along, and protects him.

steps.prompt: An uncle says he will "talk some sense" into your son at the next visit. What do you do?

options.text: Say no one lectures your son, and you'll be there throughout
options.then: The uncle grumbles but agrees. Your son hears about it and relaxes.

options.text: Let the uncle try once, since it may satisfy the family
options.then: The uncle takes your son aside. He comes back quiet and won't say what was said.

options.text: Ask the uncle to please be gentle about it
options.then: The uncle says he will be firm but fair. Your son dreads the visit.

options.text: Tell your son to avoid the uncle at the visit
options.then: Your son hides in his room until the uncle leaves.

steps.why: Nobody lectures him, and you stay right there beside him.

steps.prompt: After the visit, your son asks whether the family is angry with him. What do you say?

options.text: Say some relatives are worried, and it's never his fault
options.then: He nods slowly. "Okay. Thanks for saying so."

options.text: Say it is nothing and he shouldn't worry
options.then: He nods, though he can tell something is being hidden.

options.text: Say they will come around if he tones it down
options.then: He looks at his hands, and wonders how much to shrink.

options.text: Say you will sort out the family, and he needn't ask
options.then: He nods, but he keeps checking your face after that.

steps.why: Honesty without blame tells him the worry belongs to them, not to him.

scenarios.debrief: Protect your child from family pressure with a calm, firm boundary.
scenarios.relearn: Hold a calm boundary against family pressure to 'fix' your child.

scenarios.hook: At a clinic, a stranger lectures your distressed child that they "need to choose a side".

steps.prompt: Your child shrinks against you as the stranger goes on. What do you do?

options.text: Step between: "They owe no one an answer. We're fine."
options.then: The stranger sniffs and turns to the magazine rack. Your child grips your hand.

options.text: Ask your child to explain themselves to the stranger
options.then: Your child's voice shakes as they try. The stranger talks over them.

options.text: Ignore the stranger and look at your phone
options.then: The stranger keeps going. Your child looks at you and finds nothing.

options.text: Argue back at the stranger with everything you know
options.then: The stranger gets louder. The receptionist glares. Your child covers their ears.

steps.why: Standing between them and the stranger tells them they owe nobody an answer.

steps.prompt: You move to another seat. Your child whispers and asks whether they have to choose a side. What do you say?

options.text: Say they never have to pick a side, and they're fine as they are
options.then: They breathe out, and lean their head on your arm.

options.text: Say they should probably decide soon so people stop asking
options.then: They chew their lip. Now they feel a clock ticking.

options.text: Say it's a silly thing to worry about
options.then: They nod, but the worry stays where it was.

options.text: Say you'll help them find the right word tonight
options.then: They look at you, and their face tightens. "Tonight?"

steps.why: They owe no one a side. Being fine as they are, with no box, puts them at ease.

steps.prompt: In the car, your child asks what you'll do if a stranger does that again. What do you say?

options.text: Say you'll keep it calm, and ask what they'd like said
options.then: They think. "Just say we're fine. And hold my hand." You promise.

options.text: Promise to stay quiet next time so it's less awkward
options.then: They nod. Next time, they will face the stranger alone.

options.text: Say you'll give the next one a real piece of your mind
options.then: They frown. "But what if it makes it worse?"

options.text: Say they should ignore strangers like that
options.then: They nod. The next stranger hears nothing back.

steps.why: Keeping it calm and asking what helps respects their wish and still protects them.

scenarios.debrief: Put yourself between your child and a stranger's pressure.
scenarios.relearn: Stand between your child and a stranger's pressure; don't make them justify it.

scenarios.hook: Your child's coach quietly suggests benching them "until they sort out the gender thing".

steps.prompt: The coach says it would be easier for the team. What do you say?

options.text: Ask the coach to keep treating your child as a player
options.then: The coach shifts. "I'm just thinking of the team," he says.

options.text: Agree to bench them so it's less awkward for the team
options.then: The coach nods, relieved, and starts planning Saturday without them.

options.text: Say you'll talk to your child and get back to him
options.then: The coach is pleased. Your child hears you were "talking about" them, and worries.

options.text: Say you may just move your child to another team
options.then: The coach nods, unbothered. Your child hears that leaving is on the table.

steps.why: Asking the coach to include your child tells them they belong, not that they are a problem.

steps.prompt: The coach adds that other parents might object. What do you say?

options.text: Say your child's place on the team is not up for debate
options.then: The coach nods slowly and says he will speak to the parents himself.

options.text: Offer to talk to the other parents yourself
options.then: The coach agrees quickly. You would be explaining your child to strangers.

options.text: Say that's fair, and they can play once the parents agree
options.then: The coach says he'll see. Your child waits for a yes that may not come.

options.text: Ask if your child can train separately for now
options.then: Your child trains alone at the back. It feels like a punishment.

steps.why: Their place isn't up for a vote, and it isn't theirs to justify.

steps.prompt: At the next practice, another player mocks your child, who glances over at you. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the coach right then, and stay until it's handled
options.then: The coach stops practice and speaks to the player. Your child stays on the field.

options.text: Wave with a thumbs up and leave it
options.then: Your child plays on alone. The mocking picks up again next drill.

options.text: Confront the other player yourself in the corridor
options.then: The player's parent appears, and you're in an argument. Your child skips practice.

options.text: Signal your child to come off and go home
options.then: Your child leaves the field, and feels they've been sent away.

steps.why: Getting the coach to act at once keeps your child included and protected.

steps.prompt: On the way home, your child asks whether they are the reason for all this trouble. What do you say?

options.text: Say the trouble is other people's behaviour, not them
options.then: They exhale. "Okay. I'm glad you came."

options.text: Say sports teams can be tough on everyone
options.then: They nod slowly, unsure if that was about them.

options.text: Say maybe a different sport would be easier
options.then: They look out the window, wondering if the fault is theirs.

options.text: Say you'll make sure it never happens again
options.then: They believe you, and hide the next incident so you won't worry.

steps.why: The fault lies in how others act, and hearing that from you lifts the weight.

scenarios.debrief: Advocate for your child to stay included, not sidelined for others' comfort.
scenarios.relearn: Advocate to keep your child included; don't accept benching for others' comfort.

scenarios.hook: After a hard day with his cousins, your son is near tears.

steps.prompt: He asks whether you are embarrassed of him. What do you say?

options.text: "Never. I'm proud of you, and I'm sorry today was hard."
options.then: He falls against you. "I thought you were," he whispers.

options.text: "If you stood out less, days like this wouldn't happen."
options.then: He looks away, tears spilling. "So it's my fault."

options.text: "Don't be silly, of course not. Come and eat something."
options.then: He wipes his eyes and nibbles. The question stays unanswered.

options.text: "Some days are just hard. Let's not think about it tonight."
options.then: He nods and goes quiet. He is still not sure.

steps.why: Plain words of pride and comfort answer his real question, and leave no doubt.

steps.prompt: He tells you what a cousin said, and asks whether he should skip family events. What do you say?

options.text: Say he can decide, and you'll be with him at every one
options.then: He is quiet, then says he'd like to come to Diwali if you sit with him.

options.text: Say maybe it's best to skip them for now
options.then: He nods. The next invitation goes unanswered, and so does the one after.

options.text: Say family is family, so he must keep going to them
options.then: He nods and goes cold. He starts dreading every invitation.

options.text: Say you'll tell the cousins to leave him alone
options.then: He panics. "Please don't say anything about me."

steps.why: He chooses, and you go with him. That keeps family from becoming a place he fears.

steps.prompt: Days later, he asks what to say if the cousins tease him again. What do you suggest?

options.text: Practise a short line together, with you nearby
options.then: You try it in the mirror, and he giggles. "Okay. I can say that."

options.text: Tell him to hit back with a sharper joke of his own
options.then: He tries one, and the cousins laugh at him, not with him.

options.text: Tell him to keep well away from those cousins
options.then: He avoids them. They remain a group he isn't part of.

options.text: Tell him it only happens if he lets it upset him
options.then: He tries not to react. It happens anyway, and now he blames himself.

steps.why: A short line he owns, with you nearby, lets him answer without hiding.

scenarios.debrief: When your child asks if you're ashamed, answer with clear pride and warmth.
scenarios.relearn: Answer 'are you embarrassed of me?' with clear pride, never blame.

scenarios.hook: Your son is nervous about wearing his favourite kurta and dupatta to a family lunch.
scenarios.setup: He stands at your door, dressed and unsure.

steps.prompt: Your son says: "Do you think I should wear this? People might say things."

options.text: "Wear what makes you happy, beta. I'll be right beside you."
options.then: He straightens the dupatta. "You'll stay with me?" "The whole time."

options.text: "Maybe pick something plainer, so nobody makes a comment."
options.then: His shoulders sag. He keeps it on, but won't meet your eyes.

options.text: "You look lovely. It's your choice, so you decide."
options.then: He chews his lip. "But what if they're rude?" You have no plan.

options.text: "Wear it, and just ignore any comments."
options.then: He nods, but grips the dupatta tight.

steps.why: Backing his choice and promising to stay close lets him be himself, and safe.

steps.prompt: At the lunch, an aunt looks him up and down and asks: "Oh, what is this outfit?"

options.text: "He chose it himself. Doesn't he look lovely?"
options.then: The aunt blinks, then mumbles: "Hmm, yes, nice colour." He leans into you.

options.text: "It's just for fun. He'll wear normal clothes later."
options.then: The aunt nods, satisfied. He stares at his plate.

options.text: "Please don't comment. Let's just enjoy the lunch."
options.then: The aunt purses her lips. The comment hangs in the air.

options.text: "It's a phase. Kids like to experiment."
options.then: The aunt smiles knowingly. He tugs his dupatta close.

steps.why: A warm, proud answer keeps the moment kind, and shows him you're glad he came.

steps.prompt: Later, your son whispers: "I heard Uncle laugh. Should I change now?"

options.text: "Only if you want to. You look great, and I'm staying."
options.then: He shakes his head. "No. I'll stay like this." He straightens up.

options.text: "Yes, change. It'll make things easier for everyone."
options.then: He goes to change. He doesn't come back to the table smiling.

options.text: "Ignore Uncle. He laughs at everything."
options.then: He nods, but keeps glancing toward Uncle.

options.text: "Let's leave, then. We don't have to stay for this."
options.then: He nods, though he had wanted to play with his cousins.

steps.why: Letting him choose, with you staying close, keeps the day his and keeps him safe.

scenarios.relearn: Backing your child's expression and staying beside him lets him be himself and safe at once, without asking him to shrink.

scenarios.hook: At a family dinner, a relative starts in on your child.
scenarios.setup: Your child is at the table, listening.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "This child just needs more discipline. That's all."

options.text: "We won't discipline who our child is. They're doing fine."
options.then: Uncle frowns. "Hmm. Your house, your rules."

options.text: "You might be right. We'll see what we can do."
options.then: He nods, satisfied. Your child puts down their fork.

options.text: "Let's not talk about this at the table."
options.then: He shrugs and reaches for the roti. Your child's eyes stay on their plate.

options.text: "Please don't say that in front of the child like this."
options.then: He lowers his voice and goes on. "Then we'll talk after dinner."

steps.why: Refusing calmly, with them listening, shows them home is on their side.

steps.prompt: Your uncle presses on: "In my day, a firm hand fixed everything."

options.text: "A firm hand can't change who they are. We won't try."
options.then: He harrumphs, but goes quiet. Your child looks up at you.

options.text: "Times have changed, Uncle. Let's leave it there."
options.then: He grunts. He will bring it up again next visit.

options.text: "Okay, you win. Just finish your dinner, beta."
options.then: Your child hears you give up. They push away their plate.

options.text: "Hmm. Perhaps we could be stricter about some things."
options.then: He nods eagerly. Your child hears it and freezes.

steps.why: Saying plainly that a firm hand can't change who they are closes it kindly.

steps.prompt: After dinner, your child asks softly: "Are you angry they said that about me?"

options.text: "Not with you. I'm sorry you heard it. You're not a problem."
options.then: They lean their head on your shoulder. "Okay," they whisper.

options.text: "Uncle means well. Try not to take it to heart."
options.then: They nod, but the words have already gone in.

options.text: "Let's not talk about it now. Go and brush your teeth, beta."
options.then: They go, and the question follows them upstairs.

options.text: "Maybe try not to upset him next time."
options.then: They stare at their hands. They start editing themselves.

steps.why: Telling them you're not angry with them, and they're not a problem, lifts the weight.

scenarios.relearn: Calmly refusing to 'discipline out' who your child is, with them in the room, shows them home is firmly on their side.

scenarios.hook: Your child tells you a teacher keeps using their old name on purpose.
scenarios.setup: They say it quietly, at the end of the day.

steps.prompt: Your child says: "She does it in front of everyone. I hate that class."

options.text: "Thank you for telling me. I'll talk to the school about it."
options.then: Their shoulders drop. "You will? Thank you."

options.text: "Just let it go. It's not worth a fuss with a teacher."
options.then: They nod. By morning their stomach hurts, and they ask if you'll speak up.

options.text: "Maybe she forgets. Have you reminded her yourself?"
options.then: "Five times," they say. "She says she forgets."

options.text: "Let me march in tomorrow and give that teacher a piece of my mind."
options.then: Your child looks alarmed. "Please, not in front of everyone."

steps.why: Thanking them and offering to act shows their name matters and you will follow through.

steps.prompt: Your child says: "If you speak to the school, please don't tell them everything."

options.text: "Only what you're comfortable with. We'll decide together."
options.then: They relax. "Just my name, and that she should use it."

options.text: "I'll explain everything so they understand properly."
options.then: They go pale. "Please no. That's not yours to tell."

options.text: "I'll say as little as I can, and I won't ask you."
options.then: They nod, but feel left out of their own story.

options.text: "The school probably knows already. I'll just complain."
options.then: They look worried. "What if they don't?"

steps.why: It is their story, so they decide what the school is told.

steps.prompt: At the school office, the principal says: "We'll speak to the teacher. Updating the records may take time."

options.text: "Please ask her today to use the name. The records can follow."
options.then: The principal nods. "I'll speak to her this afternoon."

options.text: "Take the time you need. We'll wait for the records."
options.then: She thanks you. In class the next day the old name is called again.

options.text: "Can you tell the whole staff, so nobody gets it wrong?"
options.then: She frowns. "Everyone would know?" You picture how your child would feel.

options.text: "Fine. Just make sure she doesn't say anything mean."
options.then: She promises, vaguely. The old name is still on the register.

steps.why: Asking for the name to be used now doesn't have to wait for paperwork.

scenarios.relearn: Thanking your child and offering to advocate with the school shows them their name matters and you'll act on it.

scenarios.hook: In a busy market, a stranger stares and mutters at your child, who shrinks beside you.
scenarios.setup: Your child's hand finds yours.

steps.prompt: Your child whispers: "Everyone is looking at me."

options.text: "Eyes on me, beta. You've done nothing wrong. I'm here."
options.then: They breathe out. "Okay," they whisper, gripping your hand.

options.text: "Just keep your head down and walk faster so they stop."
options.then: They hurry along, head low, tears starting.

options.text: "Nobody is looking. Don't be silly."
options.then: "They are," they say, and stop believing your answers.

options.text: "Ignore those people. They're just being rude."
options.then: They nod. They can't stop feeling the stares.

steps.why: Saying they've done nothing wrong, and staying close, steadies them.

steps.prompt: The stranger steps closer and says: "That child needs a good talking-to."

options.text: "We're fine, thank you. Excuse us."
options.then: The man snorts but steps back. Your child leans against your arm.

options.text: "Sorry, sorry. We're just leaving right now."
options.then: He smirks. Your child feels caught doing something wrong.

options.text: "Mind your own business, you nosy old man!"
options.then: He shouts back. A crowd gathers. Your child freezes.

options.text: "They're just going through a phase. That's all."
options.then: He nods, pleased. Your child hears you explain them away.

steps.why: A calm, short reply stops it without a scene or an apology.

steps.prompt: At a chai stall, your child asks quietly: "Why do people stare at me?"

options.text: "Some people don't understand. There's nothing bad in you."
options.then: They think, then lean against you. "So it isn't me that's wrong?"

options.text: "Maybe if you dressed differently, they wouldn't."
options.then: They look down at their clothes and say nothing more.

options.text: "People stare at everybody. It doesn't mean anything."
options.then: They frown. They know it isn't the same.

options.text: "Don't think about it. Just drink your chai."
options.then: They sip. The question stays there, unanswered.

steps.why: An honest answer, with your love, tells them the problem is not them.

scenarios.relearn: Steadying your child and naming that they've done nothing wrong keeps you between them and a stranger's cruelty.

scenarios.hook: Your child has been carrying a worry for weeks, and finally speaks up at bedtime.
scenarios.setup: The light is low.

steps.prompt: Your child asks in a small voice: "Would you still love me if I'm not like the other kids?"

options.text: "Nothing you could be would make me love you any less."
options.then: They look at you. "Really? Nothing at all?"

options.text: "Let's not get into all that now. Of course I love you."
options.then: "Okay," they say, and the worry goes back inside.

options.text: "Of course I do, but why would you ask such a thing?"
options.then: They shrink. "Never mind. Forget I asked."

options.text: "I'll always love you, as long as you're happy and safe."
options.then: They repeat it slowly. "Happy and safe." They wonder what if they're not.

steps.why: A whole, plain answer with no conditions is what a worried child needs to hear.

steps.prompt: Your child asks: "What if other people don't love me like that?"

options.text: "Then they're missing out. I'll always be on your side."
options.then: They nod slowly, trying it on. "Always?" "Always."

options.text: "Everyone will love you. Don't worry about that."
options.then: They frown. They know that isn't always true.

options.text: "You'll have to learn not to care what they think."
options.then: They look down. It sounds like one more thing to do alone.

options.text: "We'll help them understand you, so they can love you."
options.then: They stiffen. Now their safety seems to depend on people they don't trust.

steps.why: Naming that some may not, and promising you'll stay, is honest and steadying.

steps.prompt: Your child whispers: "Can I tell you something else? You can't tell anyone."

options.text: "Yes. It stays between us unless you're in danger. Tell me."
options.then: They take a breath, and begin to tell you.

options.text: "I can't promise that. Parents need to know everything."
options.then: They shake their head. "Then never mind."

options.text: "Of course. I'll only tell your father, and nobody else."
options.then: They go quiet. "Not Papa either," they say.

options.text: "Is it something silly again? Tell me quickly."
options.then: They shrink. "It's fine. Never mind."

steps.why: A clear promise, limited only by safety, keeps the door open.

scenarios.relearn: Answering a worried child with a clear, whole 'nothing changes my love' leaves no doubt that home is unconditionally safe.

scenarios.hook: Your co-parent has been uneasy about your son for weeks.
scenarios.setup: They find you in the kitchen before dinner.

steps.prompt: Your co-parent says: "I'm talking to him tonight. He has to toughen up."

options.text: "Let's not pressure him. Let's work out how we both back him."
options.then: They pause. "Back him how? I don't even know what to do."

options.text: "Fine, do what you think is best. I don't want to argue."
options.then: They nod, and stop in the doorway. "Then I'll talk to him myself."

options.text: "Not tonight. Let's do it later, when we're both calm."
options.then: They agree, annoyed. The plan hasn't gone away.

options.text: "You're being cruel. I'm not letting you near him."
options.then: They bristle. "Cruel? I'm his parent too." The argument gets louder.

steps.why: Inviting them to back him together turns a fight into a shared plan.

steps.prompt: Your co-parent says: "I'm scared people will hurt him. I'd rather he learned to cope."

options.text: "I'm scared too. He copes best knowing we're on his side."
options.then: They exhale. "I hadn't thought of it like that."

options.text: "Nobody will hurt him. You're worrying too much."
options.then: They stiffen. "So my fear is nothing?"

options.text: "Then let's teach him to blend in a little."
options.then: They nod eagerly, relieved. It is your son who would have to blend in.

options.text: "Your fear isn't his to carry. Deal with it yourself."
options.then: They look stung. "I thought we were in this together."

steps.why: Sharing the fear and turning it toward support keeps him from carrying it.

steps.prompt: Your co-parent asks: "So what do we actually say to him? I don't know how to start."

options.text: "Just tell him you love him and you're glad he's yours."
options.then: They nod. Later you hear them in his room. His laugh follows.

options.text: "Let me talk to him. You'd only get it wrong."
options.then: They step back, hurt, and stay out of the room.

options.text: "Ask him straight out if he's gay, and listen."
options.then: They march in. He goes pale and tells them nothing.

options.text: "Let's say nothing. It'll blow over."
options.then: They agree. Weeks pass in silence, and he wonders what they think of him.

steps.why: A simple I-love-you needs no label and no speech, and it starts the trust.

scenarios.relearn: Inviting a co-parent to back the child together, instead of pressuring him, keeps both parents as safe ground.

scenarios.hook: Your child's friend, who is also gender-diverse, is over for the first time.
scenarios.setup: They stand by the door, wary of you.

steps.prompt: The friend says: "Hi, aunty. Is it okay that I'm here?"

options.text: "You're always welcome here. What do you two like to eat?"
options.then: The friend's shoulders drop. "Anything with cheese," they say, smiling.

options.text: "You can stay, but no funny business, and the door stays open."
options.then: The friend nods, stiff. Your child looks mortified.

options.text: "Of course. Do your parents know you're here?"
options.then: The friend hesitates. "They know I'm at a friend's." They look uneasy.

options.text: "Sure, sit anywhere. I'll leave you kids alone."
options.then: The friend sits on the edge of the sofa, still watching you.

steps.why: A warm welcome, with something they'd like, tells them they're safe here.

steps.prompt: The friend says: "My family uses a different name for me. Can you call me Zoya?"

options.text: "Of course, Zoya. Thank you for telling me."
options.then: Zoya smiles properly for the first time. "Thank you, aunty."

options.text: "Sure, but I'll have to use the other name in front of others."
options.then: Zoya nods, but the smile flickers.

options.text: "Sure. Should I ask your mother what she thinks?"
options.then: Zoya goes rigid. "Please, no. Don't tell her anything."

options.text: "That's a lovely name. Is it just for now?"
options.then: Zoya shrugs. "I don't know." The question sits heavy.

steps.why: Using the name they asked for, without questions, makes them feel safe.

steps.prompt: Zoya asks: "Will you tell my parents that I told you this?"

options.text: "No. It's yours to tell. You're safe here."
options.then: Zoya's eyes fill. "Thank you. I really needed to hear that."

options.text: "I won't, unless they ask me directly."
options.then: Zoya frowns. "But what if they ask?" Zoya looks uneasy.

options.text: "I think they should know. I'd be happy to tell them."
options.then: Zoya goes pale. "Please don't."

options.text: "I'll say nothing, but you should tell them soon."
options.then: Zoya nods, though soon sounds like a deadline.

steps.why: Their story is theirs to tell, and your promise keeps this a safe place.

scenarios.relearn: A warm welcome to your child's friend tells your child the people and world they love are safe and respected in your home.

scenarios.hook: You slipped and used your child's old pronoun at the table.
scenarios.setup: Everyone heard it, and your child went quiet.

steps.prompt: Your child looks up and says quietly: "That was the wrong pronoun, Papa."

options.text: "Sorry, I meant 'she'. I'm still practising."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. Thanks." She picks up her fork again.

options.text: "Ugh, sorry. This is so hard for me. Please be patient."
options.then: She says it's okay, and starts comforting you instead.

options.text: "It's a lifelong habit. It will take me time."
options.then: She looks down. "Okay," she says quietly.

options.text: "Let's not make a big thing of it at the table."
options.then: She goes quiet. Your brother snorts into his dal.

steps.why: A short sorry and a promise to practise keeps the moment yours to carry.

steps.prompt: Your brother says: "Why the fuss? It's just a word."

options.text: "It matters to her, so it matters to me."
options.then: Your brother shrugs but says no more. She glances at you gratefully.

options.text: "You're right. I don't want to make a fuss."
options.then: The table relaxes. She keeps her eyes on her plate.

options.text: "Let's talk about this some other time."
options.then: He shrugs. She notices you dropped it.

options.text: "You obviously don't understand. It's not just a word!"
options.then: He rolls his eyes and the mood sours. She squirms.

steps.why: Saying it matters to her tells everyone you're on her side, without a debate.

steps.prompt: Later she says: "Papa, sometimes it feels like I'm the one looking after you."

options.text: "Thanks for telling me. I'll talk to a friend instead."
options.then: She smiles a little. "That helps. Thanks, Papa."

options.text: "I'm doing my best. It's hard for me too."
options.then: She nods, but stops telling you things.

options.text: "You know I love you. That's what matters."
options.then: She nods. The feeling stays where it was.

options.text: "Don't worry about me. Just let my slips go."
options.then: She tries, but each slip still stings, and now she can't say so.

steps.why: Your feelings are yours to work through with another adult, not your child.

scenarios.relearn: Repairing a pronoun slip with a quick sorry and a promise to practise keeps the moment yours to carry, not your child's.

scenarios.hook: It is late and you are overwhelmed. You want to talk to someone tonight.

steps.prompt: Your child is asleep, and you can't stop your thoughts. What do you do?

options.text: Call Tele-MANAS 14416 and say you need to talk
options.then: A calm voice listens and helps you breathe. They say you can call again any night you need.

options.text: Lie awake and go over it again and again for hours
options.then: The clock reads 3 a.m. The thoughts are just as loud.

options.text: Post your worry in a big online forum
options.then: Strangers reply with loud opinions. One tells you to fix it.

options.text: Wake your spouse and argue about what to do
options.then: Your spouse is groggy and defensive. Nothing gets settled.

steps.why: A free, trained line can steady you tonight, so the worry stops looping.

steps.prompt: Days later, you ring Tele-MANAS 14416, and a counsellor asks what is on your mind. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're a parent who wants to support your child
options.then: "Thank you for calling," they say. "Tell me more."

options.text: Say it's nothing, and apologise for calling
options.then: "No need to apologise," they say gently. You almost hang up.

options.text: Ask them to tell you how to change your child
options.then: They say they can't help with that, but can talk about supporting you.

options.text: Give your child's full name, school and home address
options.then: They gently say you can get help without sharing all of that.

steps.why: Saying you want to support your child opens the right kind of help.

steps.prompt: The counsellor suggests a parents' group in your city. What do you do the next day?

options.text: Look up the group and ask about a first meeting

options.text: Decide you're fine now and let the whole thing go

options.text: Wait until you feel completely ready to make contact
