options.text: Ask your child to come along for support
options.then: Your child looks puzzled. "It's your group, isn't it?"

steps.why: A small next step turns one good night into steady support.

scenarios.debrief: You don't have to carry a heavy night alone; a trained voice on a free line can help.
scenarios.relearn: On a heavy night, a free line like Tele-MANAS 14416 can steady you.

scenarios.hook: You found a counsellor, but you aren't sure they will be affirming.

steps.prompt: Their website is warm but never mentions gender-diverse children. What do you do?

options.text: Ask up front if they support gender-diverse children
options.then: They reply the same day, warmly, but only say they welcome all families.

options.text: Book and hope they're fine
options.then: You book. Nothing tells you how they will treat your child.

options.text: Use whoever a relative recommends
options.then: Your relative's pick lists "family values coaching". You wonder what that means.

options.text: Read the reviews and decide from the star rating
options.then: Five stars, but not one review says anything about this.

steps.why: Asking up front starts your check on them, before you trust them.

steps.prompt: A line on their page says: "I help families find balance." It isn't clear what that means. What do you do?

options.text: Ask plainly if they ever try to change a child's identity
options.then: They answer directly: no, they support the child as they are.

options.text: Take it as a yes and go ahead
options.then: You book a first call, still unsure what "balance" means.

options.text: Ask a friend if they have heard good things about them
options.then: Your friend says they are very nice. That tells you nothing about their approach.

options.text: Read more of their site for a clue about what balance means
options.then: The other pages are warm and vague. You still don't know their approach.

steps.why: A plain question gets a plain answer, and a safe counsellor gives one.

steps.prompt: On the first call, the counsellor asks about your child. What do you share?

options.text: Share only what's needed, and say your child's story is theirs
options.then: They nod, and turn the talk to how you are coping.

options.text: Share your child's private details so they can help
options.then: You realise you have told a stranger things your child hasn't told anyone.

options.text: Refuse to say anything about your child
options.then: The call is short and awkward. You have gained nothing.

options.text: Ask them to talk to your child first
options.then: They suggest meeting you first. You feel your plan being set aside.

steps.why: Sharing only what's needed protects your child's privacy, and still gets you real guidance.

steps.prompt: After three sessions, your co-parent asks if the counsellor is worth the money. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes, and invite them to join the next session
options.then: They hesitate, then agree to come once, to listen.

options.text: Say it's fine and they needn't know more
options.then: They shrug and leave. They stay out of it.

options.text: Say it isn't worth it and you'll stop
options.then: You stop. The old questions come back within a fortnight.

options.text: Say the counsellor thinks you're doing everything right
options.then: They nod, and stop asking. You haven't discussed a single change.

steps.why: Inviting your co-parent in lets you both learn together, and neither carries it alone.

scenarios.debrief: Ask plainly, and ask again when the answer is vague: that screens for a safe, affirming counsellor.
scenarios.relearn: Ask plainly, and press when the answer is vague, to screen for a safe, affirming counsellor.

scenarios.hook: A relative insists on a clinic that promises to "cure" your child.

steps.prompt: Your uncle has already booked an appointment for Saturday. What do you do?

options.text: Decline calmly and say you're finding affirming support
options.then: He argues for a bit, then goes quiet when you don't budge.

options.text: Go just once to keep the peace in the whole family
options.then: Your uncle beams and confirms Saturday. Your stomach turns.

options.text: Let your uncle handle the whole thing on your behalf
options.then: He takes charge of the calls. Your child is now part of a plan you didn't make.

options.text: Ask for a few more days to think it over carefully
options.then: He agrees, and calls every day to check.

steps.why: Calmly declining, with a better plan, protects your child from a harmful approach.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says the clinic has many happy families and shows you a brochure. What do you do?

options.text: Hand it back and say you won't try to change your child
options.then: He frowns at the brochure, but takes it back.

options.text: Read it to be polite, and say you'll think about it
options.then: You skim promises of change. He takes your reading as interest.

options.text: Ask for the names of some of those happy families
options.then: He gives you two numbers. Now you are debating results, not your child.

options.text: Throw the brochure away, angry at being pressed
options.then: He gasps, and tells the others you were rude.

steps.why: Handing it back plainly shows you're not open to it, without a fight.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says the clinic is "only counselling" and very gentle. What do you do?

options.text: Say anything aiming to change a child is not counselling
options.then: She hesitates. "I hadn't thought of it that way," she says.

options.text: Ask if it might help your child a little bit anyway
options.then: She jumps in, and your uncle nods. You have left a door open.

options.text: Ask the clinic to keep the sessions very light and short
options.then: She beams and rings the clinic. The word "light" will not change what they do.

options.text: Change the subject to lunch and hope it all passes soon
options.then: Lunch comes, but the topic stays on the table.

steps.why: Naming that changing a child is the aim shows why "gentle" is beside the point.

steps.prompt: Your child asks if the clinic is because something is wrong with them. What do you say?

options.text: Say nothing is wrong with them, and they are not going to any clinic
options.then: They tear up. "Really?" "Really," you say.

options.text: Say it's just a visit to check that they're okay
options.then: They hear "check", and look worried.

options.text: Say you don't know yet, but you'll decide very soon
options.then: They nod. Waiting, they start bracing.

options.text: Say it's the family's wish, and not really yours
options.then: They realise their family wants them changed, and pull away.

steps.why: They need to hear that nothing is wrong with them, and no clinic will try to change them.

steps.prompt: A friend suggests a parents' group instead, but your uncle says a group "won't fix anything". What do you say?

options.text: Say there is nothing to fix, and you are joining the group
options.then: He grumbles. You go, and find other parents who understand.

options.text: Say you'll do both, to keep everyone happy
options.then: You are pulled two ways, and your child feels it.

options.text: Say you'll try the group for a month, to prove it helps
options.then: He nods. "Then we'll see the results." Now the group has to show a change.

options.text: Say you'll skip both for now and see
options.then: The pressure eases briefly, then returns. You are still alone with it.

steps.why: A parents' group gives real support, with nothing to fix and no cure to bargain with.

scenarios.debrief: 'Cure' clinics are discredited and harmful; decline and choose affirming support.
scenarios.relearn: 'Cure' clinics are harmful; decline them and choose affirming support.

scenarios.hook: You want a counsellor's guidance, but worry the intake form could out your child.

steps.prompt: The clinic's form asks for your child's name, school and "presenting issue". What do you do?

options.text: Ask for guidance for yourself, sharing what you choose
options.then: The receptionist says a parent-only booking is fine.

options.text: Skip help entirely, and close the form for good
options.then: You close the form. A week on, the worry is still there, so you ring the clinic.

options.text: Fill in every single detail so you seem thorough
options.then: You submit it. Then you wonder who will read it.

options.text: Have your spouse fill it in for you this evening
options.then: Your spouse writes more than you would have. You call the clinic to correct it.

steps.why: You can get guidance for yourself, and leave your child's identity off the paper.

steps.prompt: When you call to confirm, the receptionist says the counsellor keeps notes on every family. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what is written, who sees it, and how it's stored
options.then: She explains it stays with the counsellor, and that you can see the notes.

options.text: Accept it, since they know their own process best
options.then: Later you wonder what was written down.

options.text: Make up details so the notes say nothing real
options.then: You end up trying to remember what you said.

options.text: Hang up, since the whole thing feels risky
options.then: You hang up. Two days later the worry wins, and you keep the booking.

steps.why: Asking how records are kept lets you choose what to share.

steps.prompt: In the first session, the counsellor asks about your child's daily life. What do you share?

options.text: Share what helps you, and keep their private details out
options.then: The counsellor nods and turns to your own questions.

options.text: Share everything your child has told you in confidence
options.then: You feel lighter at first, then uneasy that the story wasn't yours.

options.text: Share nothing and ask for general advice only
options.then: The advice is general, and doesn't quite fit.

options.text: Ask to bring your child in to explain it themselves
options.then: The counsellor says that should be your child's choice, not yours.

steps.why: Sharing what helps you keeps your child's confidences theirs.

steps.prompt: A friend asks why you've been going out on Thursdays. What do you tell her?

options.text: Say it's parenting guidance for you, nothing more
options.then: She nods. "Good for you." She doesn't ask more.

options.text: Tell her all about your child and everything so far
options.then: She is kind, but now she knows what your child hasn't shared.

options.text: Make up a story about a Thursday gym class you joined
options.then: She invites you to the gym next Thursday. You are cornered.

options.text: Say it's a secret, and leave it at that for now
options.then: She is curious and asks others. The mystery grows.

steps.why: Naming the support without your child's story keeps both privacy and honesty.

scenarios.debrief: You can get guidance while keeping your child's identity private.
scenarios.relearn: You can get a counsellor's guidance while keeping your child's identity private.

scenarios.hook: You are ready to learn, but your co-parent is scared to seek any help.

steps.prompt: Your co-parent says only weak parents need help. What do you do?

options.text: Invite them to listen to a helpline call with you
options.then: They shrug. "Listening isn't the same as agreeing," they say.

options.text: Tell them they're a bad parent for thinking that
options.then: They snap back and leave the room. The door closes.

options.text: Go silent and do nothing about it for a while
options.then: The weeks pass, and the distance between you grows.

options.text: Go ahead alone and tell them nothing about it
options.then: You call in secret. They find out later and feel left out.

steps.why: A no-pressure invitation gives them a way in, where shame only makes them shut down.

steps.prompt: Some time later, your co-parent says they might listen in on a helpline call, but won't speak. What do you do?

options.text: Agree, and let them just listen while you talk
options.then: You call Tele-MANAS 14416 together. They listen, and nod once.

options.text: Insist they speak too, or it won't count
options.then: They fold their arms. It takes another week before they agree to only listen.

options.text: Put it off until they're more comfortable
options.then: Weeks pass. Eventually they say they're ready, and you make the call.

options.text: Call without warning, so they overhear by accident
options.then: They feel tricked. "You planned this," they say, but they stay on the line.

steps.why: Letting them just listen is a real first step, and it costs them nothing.

steps.prompt: After the call, your co-parent says it wasn't as bad as they thought. What do you do?

options.text: Thank them, and ask what stayed with them
options.then: They mention one line about love mattering most. You both sit with that.

options.text: Say you told them it would not be so bad
options.then: They stiffen. "Fine. I'll go back to my phone."

options.text: Immediately book a counselling session for them
options.then: They tense. "I said not bad. I didn't say yes."

options.text: Say nothing and let the moment quietly pass by
options.then: They go back to the TV. The door is open, but nobody has pushed it.

steps.why: Thanking them, and asking what stayed with them, builds on a good first step.

scenarios.debrief: Invite a hesitant co-parent to a first small step; shame doesn't move anyone.
scenarios.relearn: Invite a hesitant co-parent to a first small step; shared learning moves you both.

scenarios.hook: You fear your child may be in danger from a relative, and you are frightened.

steps.prompt: Your child flinches whenever that relative's name comes up. What do you do?

options.text: Keep your child away from the relative, and stay close
options.then: Your child watches you carefully, and their shoulders loosen a little.

options.text: Wait and watch to see what happens over the weekend
options.then: The relative visits on Sunday. Your child hides in the bathroom.

options.text: Confront the relative alone tonight, before it gets worse
options.then: The relative denies everything and shouts. Your child hears it all.

options.text: Tell yourself you're imagining it and it will pass
options.then: You put it aside. The flinch happens again the next week.

steps.why: Keeping your child away from the relative first is the simplest protection.

steps.prompt: Your child says quietly that the relative made them promise to keep a secret. What do you do?

options.text: Say: "I'm glad you told me. This is not your fault."
options.then: Your child's eyes fill. They lean into you.

options.text: Ask for every detail, right now
options.then: They shut down. "I don't want to say," they whisper.

options.text: Tell them to forget it, since the relative is family
options.then: They stop looking at you. The secret is heavier now.

options.text: Promise to keep it a secret from everyone
options.then: They relax, but it is a promise you can't keep safely.

steps.why: Believing them and saying it is not their fault keeps them safe, and talking to you.

steps.prompt: Your child says the relative is coming to stay tonight. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the relative not to come, and call crisis 112 if they do
options.then: You message that tonight is off. Your child stays by your side all evening.

options.text: Let the relative stay just this once
options.then: The relative arrives. Your child won't leave your side, and neither of you sleeps.

options.text: Send the relative an angry message about what you suspect
options.then: The relative denies it and warns others that you are making trouble.

options.text: Ask another relative to keep an eye on things
options.then: They agree, but sleep through the night. Your child sits awake.

steps.why: Keeping the relative away and your child close is the safe move. In immediate danger, call crisis 112.

steps.prompt: Once things are calmer, you want a clear plan for your child's ongoing safety. What do you do?

options.text: Use the Be the Safe Adult guidance to make a safety plan
options.then: The guide lists steps you can take today, one at a time.

options.text: Rely on the relative promising it won't happen again
options.then: The relative promises. Your child stops sleeping properly.

options.text: Wait for your child to bring it up again
options.then: You wait, with no plan. Days later, your child comes to you, worried.

options.text: Tell everyone in the family so someone will act
options.then: The family splits. Your child hears their story repeated in the hall.

steps.why: A clear safety plan keeps your child protected, and doesn't spread their story.

steps.prompt: Your child asks if they will get in trouble for telling. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're proud they told you, and it isn't their fault
options.then: They breathe out a long breath, and hold your hand.

options.text: Say it depends on what the family decides
options.then: They stiffen. Now telling feels dangerous.

options.text: Say you'll try to keep it from getting them in trouble
options.then: They frown. "Try?" they ask.

options.text: Say it's best not to talk about it now
options.then: They nod, and don't bring it up again.

steps.why: Saying it isn't their fault, and thanking them, tells them telling was safe.

scenarios.debrief: For immediate danger, crisis 112 reaches help; Be the Safe Adult covers ongoing safety.
scenarios.relearn: In danger, crisis 112 reaches emergency help; Be the Safe Adult covers ongoing safety.

scenarios.hook: You are torn between a "cure" camp a neighbour praised and an unfamiliar parents' group.

steps.prompt: Your neighbour hands you the camp's brochure and says it changed her nephew. What do you do?

options.text: Say no to the camp, and try the parents' group
options.then: She looks unsure, but wishes you luck.

options.text: Try the camp, since she vouches for it
options.then: The brochure promises change in a month. Your stomach knots.

options.text: Do neither, and stay on your own with the worry
options.then: Weekends pass with your worry unchanged.

options.text: Visit both and compare them side by side
options.then: The camp visit leaves your child anxious about what you are thinking.

steps.why: A parents' group gives you real allies, and a camp that promises change harms.

steps.prompt: You finally reach a parents' group, where a parent asks how you are doing. You have never said it aloud. What do you do?

options.text: Say honestly that you're scared and want to learn
options.then: Heads nod. Someone says: "We were all there."

options.text: Say everything is fine, to seem strong
options.then: The group moves on. You leave with the same worry.

options.text: Say your child is just going through a phase
options.then: They wait kindly. You hear yourself say it, and wince.

options.text: Say the neighbour's camp might be the answer
options.then: A parent gently says it harmed their own child. You go quiet.

steps.why: Saying you're scared aloud lets others help, and shows you are not alone.

steps.prompt: The neighbour asks if your child will be going to the camp this term. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're not doing it, and thank her for caring
options.then: She frowns. "You'll wonder what could have been," she says, and lets it drop.

options.text: Say you're still thinking it over, and will let her know
options.then: She smiles and starts sending you dates.

options.text: Say your child probably wouldn't like it there
options.then: She says they'd get used to it. The talk shifts to your child.

options.text: Avoid her for the next few weeks and hope she forgets
options.then: She finds you at the gate anyway.

steps.why: A clear, kind no ends the pressure sooner than avoiding her.

steps.prompt: Your child asks why you go out on Thursday evenings. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're learning how to support them better
options.then: They light up. "Can I tell you what would help?"

options.text: Say it's something to do with work
options.then: They nod, but sense something is being kept from them.

options.text: Say you're going to sort things out
options.then: They wonder what needs sorting. Their shoulders tighten.

options.text: Say it's a grown-up matter, so don't ask
options.then: They shrug. The distance stays.

steps.why: Telling them you are learning to support them shows love, and invites them in.

scenarios.debrief: A 'cure' camp harms however warmly it's praised; parents who've been there are real help.
scenarios.relearn: Choose affirming peers over any 'cure'; a group helps, a 'cure' camp harms.

scenarios.hook: Your child has seemed low since the new term began at school.

steps.prompt: They finally tell you that classmates laugh at how they dress. What do you do?

options.text: Listen, then ask the school to stop the teasing
options.then: Your child nods slowly. "Okay. Will they ask me lots of things?"

options.text: Tell them to blend in with everyone else
options.then: They nod, and put their favourite shirt at the bottom of the drawer.

options.text: Assume the other kids will sort it out
options.then: The laughing carries on for another month.

options.text: Buy them new clothes that the others would like
options.then: They wear the new clothes. They stop looking in the mirror.

steps.why: The teasing is the problem, not the clothes, so bring the school in.

steps.prompt: At the parent-teacher meeting, the teacher says: "Kids tease whoever stands out. Maybe they could stand out less." What do you say?

options.text: Say the aim is to stop the teasing, and ask for a plan
options.then: She nods slowly. "Let me speak to the class this week."

options.text: Agree, and take that advice home to your child
options.then: You tell your child to dress like the others. They fold up.

options.text: Say you'll think about it, and leave it there
options.then: She looks relieved. Nothing changes in class.

options.text: Ask for your child to be moved to another class
options.then: She says that isn't possible, and your child would lose their friends.

steps.why: Keeping the focus on the teasing, not the clothes, puts the responsibility where it belongs.

steps.prompt: A few weeks on, your child asks if they can wear what they like to school. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's theirs to choose, and you'll keep an eye out
options.then: They put on their favourite shirt the next morning.

options.text: Say to wait a whole term until things calm down
options.then: They nod, and the shirt stays in the drawer.

options.text: Say it's up to them and you'd rather not know about it
options.then: They shrug. They stop mentioning school.

options.text: Say only on weekends, just to be on the safe side
options.then: They agree. Monday mornings feel like putting on a costume.

steps.why: They keep the choice, and you keep watch. That protects them without asking them to hide.

scenarios.hook: You have dialled Tele-MANAS 14416, and someone has answered.
scenarios.setup: Your voice shakes a little.

steps.prompt: A voice says: "Tele-MANAS. How can I help?"

options.text: "I'm a parent, and I want to learn to support my child well."
options.then: "Of course," the voice says warmly. "I'm glad you called."

options.text: "Um, sorry, I shouldn't be calling. Never mind."
options.then: "Please don't hang up," the voice says. "You're welcome here."

options.text: "I'm calling for a friend, not for myself."
options.then: "That's fine," the voice says. "You can talk about yourself too."

options.text: "My child has a problem, and I need it fixed."
options.then: "I hear how worried you are," the voice says. "Tell me what you've noticed."

steps.why: Saying you want to learn to support your child sets the right tone from the first words.

steps.prompt: The voice asks: "Can you tell me a little about what's worrying you?"

options.text: "I'm scared. I don't fully understand, but I want to protect my child."
options.then: "Thank you for saying that," the voice says. "Go on."

options.text: "Mostly what the relatives will say if they find out."
options.then: "That's a common worry," the voice says. "What about your child?"

options.text: "I just need to know what to do to make it go away."
options.then: The voice pauses. "You sound frightened. Let's talk about what you're feeling."

options.text: "Let me tell you my child's name, school and all the details."
options.then: "You don't need to share those to get help," the voice says kindly.

steps.why: Sharing your fear honestly lets the counsellor help you, and you can keep details private.

steps.prompt: The voice asks: "Would it help to talk again, or to join a parents' group?"

options.text: "Yes, both please. What is the next step?"
options.then: The voice explains how to call back and find a group.

options.text: "Maybe. I'll think about it and call back."
options.then: "Of course," the voice says. "Call whenever you're ready."

options.text: "No thanks. I feel better now. I'm fine."
options.then: "I'm glad," the voice says. "We're here if the worry comes back."

options.text: "Can I just have a leaflet with instructions instead?"
options.then: The voice explains that talking or a group would go further than a leaflet.

steps.why: Saying yes to a next step turns one good call into steady support.

steps.prompt: Your child overhears the end of the call and asks: "Who were you talking to?"

options.text: "Someone who's helping me learn to support you better."
options.then: They look at you for a moment. "Thank you," they say.

options.text: "Just a work call. Nothing to worry about."
options.then: They nod, but sense it wasn't work.

options.text: "A helpline. I was so worried about you."
options.then: They look stricken. "Because of me?"

options.text: "Someone who says we can fix things. It'll be okay."
options.then: They freeze. "Fix what?"

steps.why: Telling them you called to support them shows love, and keeps your worry off their shoulders.

scenarios.relearn: A simple 'I want to learn to support my child' opens the right, affirming kind of help.

scenarios.hook: On a first call with a possible counsellor, you want to know if they are affirming.
scenarios.setup: She has just picked up.

steps.prompt: The counsellor says: "Hello, thanks for calling. Tell me what brings you."

options.text: "Before we begin, do you support gender-diverse children as they are?"
options.then: "Yes," she says. "Every child is welcome here."

options.text: "So, um, can you maybe help with, you know, this kind of thing?"
options.then: "Which kind of thing?" she asks. You still haven't asked what you need.

options.text: "I'll just tell you what's going on and see what you say."
options.then: You talk for ten minutes. You still don't know her approach.

options.text: "My child is confused and needs sorting out."
options.then: She pauses. "Tell me more about what you mean." Her tone gives nothing away.

steps.why: One direct question at the start tells you whether they are safe to trust.

steps.prompt: The counsellor says: "I work with the whole family to find balance."

options.text: "Do you ever try to change how a child sees themselves?"
options.then: "Never," she says. "I support the child as they are."

options.text: "That sounds good. Balance is what we need."
options.then: She agrees warmly. You realise you never learned what she meant.

options.text: "Fine. I'm sure you'll do what's best."
options.then: She thanks you. The question sits unasked.

options.text: "Can you help my child fit in better at school?"
options.then: She says she can talk about school stress. The real question is still open.

steps.why: A vague answer needs a plain follow-up. A safe counsellor answers straight.

steps.prompt: She asks: "May I speak with your child directly in the first session?"

options.text: "Let's begin with just me. My child can choose later."
options.then: "Of course," she says. "We'll go at your child's pace."

options.text: "Yes, book them in. They need to hear from an expert."
options.then: She notes it down. Your child knows nothing of this yet.

options.text: "Only if you promise to tell me everything they say."
options.then: She explains she keeps sessions private, and your face falls.

options.text: "No, never. I don't want my child near a counsellor."
options.then: She accepts it, but the call ends short and stiff.

steps.why: Starting with you and letting your child choose later respects their pace and privacy.

steps.prompt: At the end she asks: "Would you like to book a session for yourself?"

options.text: "Yes please. Thank you for taking my call."
options.then: "Anytime," she says. "Next Tuesday at five?"

options.text: "Let me think about it and get back to you."
options.then: "Of course," she says. The next few days pass without a plan.

options.text: "Yes. Book my child in for the same day."
options.then: She says she'll wait for your child's own wish. You feel let down.

options.text: "Maybe. But first, will you speak to my in-laws about this?"
options.then: She says she can meet family later, with your child's consent.

steps.why: Booking for yourself gets you real support now, and your child can join in their own time.

scenarios.relearn: Asking 'do you support gender-diverse children as they are?' screens for a safe, affirming counsellor.

scenarios.hook: A relative is pressing a "cure" clinic on you over chai.
scenarios.setup: Everyone else has gone quiet.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "Just try the clinic once. What's the harm?"

options.text: "There's nothing to cure. I'm finding him affirming support."
options.then: Your aunt stares into her cup. "Hmm. As you wish."

options.text: "Maybe. We'll see. I don't want to upset anyone."
options.then: She smiles, sure she has won. She asks for a date.

options.text: "Fine, one visit, to keep everyone happy."
options.then: She calls the clinic on the spot. Your son, listening, goes still.

options.text: "You have no right to say that about my son."
options.then: The room freezes. Your aunt puts down her cup, offended.

steps.why: A clear, kind no with a better plan closes the door without a fight.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "Other families have seen real results, you know."

options.text: "I'm his mother. He's fine as he is, and I won't change him."
options.then: Your aunt is silent, then says: "You're very sure."

options.text: "Show me the results and I'll think again."
options.then: She reaches for her phone. Now you are arguing results, not your son.

options.text: "You may be right. I'm just so tired of arguing."
options.then: She takes your tiredness as a yes. She begins to plan.

options.text: "Those families must be desperate. I feel sorry for them."
options.then: Her face hardens. "Some of them are our friends."

steps.why: Answering as his parent, plainly, is firm without arguing over results.

steps.prompt: Your uncle joins in: "The clinic is respected. Even doctors send people."

options.text: "Anything that promises to change him harms him. We're done."
options.then: He frowns, sees the others aren't backing him, and looks away.

options.text: "Let's not fight over chai. We can talk another day."
options.then: Your uncle shrugs. "Another day, then," he says, clearly not done.

options.text: "If doctors say so, maybe I should look at it properly."
options.then: He beams and produces a business card.

options.text: "You two are being cruel. I can't talk to you anymore."
options.then: You walk out. The two of them say your son is being spoilt.

steps.why: Naming that a cure harms your son ends the argument. You needn't debate results with your uncle.

steps.prompt: On your way out, your aunt whispers: "I only want what's best for him."

options.text: "So do I, Aunty. No clinic, but come to lunch on Sunday."
options.then: She laughs unsteadily. "Lunch, then. I'll bring sweets."

options.text: "Okay, Aunty. I'll think about the clinic again."
options.then: She nods, triumphant. You have opened a door you meant to shut.

options.text: "I know. Please just drop it now. I'm tired."
options.then: She purses her lips. The pressure eases, and the distance grows.

options.text: "You'll see I'm right when he's happy."
options.then: She shrugs. Her next call is about the clinic again.

steps.why: Keeping the relationship warm while holding your line leaves room for her to change.

scenarios.relearn: A clear 'There's nothing to cure. I'm finding him affirming support' declines a 'cure' with love.

scenarios.hook: You called a counsellor's office, and the receptionist asks for a lot of detail about your child.
scenarios.setup: You can hear her typing.

steps.prompt: The receptionist says: "Please describe the problem so we can book the right person."

options.text: "I'd like guidance as a parent. I'll share what's relevant later."
options.then: "Certainly," she says. "I'll book you a parent appointment."

options.text: "Sure. Let me tell you everything that's been going on."
options.then: She writes down all you say about your child. You feel uneasy.

options.text: "It's a bit embarrassing. Can we skip that part?"
options.then: "We need something," she says. You end up giving details anyway.

options.text: "Let me put someone from home on. They'll explain."
options.then: Someone from home takes over and says more than you would.

steps.why: Asking for parent guidance gets you help without handing over your child's story.

steps.prompt: She says: "Now, for our records, we'll need your child's name and school."

options.text: "Please book me alone for now. Details can wait."
options.then: "That's fine," she says. "I'll note the booking under your name."

options.text: "Fine, I'll spell my child's name and school for you."
options.then: She types it all in. You wonder who else will read it.

options.text: "Their name is fine, but I won't give the school."
options.then: She notes the name. You have still given a name that isn't yours to give.

options.text: "Can I just email you the details later instead?"
options.then: She says yes, and you are left with a form and a deadline.

steps.why: Booking for yourself first lets your child decide what is shared, and when.

steps.prompt: She says: "Our notes may sometimes be shared with other professionals, if needed."

options.text: "Please don't share anything without asking me."
options.then: "Understood," she says. "I'll add that to your file."

options.text: "That's fine. Do whatever is normal for you."
options.then: She thanks you. You will never quite know who has what.

options.text: "Then I'd rather cancel and not come at all."
options.then: She apologises, and you are left without help.

options.text: "Share what you need to, as long as it helps."
options.then: She writes "consent given", and you realise you never asked what that covers.

steps.why: Asking to be consulted first keeps the choice with you and your child, not the office.

scenarios.relearn: Asking for guidance for yourself, sharing what's relevant, gets help while keeping your child's story theirs.

scenarios.hook: Your co-parent is scared to seek help, and you want to ask, not push.
scenarios.setup: They are on the sofa, scrolling.

steps.prompt: Your co-parent says without looking up: "If I go to a helpline, it means I've failed."

options.text: "What if we listened together this week? No pressure, side by side."
options.then: They look up. "Just listening? Not talking?"

options.text: "You clearly don't care enough to try, so I'll just do it alone."
options.then: They set the phone down hard. "That's not fair."

options.text: "You've failed if you don't go, so go."
options.then: They stiffen and turn the TV up.

options.text: "It's okay. Forget I asked."
options.then: They relax, and the room goes quiet. The subject slips away.

steps.why: A no-pressure invitation to listen together gives them a safe way in.

steps.prompt: Later they say: "What if they judge us? What if they say it's our fault?"

options.text: "It's no one's fault. These lines are for parents like us."
options.then: They breathe out. "Okay. That helps a bit."

options.text: "Stop worrying. You always expect the worst."
options.then: They pull back. "You don't get to tell me what to feel."

options.text: "If they judge us, we'll just leave."
options.then: They nod, but now the call sounds like a test.

options.text: "You're being ridiculous. Everyone calls these lines."
options.then: They flush, and the shame sharpens.

steps.why: Saying it's no one's fault, and that these lines are for parents like you, eases the fear.

steps.prompt: Another day, they ask: "What do we say when we call?"

options.text: "That we're parents who want to support our child."
options.then: They nod. "That's true, at least. I can say that."

options.text: "Leave it to me. I'll do all the talking."
options.then: They sit back, relieved. You end up doing it alone in effect.

options.text: "We'll ask them what we should do to stop this."
options.then: They nod, but the question tastes wrong even to them.

options.text: "We don't need to prepare. We'll figure it out."
options.then: They shrug. "Fine. We'll just dial and see."

steps.why: A simple, honest line is enough to open the right kind of help.

steps.prompt: After the call they say: "I felt better than I expected. Can we do it again?"

options.text: "Yes. Let's pick a time each week, at your pace."
options.then: They nod. "Thursday evenings? I'll clear the diary."

options.text: "Great. Now we can tell the whole family together."
options.then: They stiffen. "Not yet. That's not ours to tell."

options.text: "See? I told you it would be fine. I was right."
options.then: They shrug, and the mood dims.

options.text: "Maybe later. We can't rush things just yet."
options.then: They nod. Later doesn't arrive.

steps.why: A steady, agreed rhythm builds on a good start, and their pace keeps it comfortable.

scenarios.relearn: A no-pressure invitation to a first shared step moves a hesitant co-parent further than blame.

scenarios.hook: A parent you know from school looks shaken and asks to talk.
scenarios.setup: You are both waiting outside a school hall.

steps.prompt: They say: "My family won't even talk about it. I have no one."

options.text: "You're not alone. There are groups and helplines. Let's find one."
options.then: Their eyes fill. "Thank you. I didn't know."

options.text: "Honestly, it's a nightmare. I don't know how any of us cope."
options.then: They go pale. "So it doesn't get easier?"

options.text: "Families always come around. Just give it time."
options.then: They nod. "How much time?" You have no answer.

options.text: "You shouldn't tell your family anything more."
options.then: They nod, but it feels like advice to hide.

steps.why: Telling them they are not alone, and pointing to real support, eases the isolation.

steps.prompt: They say: "I'm scared I'll get it wrong and hurt my child."

options.text: "You'll slip, then repair it. Love first, learning after."
options.then: They laugh unsteadily. "That I can do."

options.text: "You can't get it wrong. Everything will be just fine."
options.then: They frown. They know that isn't true.

options.text: "Then leave it to the experts and stay out of it."
options.then: They shrink. "But I'm the parent."

options.text: "Read every book first, and then talk to your child."
options.then: They nod eagerly. Their child waits, unspoken to.

steps.why: You don't need to be perfect. Love, repair and learning are enough.

steps.prompt: They ask: "Should I tell everyone at the school what's going on?"

options.text: "That's your child's story. Share what they're okay with."
options.then: They nod slowly. "I hadn't thought about asking them."

options.text: "Yes, tell everyone. Then no one can gossip behind your back."
options.then: They look worried. "Won't that make things harder for them?"

options.text: "No, hide it from everyone. It's safer."
options.then: They nod, but the word "hide" lingers on their face.

options.text: "Tell the teachers, and leave the parents out."
options.then: They nod. Their child's teachers now know more than the child chose to share.

steps.why: Whether and when others know is your child's choice, so ask them first.

steps.prompt: They ask: "There's a parents' group near here. Will you come with me next week?"

options.text: "Yes, I'll be there. Let's meet outside and walk in together."
options.then: Their shoulders drop. "Thank you. That makes it easier."

options.text: "I'd love to, but I'm swamped. Maybe another time."
options.then: They nod politely. The next week goes by without company.

options.text: "You go first, and tell me how it was."
options.then: They go alone, and come back quiet.

options.text: "Sure. But you talk, and I'll sit at the back."
options.then: They nod. "Alright. I just hoped you'd sit beside me."

steps.why: Going along with them turns advice into real company.

scenarios.relearn: Telling a frightened parent 'you're not alone' and naming real support helps them be their child's safe place.

scenarios.hook: You're thinking of joining a parents' group for families like yours, but privacy worries you.
scenarios.setup: You meet the organiser before the first session.

steps.prompt: The organiser asks: "Anything you want to know first?"

options.text: "How confidential is this group? What stays private?"
options.then: She nods. "What's said here stays in the room. We never share names outside."

options.text: "It's fine. I'll share my whole family's situation and hope."
options.then: She pauses. "Share only what you want. You needn't tell it all today."

options.text: "Is this group safe? I've heard some groups gossip."
options.then: She says they don't gossip and moves on. You still don't know how privacy is kept.

options.text: "Nothing. I don't want to sound suspicious."
options.then: She says "Take your time" and hands you a schedule.

steps.why: Asking exactly what stays private gets you a clear answer before you share anything.

steps.prompt: A few days on, the organiser messages: "We also have a members' WhatsApp group. Shall I add you?"

options.text: "Please tell me who can see it first. I'll say yes once I know."
options.then: She replies: "Only members, and no photos or screenshots. I'll add you when you say."

options.text: "Yes, add me. Everyone seems so nice."
options.then: You're added at once. Your name and number now show to every member.

options.text: "Add me. I'll post my child's name so people know who I mean."
options.then: Warm replies come in. Your child's name now sits in a chat you don't control.

options.text: "Send me the link and I'll forward it to my sister."
options.then: Your sister joins by the link. The organiser hadn't agreed to outsiders.

steps.why: Learning who can see the chat lets you choose what to share and when.

steps.prompt: At the first session, another parent asks: "Which school does your child go to?"

options.text: "I'd rather keep that private. I'm happy to share how I feel."
options.then: She smiles. "Of course. That's how it works here." The talk turns to feelings.

options.text: "Oh, the one near Model Town. Do you know it?"
options.then: She does, and knows a teacher there. Your child's school feels a little less private.

options.text: "Ask the organiser. She knows all about us."
options.then: The organiser looks startled. She hadn't planned to say anything about you.

options.text: "I can't say. No one here can be trusted."
options.then: The room goes quiet, and you feel more alone than when you walked in.

steps.why: You can keep details private and still take part fully.

scenarios.relearn: Asking how confidential a group is, before you join, protects your family's privacy from the start.

scenarios.hook: Your brother-in-law wants your son to stay with him these holidays, and you sense it isn't safe.
scenarios.setup: Your brother-in-law calls on a Sunday evening.

steps.prompt: He says: "The boy needs toughening up. Send him to me for a month."

options.text: "He's staying with us. His safety comes first."
options.then: He goes quiet. "You're making a fuss over nothing." But he lets it drop tonight.

options.text: "Let me think about it. I'll tell you next week."
options.then: "Fine, but everyone expects a yes." The question stays open and the pressure builds.

options.text: "He can come for a few days, just not the whole month."
options.then: "A few days is a start," he says, and begins planning the trip.

options.text: "Talk to my spouse. It's really their decision."
options.then: He sighs and calls them. Your spouse hears it as you dodging the question.

steps.why: A plain, firm answer keeps your son safe without needing a fight.

steps.prompt: Two days later he calls again: "Everyone says the boy should come for the full month. What are you afraid of?"

options.text: "The answer is no, and it isn't about you."
options.then: He is silent, then hangs up. The family chat is quiet for a day.

options.text: "You're right. I'm overreacting. Send me the dates."
options.then: He is delighted and books the tickets. Your stomach sinks.

options.text: "Let's ask your father to decide what's best for the boy."
options.then: His father sides with him at once. Now more people are pressing you.

options.text: "I'll explain my reasons to the whole family."
options.then: He is furious. Half the family now has opinions about your son.

steps.why: A short no keeps your son safe and keeps his story out of the family debate.

steps.prompt: That evening your son, who overheard part of the call, asks: "Uncle wants me to come. Do I have to go?"

options.text: "No. You're staying with us. Tell me anything, and I'll get help."
options.then: His shoulders drop, and he hugs you. "Okay. Thanks."

options.text: "Don't worry. Grown-ups are just talking."
options.then: He nods, but keeps watching your face for what you aren't saying.

options.text: "Do you want to go? It's your choice."
options.then: He shrugs, unsure. Being asked to decide feels heavy for him.

options.text: "You'll be fine. Everyone visits relatives sometimes."
options.then: He nods slowly. He doesn't look fine.

steps.why: He needs to hear he is staying and that you are safe to tell. None of this is his fault.

scenarios.relearn: Holding the line, 'his safety comes first', protects a child even when it ruffles family feathers.

scenarios.hook: "He saw it on a phone or a show, that's where this came from."

myth.un: He saw it on a phone or a show, that's where this came from.
myth.re: Screens don't make a child gender-diverse; they may just give a name to what was already true.
myth.why: Who a child is isn't downloaded from a screen.

scenarios.relearn: Screen time doesn't cause a child's identity; it may only give them words for who they already are.

scenarios.hook: "He started this after a new friend, so the friend must have spread it."

myth.un: He started this after a new friend, so the friend must have spread it.
myth.re: Identity isn't caught like a cold; a safe friend may just be the first place a child felt free to be open.
myth.why: A friend gives safety, not an identity.

scenarios.relearn: Identity isn't 'caught' from friends; a safe friend can just be where a child first felt free to be open.

scenarios.hook: "This is a foreign, Western idea that doesn't belong in our culture."

myth.un: This is a foreign, Western idea that doesn't belong in our culture.
myth.re: Gender-diverse people have lived in India for centuries; what's foreign is the shame, not the people.
myth.why: India's own history holds many gender stories.

scenarios.relearn: Gender diversity isn't a Western import; it has long roots in India. The shame is what's borrowed, not the child.

scenarios.hook: "It's just a trend going around, he'll grow out of it like a fashion."

myth.un: It's just a trend going around, he'll grow out of it like a fashion.
myth.re: Who a child is isn't a passing fashion; whether it shifts or stays, they deserve respect right now.
myth.why: You honour a child as they are today.

scenarios.relearn: A child's identity isn't a fad to wait out; respect them as they are now, whether it stays the same or shifts.

scenarios.hook: "My son likes dresses, so he must be gay."

myth.un: My son likes dresses, so he must be gay.
myth.re: Liking dresses is about expression, not about who he'll love; clothes don't tell you a child's orientation.
myth.why: Expression and attraction are separate things.

scenarios.relearn: What a child wears is expression, not orientation; clothes don't reveal who a child is attracted to.

scenarios.hook: "A girl who acts like a 'tomboy' has something going wrong."

myth.un: A girl who acts like a 'tomboy' has something going wrong.
myth.re: A girl who climbs, plays rough or loves trucks is just a girl with her own interests, not a problem.
myth.why: Interests have no gender to break.

scenarios.relearn: A girl who loves so-called 'boy things' isn't broken; she's a child with her own interests.

scenarios.hook: "If I'd been stricter, he wouldn't be like this."

myth.un: If I'd been stricter, he wouldn't be like this.
myth.re: No amount of discipline creates or removes who a child is; strictness only teaches them to hide from you.
myth.why: Identity isn't a behaviour you can drill away.

scenarios.relearn: Discipline doesn't cause or fix a child's identity; harshness only teaches them to hide who they are.

scenarios.hook: "A relative says it's the mother's fault for raising him 'too soft'."

myth.un: A relative says it's the mother's fault for raising him 'too soft'.
myth.re: No parenting style makes a child gender-diverse; blaming the mother is a myth, not a cause.
myth.why: It isn't caused by how you raised them.

scenarios.relearn: Being gender-diverse isn't caused by parenting style; blaming the mother for 'softness' is a myth.

scenarios.hook: "If he stops wearing girls' clothes, the feelings will stop too."

myth.un: If he stops wearing girls' clothes, the feelings will stop too.
myth.re: Taking away the clothes only hides expression; a child's inner sense of self doesn't switch off with an outfit.
myth.why: You can hide expression, not erase identity.

scenarios.relearn: Removing the clothes hides expression but doesn't change identity; the inner sense of self stays.

scenarios.hook: "She's only saying this for attention."

myth.un: She's only saying this for attention.
myth.re: Telling a parent something this tender is rarely a stunt; it usually took courage and trust to say at all.
myth.why: Honesty about the self is brave, not a show.

scenarios.relearn: Sharing who they are isn't attention-seeking; it usually takes real courage and trust to tell a parent.

scenarios.hook: "He's just confused, he's too young to know anything about himself."

myth.un: He's just confused, he's too young to know anything about himself.
myth.re: Children sense who they are early, much as they sense being a boy or a girl; clarity, not confusion.
myth.why: Self-knowledge can come young.

scenarios.relearn: A child isn't automatically 'confused'; kids can sense who they are early, just as they sense being a boy or girl.

scenarios.hook: "If I allow it, my other children will 'become' the same."

myth.un: If I allow it, my other children will 'become' the same.
myth.re: Accepting one child doesn't change another's identity; it only teaches all of them that home is safe.
myth.why: Acceptance spreads safety, not identity.

scenarios.relearn: Accepting one child doesn't make siblings gender-diverse; it just teaches every child that home is safe.

scenarios.hook: "A boy who plays with dolls is being 'turned into' something."

myth.un: A boy who plays with dolls is being 'turned into' something.
myth.re: A doll is a toy for nurturing play, not a switch; no toy turns a child into anything they aren't.
myth.why: Toys don't rewrite who a child is.

scenarios.relearn: Playing with a doll is just play; toys don't 'turn' a child into anything. Interests aren't gendered.

scenarios.hook: "A doctor cousin said this is a condition that needs treatment."

myth.un: A doctor cousin said this is a condition that needs treatment.
myth.re: Being gender-diverse isn't an illness and major health bodies don't treat it as one; there's nothing to cure.
myth.why: It's part of human diversity, not a disease.

scenarios.relearn: Being gender-diverse isn't an illness or a condition to treat; it's part of human diversity, not a disease.

scenarios.hook: "Gay, transgender, it's all the same thing really."

myth.un: Gay, transgender, it's all the same thing really.
myth.re: Gay is about who you love; transgender is about your gender; they're different, and a person can be either or both.
myth.why: Attraction and gender are two questions.

scenarios.relearn: Gay (orientation) and transgender (gender identity) aren't the same; they answer two different questions.

scenarios.hook: A relative insists your son's love of dresses is 'just a phase he'll outgrow'.

steps.prompt: She waits for you to agree. What do you say?

options.text: Say you respect him now, whether it lasts or not
options.then: She says "Hmm." Across the room, your son looks up and smiles at you.

options.text: Agree it's a phase, just to end the talk quickly
options.then: She nods, pleased, and the talk ends. Nearby, your son looks down at his dress.

options.text: Say it's none of her business how he dresses
options.then: She stiffens. "I'm only worried." The room turns tense.

options.text: Say you'll ask a doctor whether it's a phase
options.then: She says "Yes, ask someone." The idea that something is wrong stays in the air.

steps.why: Respecting him whether or not it lasts tells him his feelings count now.

steps.prompt: Days later, your son asks to wear his dress to a cousin's birthday. What do you do?

options.text: Let him, and stay close at the party
options.then: He twirls in front of the mirror. At the party a cousin asks about it and you answer calmly.

options.text: Tell him to wear it only at home
options.then: He nods. The dress goes back in the cupboard, and so does his smile.

options.text: Suggest trousers, since people will talk
options.then: He agrees quietly. He looks at you for a long moment before leaving.

options.text: Let him, and leave him to handle any comments
options.then: He wears it happily until an uncle jokes. He looks around for you and you're busy chatting.

steps.why: Saying yes and staying close protects him if anyone comments.

steps.prompt: That night your son asks whether you like him in his dress. What do you say?

options.text: Say you love him, in a dress or in anything
options.then: He hugs you tight. "Okay!" he says, and falls asleep smiling.

options.text: Say it's nice, but people may not understand
options.then: He tilts his head. "Who won't understand?" You don't have an answer.

options.text: Say you like him best in his usual clothes
options.then: His smile fades a little. He tucks the dress under his pillow.

options.text: Say you'll talk about it when he's older
options.then: He nods, though his eyes drop. He wonders if he asked something wrong.

steps.why: A warm, simple answer tells him he is loved and welcome as he is.

scenarios.debrief: Whether or not it lasts, respect the child now; 'just a phase' tells them they don't count.
scenarios.relearn: Respect a child as they are now, whether it lasts or not; 'just a phase' teaches them their feelings don't matter.

scenarios.hook: You catch yourself wanting to blame phones and the internet for your child's identity.

steps.prompt: Your teen is on their phone late again, and your worry spikes. What do you do?

options.text: Read affirming sources first, then ask what they watch
options.then: You learn the videos have given them words for how they feel. Your worry eases.

options.text: Take all their screens away until it passes
options.then: Your teen goes silent. The screens are gone, and so is the talking.

options.text: Ask to see what they watch, then argue with each video
options.then: They show you one clip, then close the phone. They don't show you another.

options.text: Check their messages after they fall asleep
options.then: You read things you weren't meant to. Now you're hiding something too.

steps.why: Learning the facts first lets you ask with curiosity, not fear.

steps.prompt: At a family gathering, a relative says too much internet is why kids these days say they're different. What do you say?

options.text: Say kids find words online for what they already feel
options.then: She frowns. "Words for what they feel? Hm." She stops arguing.

options.text: Agree, and say you're cutting their screen time
options.then: She is pleased. Your teen, hearing about it later, feels blamed.

options.text: Say nothing, to avoid a scene
options.then: She takes your silence as agreement and tells others.

options.text: Say she has no right to comment on your family
options.then: She goes red. The talk ends, and the fact is never said.

steps.why: Screens can give a child words, but they don't make the child who they are.

steps.prompt: Your teen asks what you really think about their online friends. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're glad they found people who understand them
options.then: They relax. "Want to meet one? They're really nice." You say yes, gladly.

options.text: Say it's fine if they tell you everything they chat about
options.then: They shrug. Being watched isn't the same as being trusted.

options.text: Say you'd rather they had friends in real life instead
options.then: They nod slowly. They stop mentioning their friends at home.

options.text: Say they can keep them only if you approve each one
options.then: They look worried. Now their support depends on your approval.

steps.why: Welcoming their friends supports them and keeps trust open.

scenarios.debrief: Screens don't cause identity; check the facts instead of acting on the fear.
scenarios.relearn: Screens don't cause a child's identity; learn the facts rather than banning devices to 'reverse' who they are.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter says she's a trans girl, and you assume that means she's saying she's gay.

steps.prompt: She looks at you nervously, waiting. What do you say?

options.text: "Thank you for telling me. What does that mean?"
options.then: She takes a breath. "It means I'm a girl. It's not about who I like."

options.text: "So do you like girls or boys? Tell me plainly."
options.then: She looks confused and a little hurt. "That's not what I said."

options.text: "Okay, call it whatever you want. We'll just see."
options.then: She nods, but her shoulders tighten. She stops explaining.

options.text: "Are you sure? You're so young to know for certain."
options.then: She looks down. "I've known for a long time."

steps.why: Thanking her and asking lets her explain in her own words.

steps.prompt: Later, your spouse asks if trans and gay mean the same thing. What do you say?

options.text: Say trans is who she is, and gay is who you love
options.then: Your spouse nods slowly. "So they're two different things." They ask how they can help.

options.text: Say they're basically the same thing, just two words
options.then: Your spouse shrugs. "Fine." You both carry a muddled idea forward.

options.text: Say it doesn't matter what it's called right now
options.then: Your spouse nods, relieved. Nobody learns anything new.

options.text: Say you'll ask the relatives what they think
options.then: The relatives now know about her, and every one of them has an opinion.

steps.why: A simple, accurate line helps the family understand her instead of guessing.

steps.prompt: At school pick-up, a friend asks whether your daughter is gay. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's not yours to share, and change the subject
options.then: She looks a little surprised, then starts talking about homework.

options.text: Say she's gay, because it's simpler to explain
options.then: Your friend nods. Now a wrong label about your daughter travels around school.

options.text: Explain it all so she understands it properly
options.then: She listens closely, then tells two other mothers by evening.

options.text: Laugh it off and say kids are just kids these days
options.then: Your friend laughs. Your daughter, waiting nearby, wonders why you laughed.

steps.why: Her identity is hers to share, and a calm deflection protects her privacy.

scenarios.debrief: Gender and attraction are different; ask and learn rather than assuming one means the other.
scenarios.relearn: Transgender is about gender, and gay is about attraction; ask and learn rather than assuming one means the other.

scenarios.hook: An elder advises that firm discipline will 'straighten out' your gender-diverse child.

steps.prompt: He says you're too soft and offers to 'have a word' with your child. What do you do?

options.text: Thank him, decline, and say your child is fine as they are

options.text: Say you'll try a stricter routine at home

options.text: Tell him he's old-fashioned and walk away
options.then: He is offended, and the family hears his side before you can explain.

steps.why: Declining kindly and firmly keeps your child from being lectured or shamed.

steps.prompt: Days later, your child comes home from a family visit unusually quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with them and say they're loved just as they are
options.then: They lean against you. After a while they say, "Uncle said something at lunch."

options.text: Tell them to ignore it because family means well
options.then: They nod, but say nothing more about it that day.

options.text: Tell them it's nothing and they'll get over it soon
options.then: They stay in their room. Dinner is quiet, and nobody brings it up.

options.text: Quiz them about every word that was said
options.then: They answer in one word each time. It feels like an interrogation.

steps.why: Sitting close and saying you love them as they are opens the door without pushing.

steps.prompt: Your child asks if they have to act differently when the elder is around. What do you say?

options.text: Say they never need to hide who they are
options.then: Their face softens. "Even at home?" "Especially at home," you say.

options.text: Say to keep quiet just while he is visiting
options.then: They nod. For the whole visit they hardly speak.

options.text: Say it's up to them how they handle it
options.then: They shrug, looking small. Nobody has told them what is safe.

options.text: Say he'll come round if they try harder
options.then: They nod. Now they think his approval is their job.

steps.why: Pressing a child to mask harms them. Home is where they can be themselves, and it is never their fault.

steps.prompt: At the next visit, the elder asks to speak to your child alone. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll all sit together, and stay beside your child
options.then: He grumbles, but sits with everyone. Your child stays next to you.

options.text: Let them talk, and ask how it went afterwards
options.then: When they return, your child stares at their hands and says "Fine."

options.text: Whisper to your child to just nod and get through it
options.then: They nod. On the way home they say nothing at all.

options.text: Refuse, and tell the elder off in front of everyone
options.then: He storms out, and your child feels the whole family's eyes on them.

steps.why: Staying beside your child shields them from pressure without a scene.

scenarios.debrief: Discipline can't change identity; it only teaches a child to hide. Keep home safe and open instead.
scenarios.relearn: Discipline can't 'straighten out' identity; it only teaches a child to hide. A safe, open home keeps them close.

scenarios.hook: Someone offers a 'treatment' that promises to change who your child is.

options.text: Say you'll try it for one month and then stop

options.text: Say you would rather not argue about it tonight
options.then: The website stays open on the laptop. The subject is back tomorrow.

options.text: Say your partner is being foolish to consider it
options.then: Your partner shuts the laptop and stops sharing what they read.

steps.why: Naming the harm and offering to look together brings your partner along without a fight.

steps.prompt: Later, your child says they overheard you both, and asks if you want them to change. What do you say?

options.text: Say nothing needs changing and you won't send them
options.then: They breathe out and lean on you. "Okay. I was scared."

options.text: Say you're only exploring every option for now
options.then: They look at you. "So maybe you do want me to change."

options.text: Say it was only worry, and not to think about it
options.then: They nod, but ask again the next day, more quietly.

options.text: Ask if they'd like to try it, just to be fair
options.then: They shrug. "If it makes you happy." They're trying to please you.

steps.why: A clear promise that they won't be changed makes them feel safe again.

scenarios.debrief: There's nothing to cure; 'treatments' to change a child are discredited and harmful. Choose affirming support.
scenarios.relearn: There's nothing to cure; 'cures' are harmful and discredited. Refuse them and choose affirming support instead.

scenarios.hook: Your son keeps choosing the kitchen and dance over cricket, and a relative calls it a 'concern'.

options.text: Sign him up for cricket alongside dance

steps.prompt: A neighbour who has seen him dance says he's 'so talented for a boy'. What do you say?

options.text: Thank her, and say he is talented and loves it

options.text: Smile and say nothing

scenarios.hook: Your child's grandfather says this 'identity business' is a foreign idea with no place in your home.

options.text: Agree, to keep the peace at the table
options.then: The table relaxes. Your child looks down at their plate.

options.text: Say he is the one who's behind the times
options.then: He bristles. Now the argument is about him, not your child.

options.text: Say it doesn't matter where it came from
options.then: He says "Exactly, so drop it." He thinks you agree with him.

steps.prompt: At a family function, a cousin repeats that it's just a foreign fashion. What do you do?

options.text: Point to old Indian communities and stories with many genders
options.then: She has heard of some. "Hm, I suppose that's true."

options.text: Send her a long article and walk off
options.then: She skims the first line. The article is never mentioned again.

options.text: Say you're not sure, and drop it
options.then: She takes that as a win and tells others.

options.text: Say your family doesn't care what history says

steps.prompt: Your child asks if some people think they don't belong here. What do you say?

options.then: They lean into you. "Even to Dadaji?" "Even to Dadaji," you say.

options.text: Say some people are just old-fashioned
options.then: They nod, but don't ask again. They are still unsure.

options.text: Say to avoid people who talk like that
