options.text: Say you'll sort it out and they needn't worry
options.then: They nod. Nothing has been said about where they belong.

steps.why: Telling them plainly that they belong makes home the safe place.

scenarios.debrief: Gender diversity isn't a Western import; it has deep Indian roots. Answer the myth with the fact.
scenarios.relearn: Gender diversity has long roots in India, not a foreign import; meet the 'it's not ours' myth with the fact.

scenarios.hook: You want to support your child, but you worry you'll say the wrong thing.

steps.prompt: At dinner your child talks fast about words their friends use, and you're lost. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're new to this and ask them to help you understand
options.then: Your child slows down and explains a word. "Thanks for asking," they say.

options.text: Nod and say "Mm-hm" until they finish
options.then: They finish. You still don't know what a single word meant.

options.text: Change the subject to their exams
options.then: They answer, but the conversation about themselves is over.

options.text: Promise to read up, and skip the conversation for now
options.then: They shrug. "Okay." The talk you were meant to have doesn't happen.

steps.why: Admitting you are new to it invites your child in instead of shutting the topic down.

steps.prompt: Days later, your child tries another new word on you, more nervously. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what it means and say it back to check
options.then: They smile. "Yes, exactly." Their shoulders relax.

options.text: Say you've got it and move on
options.then: They can tell you're guessing. They stop trying.

options.text: Ask them to write a list of every word to study
options.then: They spend an evening on it. Home starts to feel like a classroom.

options.text: Say you can't keep up with these things
options.then: They nod slowly and swallow whatever they wanted to say.

steps.why: Asking and repeating it back shows you are really trying, in a way they can feel.

steps.prompt: A relative asks you to explain what your child 'is'. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're still learning, and their story is theirs to share
options.then: She sniffs but lets it go. From the hall, your child hears you.

options.text: Repeat your child's new words to sound informed
options.then: She asks more, and you find yourself telling her things your child said privately.

options.text: Say you're as confused as she is
options.then: She agrees it's all confusing and starts giving advice.

options.text: Change the subject and avoid her all evening
options.then: She corners you later, and your child notices you hiding.

steps.why: Being honest that you are learning, while guarding their privacy, protects trust.

scenarios.debrief: It's fine to be a beginner; ask and learn together rather than pretending or avoiding the subject.
scenarios.relearn: You can be a beginner; ask your child to help you understand rather than pretending or avoiding it.

scenarios.hook: Your spouse keeps saying 'gay' and 'trans' as if they mean the same thing.
scenarios.setup: After dinner, your spouse says it again.

steps.prompt: Your spouse says: "So is our child gay or trans? It's the same thing, no?"

options.text: "Gay is who you love. Trans is who you are."
options.then: Your spouse blinks. "Oh. I honestly didn't know that."

options.text: "It doesn't matter. It's all the same anyway."
options.then: Your spouse nods. "So it's one thing, then." The muddle stays.

options.text: "You're confused. Go and read something about it."
options.then: Your spouse's jaw sets. "Don't talk to me like that."

options.text: "Let's ask a doctor to tell us which one it is."
options.then: Your spouse agrees quickly. Nobody has asked your child.

steps.why: A calm, simple line gives your spouse a fact without making them feel foolish.

steps.prompt: The next evening your spouse asks: "If our child is trans, will they like boys or girls?"

options.text: "Gender and attraction are separate. Only they can say."
options.then: Your spouse nods slowly. "So we don't have to guess."

options.text: "Probably boys, I think. That is how it usually goes."
options.then: "Hm," says your spouse, filing it away as a fact.

options.text: "Who cares who they like? That is years away."
options.then: Your spouse frowns. "But shouldn't we know?"

options.text: "I'll find out from them and then tell you all."
options.then: Your spouse relaxes. Your child hasn't been asked what they want shared.

steps.why: Gender and attraction are different things, and your child will share their own story.

steps.prompt: Your spouse says: "How do I explain all this to my mother?"

options.text: "Let's ask our child what they're okay with."
options.then: Your spouse nods. "It's theirs to tell. I'll wait."

options.text: "Tell her everything, so she can't say we hid it."
options.then: Your spouse picks up the phone. Your child's news will be in the family chat by night.

options.text: "Say it's a phase and we're waiting."
options.then: Your spouse is relieved. Your child, walking in, catches the word 'phase'.

options.text: "You explain it. You're better with her."
options.then: Your spouse nods and starts planning what to say. Nobody asks your child.

steps.why: Their identity is theirs to share, so asking your child first comes before telling anyone.

scenarios.relearn: Gay is about attraction and trans is about gender; explaining the difference helps the whole family understand the child.

scenarios.hook: Your child's grandmother has been quietly worried since she saw your son in a dress.
scenarios.setup: She takes you aside after lunch.

steps.prompt: Your mother says: "Isn't this just a phase he'll outgrow?"

options.text: "Maybe it shifts, maybe not. Either way, he deserves respect now."
options.then: She is quiet. "Respect. Yes, of course he does."

options.text: "Yes, surely. Let's just ignore it until it passes."
options.then: She pats your hand, pleased. Nearby, your son hears the word 'ignore'.

options.text: "Ma, please don't say that in front of him."
options.then: She pulls back, hurt. "I'm only asking. I love him."

options.text: "I don't know. Let's wait and see what he does."
options.then: She nods. "Wait and see, yes." Your son senses he is being watched.

steps.why: Whether it lasts or not, he deserves respect today.

steps.prompt: Your mother says: "But what if he is like this at fifteen? What then?"

options.text: "Then we'll love him at fifteen just as we do now."
options.then: She takes your hand. "I suppose that is what matters."

options.text: "He won't be. Children always grow out of this."
options.then: She smiles with relief. You have promised something you can't know.

options.text: "That is too far ahead to talk about."
options.then: She presses her lips together. The worry stays in the room.

options.text: "Then we'll take him to a doctor."
options.then: Her face clears. "A doctor, yes." The idea that something needs fixing settles in.

steps.why: Promising love, not a particular outcome, is honest and steadying.

steps.prompt: Your mother asks: "What should I do when he visits me?"

options.text: "Let him play as he likes, and say you're glad he's here."
options.then: She wipes her eyes and smiles. "That I can do."

options.text: "Say nothing about it. Pretend you don't notice."
options.then: She nods. He senses her stiffness whenever he dresses up.

options.text: "Tell him boys can't wear dresses outside the house."
options.then: She agrees. Her first visit ends with him quiet in a plain shirt.

options.text: "Ask your friends what to say to him."
options.then: Her friends give advice. She returns with three opinions and no ease.

steps.why: Simple warmth from a grandparent is one of the kindest things a child can get.

scenarios.relearn: Whether an identity lasts or shifts, the child deserves respect now; 'just ignore it' teaches them they don't count.

scenarios.hook: A relative tells your wife that the child 'turned out this way' because of her parenting.
scenarios.setup: Your wife's face falls as everyone hears it.

steps.prompt: Your relative says: "It is because you were too soft on him, beta."

options.text: "No parenting causes this. It's who our child is."
options.then: She purses her lips. Your wife looks up at you, surprised.

options.text: "Maybe we did something wrong when he was small."
options.then: Your wife looks at you, stricken. "You think it's my fault?"

options.text: "Aunty, please don't say such things in front of everyone."
options.then: She sighs. "I'm only telling the truth, beta." Your wife stares at her plate.

options.text: "She's done her best. Leave her alone."
options.then: The relative shrugs. "Best or not, look at the result." Your wife looks away.

steps.why: Naming the fact plainly lifts the blame from both of you.

steps.prompt: Later your wife says quietly: "What if she is right? What if it is me?"

options.text: "It isn't you. Nothing you did caused this."
options.then: She leans against you. "I needed to hear that."

options.text: "She is old and out of touch. Just forget it."
options.then: She nods, but the doubt stays with her.

options.text: "We can ask a doctor if we did anything wrong."
options.then: She agrees quietly. The idea of blame now has a place to live.

options.text: "You're overthinking. Stop worrying about it."
options.then: She goes silent and turns off the light.

steps.why: Telling her plainly that it isn't her fault steadies her.

steps.prompt: Your child asks: "Did I do something wrong? Why was Aunty upset with Mama?"

options.text: "No. You did nothing wrong, and we love you."
options.then: He breathes out. "Okay. I thought it was because of me."

options.text: "Grown-ups argue sometimes. Don't worry."
options.then: He nods, unconvinced. He still thinks it's his fault.

options.text: "Aunty is a bit silly. Don't listen to her."
options.then: He giggles a little, but still wonders what she said.

options.text: "That is for Mama and me to sort out."
options.then: He nods, but he is left holding his own guess.

steps.why: A child needs to hear plainly that nothing about them is wrong or anyone's fault.

scenarios.relearn: No parenting style causes a child's identity; correcting the blame protects both the parent and the child from shame.

scenarios.hook: A cousin insists your son 'got these ideas' from too much time on the phone.
scenarios.setup: She says it while he plays in the next room.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says: "It's all that phone. Take it away and he'll be normal."

options.text: "A phone doesn't make him who he is. He's just himself."
options.then: She frowns. "Hm." In the next room, your son laughs at his game.

options.text: "You're right. I'll take his phone away and see."
options.then: She is pleased. "Good. You'll see the difference in a week."

options.text: "Maybe it's a phase. Let's wait and see if it passes."
options.then: She nods. "Phases pass. Just don't encourage it."

options.text: "Maybe. I'll ask the other relatives if they've noticed it too."
options.then: She nods. "Everyone has. Ask anyone." He looks up from the next room.

steps.why: A calm, simple fact answers the blame without punishing him.

steps.prompt: Your cousin goes on: "He was different before he got that phone. Anyone can see it."

options.text: "Phones give him words. They don't make him who he is."
options.then: She thinks about it. "Words. I suppose everyone finds words somewhere."

options.text: "Maybe. I honestly can't be sure of anything now."
options.then: She latches on. "Exactly. So why risk it?"

options.text: "Fine. I'll watch what he looks at from now on."
options.then: She approves. Your son will soon feel watched in his own home.

options.text: "I don't want to discuss this any more. Please stop."
options.then: She stops, huffing. She goes home with the same idea intact.

steps.why: A phone can give him words for what he feels, but he is who he is either way.

steps.prompt: Your son wanders in and asks: "Mama, were you and Aunty talking about my phone?"

options.text: "Aunty worries. But you're just being you, beta."
options.then: He grins. "I am just me." He leans against you.

options.text: "Just grown-up talk, beta. Go back and play, okay?"
options.then: He goes, but hovers at the door a moment first.

options.text: "Aunty says you spend too much time on the phone."
options.then: He looks down at the phone. "Am I in trouble?"

options.text: "We may need to take the phone away for a while."
options.then: His face crumples. "But I didn't do anything."

steps.why: Telling him plainly that he is just being himself keeps him from feeling blamed.

scenarios.relearn: Screens don't cause identity; a phone may give words for who a child already is, but it doesn't create it.

scenarios.hook: At a family lunch, an uncle mocks your son for loving dance.
scenarios.setup: He laughs across the table, loudly, in front of everyone.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "Dance? Let him play like a boy, yaar!"

options.text: "He loves dance. Interests don't have a gender."
options.then: The table goes quiet. Your son looks up at you, surprised and glad.

options.text: "You're right. I'll make sure he sticks to boys' games."
options.then: The uncle nods, pleased. Your son stares at his plate.

options.text: "Uncle, please don't do this. He's sitting right here."
options.then: The uncle chuckles. "Only joking!" The laughter around the table carries on.

options.text: "It's just for now. He'll move on to other things."
options.then: The uncle smirks. "Of course he will." Your son's spoon stops.

steps.why: One clear, warm line tells him what he loves is welcome.

steps.prompt: The uncle laughs harder: "Next he'll want to wear ghungroos!"

options.text: "If he wants to, he can. We're proud of him."
options.then: A cousin looks down, smiling. Your uncle mutters and reaches for the rice.

options.text: "Ha, ha. That is enough now, Uncle. Please."
options.then: The laughter dies awkwardly. Your son isn't sure whether he has been defended.

options.text: "Yes, I'll keep him away from all that dancing."
options.then: "Sensible," says your uncle. Your son stops eating.

options.text: "Come on, everyone. The food is getting cold."
options.then: Everyone eats, but your son shrinks in his chair.

steps.why: Standing behind him in front of the family shows him he can be himself at the table.

steps.prompt: Later, your son asks: "Why does Uncle think dance is bad?"

options.text: "He's mistaken. I love watching you dance."
options.then: He grins. "Will you come to my next show?"

options.text: "He's old-fashioned. Try not to take it to heart."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay." He is quiet at practice the next day.

options.text: "Maybe dance is better kept for home for now."
options.then: He nods slowly and puts his dance shoes at the back of the cupboard.

options.text: "Some people think differently. Just ignore him."
options.then: He nods. He wonders which other people think like that.

steps.why: He needs to hear that his love of dance is fine and that you enjoy it too.

scenarios.relearn: Interests have no gender; defending a child's love of dance teaches him that what he enjoys is welcome.

scenarios.hook: Your teen has asked to talk to you alone, and you can tell it matters to them.
scenarios.setup: They watch your face, barely breathing.

steps.prompt: Your teen says: "I'm non-binary. I'm not a boy or a girl."

options.text: "I'm still learning what that means, but I love you."
options.then: Their eyes fill. "You don't have to get it yet. I just needed you to know."

options.text: "That's not a real thing. You're overcomplicating this."
options.then: Their face closes. "I knew you'd say that."

options.text: "Are you sure? Maybe it's only a phase for now."
options.then: They stiffen. "It isn't. I've thought about this for years."

options.text: "Okay. I'll need some time on my own with this."
options.then: They nod slowly, but look hurt. You haven't said you love them.

steps.why: Honesty about learning, with love first, is what a teen most needs to hear.

steps.prompt: A few days later your teen asks: "Could you use 'they' for me at home?"

options.text: "Yes, I'll try. Tell me if I slip, and I'll keep trying."
options.then: Relief crosses their face. "Thank you. I know it's hard."

options.text: "I'll just use your name. That's easier for me."
options.then: They nod, a little deflated. The name is fine, but their request went unanswered.

options.text: "Let me think about it for a while and tell you."
options.then: They nod and wait. Weeks later, the question is still open.

options.text: "I'll use it once you're older and sure about this."
options.then: They go quiet. "So not now. Maybe never."

steps.why: Using the words they ask for, slips and all, is a daily act of affirmation.

steps.prompt: Your teen says: "I don't want relatives to know yet. Can you keep it private?"

options.text: "Yes. It's your story. You decide who knows and when."
options.then: Their shoulders drop. "Thank you. I'll tell them when I'm ready."

options.text: "Okay, but your grandmother has a right to know."
options.then: They go still. "So it's not really my choice."

options.text: "I'll tell them gently so it isn't a shock later."
options.then: They stare at you. "Please don't."

options.text: "Fine, but you will have to tell them soon enough."
options.then: They agree, but the deadline sits heavy on them.

steps.why: Their identity is theirs to share, and they decide when.

scenarios.relearn: You can admit you're still learning while affirming love; honesty plus warmth beats pretending or dismissing.

scenarios.hook: A well-meaning aunt has come to your house with a plan for your child.
scenarios.setup: She sits down with her tea and gets straight to it.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "I know a doctor who can cure this. Just one visit, beta."

options.text: "There's nothing to cure. We'll find support for him."
options.then: She looks taken aback. "Nothing? But I only want what is best for him."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. Let's see if he can fix it."
options.then: Her face lights up. "I'll book it today."

options.text: "Thanks, Aunty. We'll think about it for a while."
options.then: "Don't think too long, beta," she says, stirring her tea.

options.text: "Only if the doctor just talks to him, nothing more."
options.then: She hesitates. "Well, he will try to help him change, of course."

steps.why: There is nothing to cure, and a clear no protects him.

steps.prompt: Your aunt adds: "He is very well known, you know. Everyone says he is good."

options.text: "I know you care. Trying to change a child hurts him."
options.then: She looks stung, then thoughtful. "I only wanted him to be happy."

options.text: "Then give me his card. I'll keep it, just in case."
options.then: She hands it over, glowing. The card waits in your drawer.

options.text: "I can't discuss this. Please leave now, Aunty."
options.then: She stands, hurt, then stops at the door. "One more thing, beta."

options.text: "Does he have success stories? I'd like to see."
options.then: She names three families. Nobody mentions asking the children.

steps.why: Kind and firm together respects her care and still protects him.

steps.prompt: Your aunt asks: "So tell me, beta. What is your plan for him?"

options.text: "Love him, listen to him, and find affirming support."
options.then: She is silent. "Affirming. I don't know that word." She lets you explain.

options.text: "Honestly, I don't know yet. I'm still thinking."
options.then: She says, "Then keep the doctor in mind." The door stays open for her idea.

options.text: "Keep him busy with sports and hope it settles."
options.then: She nods approvingly. His weekends fill with matches he doesn't enjoy.

options.text: "Wait. Children often grow out of these things."
options.then: She nods. "True, it may pass." He goes on feeling he has to change.

steps.why: Love, listening and affirming support are what actually help.

scenarios.relearn: There's nothing to cure; affirming support helps a child, while 'cures' are harmful. Decline them kindly but clearly.

scenarios.hook: "I have to feel completely at peace with this before I can support my child."

myth.why: Your upbringing isn't your limit.

myth.un: Once I've apologised for one hurtful reaction, I should be back to normal and never wobble again.
myth.re: Growth isn't a straight line; an honest 'I'm still learning, bear with me' keeps repair going, slips and all.
myth.why: Repair is ongoing, not one event.

myth.why: Supported parents parent better.

myth.why: Named fear stops steering you blind.

myth.re: Acceptance isn't a verdict you reserve; your child needs to feel safe with you now, not on probation.
myth.why: A child shouldn't live on probation.

scenarios.relearn: Acceptance isn't a verdict to reserve for later; your child needs to feel safe with you now, not on probation.

'It's too late for me to change'

scenarios.relearn: Hold the kind, true thoughts about your journey; drop the harsh untrue ones that say fear means no love or it's too late.

scenarios.hook: Sort: holds your worry yourself, or lands it on your child?

items.text: Journalling your fears for yourself
Pulling away coldly when they're near
Talking it through with your partner
Telling your child you're ashamed of them
Booking an affirming counsellor
Making your child comfort you

scenarios.relearn: Hold your worry yourself, with a partner, journal or counsellor; don't land it on your child as distance, shame or comfort-work.

scenarios.hook: A relative makes a cruel joke about 'boys like that'. Your child is in earshot.

steps.prompt: The room laughs, and your child freezes in the doorway. What do you do?

options.text: Walk over and stand beside your child
options.then: Their hand finds yours. The laughter fades awkwardly.

options.text: Stay silent and hope they didn't hear
options.then: They heard. They look at you and see nothing change.

options.text: Laugh a little to keep the peace
options.then: The joke passes. Your child watches you laugh with the room.

options.text: Send your child off to play and say nothing
options.then: They go, uneasy. The joke stays in the room, and so does the silence.

steps.why: Standing beside them shows whose side you are on, without a scene.

steps.prompt: Later that evening your child is very quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with them: "That was wrong. I'm on your side."
options.then: They lean against you and finally let out a long breath.

options.text: Say your relative didn't really mean it at all
options.then: They nod. They still don't know what you think.

options.text: Ask them what they did to bring it on today
options.then: Their eyes fill. They hear that you side with the joke.

options.text: Wait quietly, hoping they will forget by morning
options.then: They don't forget. They lie awake replaying the laughter.

steps.why: Saying you are on their side, in private, tells them home stays safe.

steps.prompt: Next week the same relative invites the family to a festival. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him those jokes must stop before you come
options.then: He grumbles and won't promise. Your child heard you say it, and stands taller.

options.text: Accept and hope he behaves better this time
options.then: At the festival, he starts again. Your child looks for you across the crowd.

options.text: Go, and leave your child with a neighbour
options.then: Your child stays behind, sure it was their fault.

options.text: Decline politely without ever saying why
options.then: He is confused, and the invitations continue.

steps.why: Naming the limit shows your child you will shield them, even if the relative doesn't change.

scenarios.debrief: You can't always silence a relative, but you can always show your child you're on their side.
scenarios.relearn: You can't always silence a relative, but you can quietly tell your child you're on their side.

scenarios.hook: You catch yourself wanting to 'test' if it's a phase before you accept your child.

steps.prompt: Your child asks for a haircut they have wanted for months. What do you do?

options.text: Take them for it this week
options.then: They look in the mirror and beam. It is the first time in months they hold your hand.

options.text: Say yes if they still want it in six months
options.then: They sigh and start counting the days.

options.text: Say yes if their marks stay high
options.then: They study hard, and feel their happiness has to be earned.

options.text: Say yes, but only in the holidays
options.then: They nod. Weeks pass with the wish held back.

steps.why: Saying yes now shows them they don't have to pass a test to be accepted.

steps.prompt: A relative says to wait a year and see if it passes. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're not waiting, and you support them
options.then: She purses her lips. "As you wish." But she doesn't argue.

options.text: Say you will watch quietly and see what happens
options.then: She nods. Your child feels the watching every day.

options.text: Say you will decide once the year is over
options.then: She smiles, satisfied. Your child's year starts on trial.

options.text: Say nothing and steer the talk to something else
options.then: She takes your silence as agreement.

steps.why: A test period tells a child their acceptance is on hold. Today is when they need you.

steps.prompt: Your child asks if you are waiting for them to change their mind. What do you say?

options.text: Say you love them as they are and there is no test
options.then: They let out a breath and hug you hard.

options.text: Say you only want them to be very sure
options.then: They nod, but their smile is smaller.

options.text: Say you hope they have made the right choice
options.then: They look away. Now they are afraid of getting it wrong.

options.text: Say you have not decided yet, but you are trying
options.then: They nod slowly. They stay careful around you.

steps.why: No audition for your love: they should hear they are accepted as they are.

scenarios.debrief: No audition for your love.
scenarios.relearn: Don't make your child audition for your acceptance; support them as they are now.

scenarios.hook: Late at night your fear spikes and you want to message your child something heavy.

steps.prompt: It is past midnight and your thumb hovers over Send. What do you do?

options.text: Hold the message and call Tele-MANAS 14416 for yourself
options.then: The counsellor listens without hurry. By the end, you can breathe again.

options.text: Send it now and get the fear off your chest
options.then: Your child reads it at dawn and goes pale.

options.text: Send a short "We need to talk tomorrow" instead
options.then: Your child stares at it all morning, dreading what it means.

options.text: Stay awake and stew in the fear all night alone
options.then: By morning you are exhausted and short with everyone.

steps.why: Taking the fear to a helpline lets you settle without your child having to hold it.

steps.prompt: At breakfast your child notices your red eyes and asks if you are okay. What do you say?

options.text: Say it was a hard night, but it is yours to handle
options.then: They nod. "Okay. I'm here if you want to talk."

options.text: Tell them everything you were afraid of last night
options.then: They listen, pale. Now they are trying to comfort you.

options.text: Say you are fine and turn away to make the tea
options.then: They can see you are not fine, and wonder if it is their fault.

options.text: Say they have been worrying you a lot lately
options.then: Their face drops. "Sorry."

steps.why: A short, calm answer is honest without handing your child your worry.

steps.prompt: Two days later the fear spikes again at dinner. What do you do?

options.text: Excuse yourself for a few minutes to breathe
options.then: You step out, breathe, and come back steadier. Dinner carries on.

options.text: Say out loud what you are afraid of, at the table
options.then: Your child stops eating and watches your face for what comes next.

options.text: Go silent and stare at your plate
options.then: The table tenses. Your child wonders what they have done.

options.text: Snap at your child about something small
options.then: They flinch. The real fear stays hidden and the dinner is spoiled.

steps.why: A short pause lets the wave pass before it lands on anyone else.

steps.prompt: A friend offers to be your listener whenever the fear comes. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes, and agree when you can call them
options.then: Your friend agrees. Now the fear has somewhere to go before it reaches your child.

options.text: Say thanks, but you should manage on your own
options.then: Your friend nods. The next spike again finds only you.

options.text: Say yes, but only if they will agree with you
options.then: Your friend goes quiet. A listener who has to agree cannot help much.

options.text: Say you will call only when it is really bad
options.then: Your friend waits. By then, the fear has usually spilled.

steps.why: A steady listener helps your feelings find a safe place before they reach your child.

scenarios.debrief: Pause; route it to an adult.
scenarios.relearn: When fear floods you, pause; take it to a supportive adult or helpline, not to your child.

scenarios.hook: Your partner wants to leave the topic alone, hoping it will sort itself out. You feel the pull to agree.

steps.prompt: Your partner says "Let's not talk about it" again at dinner. What do you do?

options.text: Say ignoring it isn't neutral, and offer to learn
options.then: Your partner sighs. "Fine. But I do not know where to start."

options.text: Agree to leave it alone for now, to keep the peace
options.then: The house is calm. Your child hears silence and reads it as shame.

options.text: Raise your voice, even though your child is nearby
options.then: Your child hears every word from the next room and goes still.

options.text: Say fine, and quietly read up on it alone instead
options.then: You learn a lot. Your partner keeps old ideas, and you carry it alone.

steps.why: Saying avoidance is not neutral, and offering to learn together, keeps you on the same team.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your partner suggests just watching what your child does for a while. What do you say?

options.text: Suggest reading one affirming source each
options.then: Your partner agrees, a little reluctantly. "One article. Just one."

options.text: Agree to watch what your child does for now
options.then: Your child feels watched and stops sharing things at dinner.

options.text: Agree to watch, but only for a month or so
options.then: A month passes. Your child is still waiting to be seen.

options.text: Say your partner is causing your child to struggle
options.then: Your partner goes cold. They stop speaking about it entirely.

steps.why: Reading together turns watching into learning, without blame.

steps.prompt: Your child notices the strain between you both and asks what is going on. What do you do?

options.text: Say you are learning together, and love them
options.then: Their face relaxes. "Okay. Thanks for telling me."

options.text: Say it is only grown-up talk and nothing to worry about
options.then: They nod, but the strain still feels like it is about them.

options.text: Ask your partner to explain it all to them
options.then: Your partner fumbles. Your child watches you both, uneasy.

options.text: Say everything is fine and go back to eating
options.then: They look from one face to the other, unconvinced.

steps.why: Telling them you are learning and love them keeps silence from becoming shame.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, your partner admits they have been thinking about it more than they let on. What do you do?

options.text: Thank them, and ask what has been on their mind
options.then: They pause. "Whether our child feels rejected." It is the first real opening.

options.text: Say "I told you so" and leave the table
options.then: Your partner goes quiet and doesn't raise it again.

options.text: Drop the subject so the evening stays pleasant
options.then: The evening is pleasant. The topic waits for another day.

options.text: Send five articles to their phone that night
options.then: Your partner scrolls, overwhelmed, and puts the phone away.

steps.why: Thanking them and asking what is on their mind keeps the learning safe and moving.

scenarios.debrief: Avoidance isn't neutral.
scenarios.relearn: Avoidance isn't neutral; invite your partner to learn alongside you rather than burying it.

scenarios.hook: You feel guilt-frozen, sure you've done too much damage to bother trying now.

steps.prompt: Your child is at the breakfast table, and you have the chance to say something small. What do you do?

options.text: Say one warm sentence, however awkward
options.then: Your child looks up, surprised. "Thanks," they say, and stay a moment longer.

options.text: Decide it is too late and stay quiet
options.then: They finish their tea and leave. The chance passes by.

options.text: Wait until you feel you deserve to begin
options.then: You wait. Days pass, and nothing changes.

options.text: Give a long apology covering everything at once
options.then: Your child sits stiffly through it and says "Okay." You feel worse.

steps.why: One small warm step reaches your child. Waiting to feel worthy does not.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your child tells you a small thing about their day. What do you do?

options.text: Listen fully and ask one gentle question
options.then: They tell you a little more. The kitchen feels warmer.

options.text: Answer briefly while looking at your phone
options.then: They stop mid-sentence and leave the room.

options.text: Launch into a long apology instead of listening
options.then: They shift in their seat, uncomfortable, and say it is fine.

options.text: Say you are busy and ask them later
options.then: Later never quite comes, and they stop offering.

steps.why: Listening is the repair. Another apology can wait.

steps.prompt: A relative says it is too late and the damage is done. What do you say?

options.text: Say it is never too late, and you are starting now
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. You feel steadier for having said it.

options.text: Sigh and agree that you handled it badly
options.then: You leave feeling smaller. The old guilt settles in.

options.text: Ask her what you should do to fix it
options.then: She gives you a long list, and none of it is about your child.

options.text: Say you do not want advice
options.then: She goes quiet. Your own doubts do not.

steps.why: Starting late still counts, and saying so guards you against the guilt spiral.

steps.prompt: One evening your child asks why you have been so distant. What do you say?

options.text: Say you were scared and slow, and you are here now
options.then: They nod. "Thanks for saying so." A small smile follows.

options.text: Say you were trying all along
options.then: They look at you, unsure. It doesn't match what they remember.

options.text: Say you needed to think it over first
options.then: They shrug. "Think what over?" It still doesn't explain much to them.

options.text: Say it does not matter now
options.then: They go quiet. Something important was closed off.

steps.why: Being honest that you were slow and are here now is what rebuilds trust.

scenarios.debrief: One step beats frozen guilt.
scenarios.relearn: Guilt-freezing helps no one; one small repairing step today, however late, still matters.

scenarios.hook: A WhatsApp 'uncle' shares a video promising to 'fix' children like yours.

steps.prompt: The comments under it are full of praise. What do you do?

options.text: Delete it, and look for affirming support
options.then: You find a parents' group built on understanding. The video fades from your mind.

options.text: Watch it all the way through, just in case
options.then: The presenter sounds sure and kind. You feel a flicker of hope.

options.text: Forward it to your partner to think about
options.then: Your partner replies with a thumbs-up and a question. "Can we call them?"

options.text: Message the uncle to ask for the clinic's number
options.then: He sends it in minutes, with a discount code.

steps.why: Deleting it and reading affirming sources keeps you learning from real help.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your partner mentions the video and asks if it is worth a try. What do you say?

options.text: Say those cures harm, and offer to find real support
options.then: Your partner blinks. "Harm? I did not know that."

options.text: Say you are not sure and would rather leave it there
options.then: Your partner nods. The video stays in their head.

options.text: Say it cannot hurt to try it just once or twice
options.then: Your partner looks relieved and starts looking up dates.

options.text: Say you will ask your child what they think of it
options.then: Your child hears about it and looks hurt.

steps.why: Naming the harm plainly and offering an alternative stops a well-meant mistake.

steps.prompt: A relative in the group asks why you did not share the video. What do you say?

options.text: Say you looked into it, and cures harm children
options.then: She goes quiet. "I did not know."

options.text: Say you were too busy to watch it properly
options.then: She says she will send it again. The pressure returns.

options.text: Say nothing, and quietly leave the group chat
options.then: Others in the group take it as a sign, and you are left with unanswered questions.

options.text: Say you will share it with everyone later on
options.then: She thanks you, and the video ends up in more phones.

steps.why: A short, calm answer stops the video from spreading through you.

scenarios.debrief: Nothing to cure.
scenarios.relearn: There's nothing to cure; 'cures' are discredited and harmful. Only affirming support helps.

scenarios.hook: A comment you made yesterday, born of your fear, clearly stung your child.

steps.prompt: Your child is avoiding you this morning. What do you do?

options.text: Go to them, own it, and say you love them
options.then: Their eyes are wary, but they listen. "Okay," they say quietly.

options.text: Act as if yesterday never happened at all
options.then: Breakfast is normal. The sting stays under the table.

options.text: Explain that you were only being honest with them
options.then: Their face closes. "Then I guess that's what you think."

options.text: Wait for them to come to you, whenever they are ready
options.then: They don't. The day ends with both of you carrying it.

steps.why: Going back yourself, and saying you love them, does the repairing so they don't have to.

steps.prompt: Your child asks in a small voice why you said it. What do you say?

options.text: Say it came from your fear, not the truth
options.then: They think, then nod. "Okay. I thought it was because of me."

options.text: Say you were tired and it meant nothing at all
options.then: They frown. "It felt like it meant something."

options.text: Say it was because of how they had been acting
options.then: Their shoulders fall. They now think it was their doing.

options.text: Say you will explain it properly when they are older
options.then: They nod slowly and stop asking.

steps.why: Naming it as your fear, and not their fault, heals the sting.

steps.prompt: A week later, a similar comment nearly slips out at dinner. What do you do?

options.text: Stop, breathe, and say something warm instead
options.then: You tell them you are glad they are at this table. Their face softens.

options.text: Say it, then quickly add that you were joking
options.then: Nobody laughs. The comment lands anyway.

options.text: Say it again in a softer tone this time
options.then: The words are gentler. They still say the same thing.

options.text: Leave the table quickly without a word
options.then: Your child watches the empty chair. They wonder what they did.

steps.why: A pause before speaking gives you room to choose warmth over the old fear.

steps.prompt: Your child says it hurt, and asks if you have really changed. What do you say?

options.text: Say you are still learning, and you will keep trying
options.then: They nod. "Okay. I'll tell you when it hurts."

options.text: Promise you will never slip again, not once
options.then: They nod, but they know you will. The next slip will feel like a broken promise.

options.text: Say they should not hold one comment against you
options.then: They look down. Their hurt has been made small.

options.text: Say you do not want to talk about it any more
options.then: They shrug and leave. The door they opened is closed again.

steps.why: Being honest that you are still learning is more trustworthy than a promise of perfection.

scenarios.debrief: Own it; reaffirm love.
scenarios.relearn: A hurtful comment from your fear can be repaired: go back, own it, reaffirm your love.

scenarios.hook: You're calling Tele-MANAS 14416 for your own support, and you're nervous to say it aloud.
scenarios.setup: The line picks up after a few rings.

steps.prompt: The counsellor says: "Hello. What is on your mind?"

options.text: "I love my child. I'm struggling and want support."
options.then: Her voice is warm. "Thank you for saying that. You're not alone."

options.text: "My child has a problem. Tell me how to change them."
options.then: She stays calm. "I hear you're worried. Let's begin with what you feel."

options.text: "I'm calling for a friend, whose child is struggling."
options.then: "Of course. What would your friend like to know?"

options.text: "Nothing, really. I probably shouldn't be calling."
options.then: "You're welcome to stay on," she says. "Most callers start just like that."

steps.why: Framing it as your feelings to work on is what gets you real help.

steps.prompt: The counsellor asks gently: "What has been the hardest part lately?"

options.text: "Fear of what people say, and grief for my old plans."
options.then: "Both are real," she says. "You can grieve and still love your child."

options.text: "My child, honestly. They've changed everything."
options.then: "I hear that," she says. "Shall we look at what is changing for you?"

options.text: "My spouse won't help, and it's all falling on me."
options.then: "That sounds lonely. Shall we come back to how you feel today?"

options.text: "Everything. I can't even begin to explain it."
options.then: "That's okay. We can go slowly, one piece at a time."

steps.why: Naming the fear and the grief, honestly, is where the real work starts.

steps.prompt: The counsellor asks: "Does your child know you are calling?"

options.text: "No. This is mine to work through for now."
options.then: "All right," she says. "Then let's keep this space just for you."

options.text: "Yes. I told them I'm calling to sort them out."
options.then: She pauses. "I'd gently suggest that isn't what this call is for."

options.text: "Yes. They said I need help, so I finally called."
options.then: "That's okay," she says. "Let's make sure the help is for you."

options.text: "No, and I'll keep it secret from them forever."
options.then: "Secrets can weigh heavy," she says. "Maybe we can look at that later."

steps.why: Your inner work belongs with a supportive adult, not on your child.

steps.prompt: The counsellor asks: "What would help you most in the next week?"

options.text: "Someone I can call when the fear comes."
options.then: "You can call here anytime. We can also point you to support near you."

options.text: "A script to change my child's mind."
options.then: "Nothing I can give would do that, and it wouldn't help them," she says.

options.text: "To be told it will all be fine."
options.then: "I can't promise that," she says. "But I can promise you're not alone."

options.text: "An article proving I did nothing wrong."
options.then: "There's good reading on that," she says. "But talking usually helps more."

steps.why: A person to call in the moment is the most practical support when fear rises.

scenarios.relearn: Reaching out for your own support, framed as your feelings to work on, gets you help without making it the child's fault.

scenarios.hook: Since your child came out, you have kept a brave face with most people.
scenarios.setup: Over chai, a close friend puts down her cup and waits.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "How are you really coping?"

options.text: "Some days are hard. Talking to you helps me carry it."
options.then: She squeezes your hand. "I'm glad you can say it here."

options.text: "It's been awful. I keep telling my child how upset I am."
options.then: Her smile fades. "Oh. And how is your child taking that?"

options.text: "I'm fine. Everything is fine. Please don't worry about me."
options.then: She studies you. "You don't sound fine." She waits, not changing the subject.

options.text: "Honestly, I'd rather not talk about it. Not even with you."
options.then: "Okay," she says gently, and lets the silence sit for a while.

steps.why: Being honest with a friend gives your feelings a safe place, away from your child.

steps.prompt: A little later, your friend says: "You don't have to be strong for everyone. What do you need?"

options.text: "A place to say the messy parts, away from my child."
options.then: She nods. "You have that here. Anytime."

options.text: "I need my child to see just how hard this is for me."
options.then: She looks worried. "Would that help them, though?"

options.text: "I need someone to tell me it will all pass soon."
options.then: "I can't promise that," she says. "But I'll be here."

options.text: "I need someone to agree this is far too much to bear."
options.then: "It's a lot," she says. "But your child is carrying a lot too."

steps.why: Asking for a listening ear, away from your child, is a healthy way to get support.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "How much of all this do you share with your child?"

options.text: "Not the details. Only that I'm learning, and love them."
options.then: She smiles. "That sounds like enough for a child to hear."

options.text: "Everything. I tell them every fear, so we are both honest."
options.then: She winces. "Every fear? That's a lot for a child to hold."

options.text: "Nothing. I hide it all so that they never worry at all."
options.then: "They may still sense it," she says. "Hiding is tiring."

options.text: "They can tell already. I don't need to say a word."
options.then: "Kids often can," she says. "But they might read it as blame."

steps.why: Sharing that you are learning and love them is honest, without handing them your fears.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Shall we meet every week, just for this?"

options.text: "Yes, please. It helps me be a calmer parent."
options.then: She smiles. "Same time, same chai."

options.text: "No. I should manage this without leaning on anyone."
options.then: She nods, a little hurt. The hard days stay yours alone.

options.text: "Yes, but only if you just listen and never ask me anything."
options.then: She hesitates. "I can listen. I might still ask."

options.text: "Maybe. I'll call you when it is a real emergency."
options.then: She nods. Until then, the hard days have nowhere to go.

steps.why: A regular, honest listener keeps hard feelings from reaching your child.

scenarios.relearn: Being honest with a supportive friend lets you carry the hard days without making your child manage your feelings.

scenarios.hook: Your mother wants you to be stricter with your child, and you don't want a war.
scenarios.setup: She arrives with a box of laddoos and a serious face.

steps.prompt: Your mother says: "Beta, put your foot down now, before it's too late."

options.text: "I hear you, Ma. I've decided my child needs my support."
options.then: She purses her lips. "Support. Hm." But she doesn't argue.

options.text: "Fine. I'll be stricter with them, so you stop nagging me."
options.then: She beams. "Finally." Down the hall, your child's door shuts softly.

options.text: "Ma, this is a different time. You wouldn't understand."
options.then: She waves a hand. "Times change. Children still need rules."

options.text: "Let me think about it for a while, Ma. I'll tell you."
options.then: She nods. "Don't take too long." The question stays on the table.

steps.why: Hearing her worry while stating your decision keeps the peace and protects your child.

steps.prompt: Your mother says: "What will the neighbours think of you?"

options.text: "Their opinions matter less to me than my child does."
options.then: She sighs. "You were always stubborn." The edge has gone from her voice.

options.text: "You're right. I'll keep my child indoors more often."
options.then: She nods, relieved. Your child hears the new rule at dinner.

options.text: "I'll tell them my child is just going through a phase."
options.then: She smiles. Your child is now a phase at every neighbour's door.

options.text: "Let's move away, then, where nobody knows us at all."
options.then: She looks shocked. "Move? Because of this?"

steps.why: Your child matters more than the neighbours, and saying so calmly keeps your line clear.

steps.prompt: Your mother says: "Then tell me what I should do. I want to help."

options.text: "Love them, listen to them, and come to a parents' group."
options.then: Her eyes fill. "A group? For people like us? I'll come."

options.text: "Just don't say anything about it, and it will be fine."
options.then: She nods, tight-lipped. Her silence is loud at family dinners.

options.text: "Gently tell them that they should try to fit in more."
options.then: She agrees happily. Your child hears it at the next visit and shrinks.

options.text: "Keep telling me what to do, until something changes."
options.then: She is pleased. You are back to arguing every week.

steps.why: Giving her something real to do turns her worry into help.

scenarios.relearn: You can honour your parent's worry while holding your line: your child's support is decided, and you invite help, not control.

scenarios.hook: You slipped into comparing your child to 'normal' kids out loud.
scenarios.setup: You see their face fall as you finish the sentence.

steps.prompt: Your child says quietly: "So I'm not normal?"

options.text: "That came out wrong. There's nothing abnormal about you."
options.then: Their eyes rise to meet yours. "Really?"

options.text: "I didn't mean it like that. Don't take it so seriously."
options.then: They look down. "Okay."

options.text: "Well, you're not like the other children. That's all."
options.then: Their face crumples. "So I'm different, and that's bad."

options.text: "Let's just forget I said it. It doesn't matter now."
options.then: They nod, but the words stay with them.

steps.why: Correcting yourself straight away tells them the words were wrong, not them.

steps.prompt: Your child asks: "Do you think that about me, deep down?"

options.text: "No. That's an old idea I grew up with. I'm unlearning it."
options.then: They think about it. "Okay. So it's not about me."

options.text: "No. Other people say it, and I just repeated it."
options.then: They frown. "But you said it."

options.text: "A little, because you keep doing things that stand out."
options.then: They stare. "So it's my fault for standing out."

options.text: "I don't know. Please stop asking me so many questions."
options.then: They stop. The question goes unanswered.

steps.why: Naming the old idea as yours, not theirs, takes the blame off them.

steps.prompt: Your child says: "I don't feel safe telling you things if you say that."

options.text: "That matters to me. I want you to feel safe with me."
options.then: Their voice is small. "I want that too."

options.text: "You can tell me anything. I'll just try not to react."
options.then: They nod, doubtful. "But you might."

options.text: "I'm your parent. You should be able to tell me anything."
options.then: They look away. "Should doesn't make it so."

options.text: "You're being dramatic. It was only one word."
options.then: They go still. "Okay."

steps.why: Taking their fear of speaking seriously, and saying you want to be safe, keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: Your child asks: "What will you do when you slip again?"

options.text: "I'll stop, say sorry, and say it better. Remind me."
options.then: A small smile. "I can do that."

options.text: "I won't slip again. I have learned my lesson for good."
options.then: They nod, but their eyes say they will believe it when they see it.

options.text: "Then we'll just move on and not make a fuss."
options.then: They nod. Ignoring hurt becomes something they are expected to do.

options.text: "Then I'll buy you a treat, to make up for it later."
options.then: They smile a little. It feels a bit like being paid off.

steps.why: Promising to catch yourself and repair, and asking for a reminder, is honest and realistic.

scenarios.relearn: Catching your own slip and naming it as old ideas you're unlearning protects your child and models honest growth.

scenarios.hook: Your child has felt the tension in the house for weeks.
scenarios.setup: They stand at the kitchen door, twisting their sleeve.

steps.prompt: Your child asks: "Are you ashamed of me?"

options.text: "Never ashamed. My fears are mine to work on, not yours."
options.then: Their shoulders drop. "Okay. I just needed to hear it."

options.text: "A little at times. You'll understand when you're a parent."
options.then: Their eyes fill. "A little?" They say nothing more.

options.text: "Of course not. Why on earth would you ask me that?"
options.then: They flinch. "Because you looked away when I came in."

options.text: "It's complicated, and we'll talk when you're older."
options.then: They nod. They hear that it is complicated, and that they are the cause.

steps.why: A clear never, plus owning your fears, lifts the shame off them.

steps.prompt: At dinner the next day, your child asks: "You're still so quiet. Is it because of me?"

options.text: "It's my own worries, and none of it is your doing."
options.then: They breathe out. "I thought it was because of something I did."

options.text: "Yes. I have been thinking a lot about what you told me."
options.then: They nod, gripping their sleeve. They take it as a verdict.

options.text: "No. I've just been very busy with work lately."
options.then: They look unconvinced. They can tell when they aren't hearing the truth.

options.text: "Don't you worry about my feelings. Just eat your dinner."
options.then: They pick at their plate, still holding the question.

steps.why: Telling them it is your worry, not their doing, removes a guilt they were carrying.

steps.prompt: Your child asks: "What are you scared of? Can I help?"

options.text: "That's kind of you. It's my job to handle, not yours."
options.then: They look relieved and a little proud. "Okay. Tell me if you want a hug."

options.text: "Yes. You could stop making all of this so hard for me."
options.then: Their face falls. "I'm making it hard?"

options.text: "Yes. Just sit with me when I feel low, and cheer me up."
options.then: They agree. Now they check on your mood every evening.

options.text: "Yes. Promise me you'll be careful and stay out of trouble."
options.then: They promise. Now they are in charge of your fears.

steps.why: Thanking them but keeping your worries with adults spares them from managing your feelings.

steps.prompt: Your child asks: "Will you still be scared next year?"

options.text: "Maybe sometimes. But I'll keep loving you and learning."
options.then: They lean on you. "Okay. I'll keep loving you too."

options.text: "No. I'm sure it will all be sorted out by then."
options.then: They nod, but they know it is a promise you can't keep.

options.text: "That depends on how you act between now and then."
options.then: They go pale. Your fear has become their responsibility.

options.text: "I don't know. Please don't ask me that ever again."
options.then: They nod. The subject closes, and so does the door.

steps.why: Being honest that fear may return, while promising love, is steadying and true.

scenarios.relearn: Telling your child the tension is your own work to do, never shame at them, keeps them safe from carrying your feelings.

scenarios.hook: You have been invited to share at a parent support group for the first time.
scenarios.setup: The circle turns to you, and the room goes quiet.

steps.prompt: The facilitator says: "Would you like to share a little today?"

options.text: "I'm new to this and scared. I'm here because I love my kid."
options.then: Her face softens. "Thank you. Many of us started right there."

options.text: "I'm here because someone made me. I don't believe any of this."
options.then: A few parents look down. She nods. "Listening is fine today."

options.text: "Let me tell you what I think is wrong with my child first."
options.then: The room goes quiet. A parent shifts in her seat.

options.text: "I'm doing great, thanks. I don't know why I'm here."
options.then: A few smile politely. The circle moves on.

steps.why: Honest, humble sharing, even when scared, is what makes a group work.

steps.prompt: At the tea break, another parent asks you gently: "How did you feel when you first found out?"

options.text: "Frightened, and a bit ashamed of being frightened."
options.then: She nods. "Same," she whispers.

options.text: "I felt sure someone must have influenced them at school."
options.then: The parent nods kindly. "I thought that too. I learned it doesn't work that way."

options.text: "I felt betrayed, and I told my child exactly that."
options.then: She goes quiet. "That one needs a repair, and it's not too late," she says gently.

options.text: "It doesn't matter how I felt. This is all about the kids."
options.then: She nods. The moment for honest sharing passes.

steps.why: Saying the frightened, messy truth helps other parents feel less alone.

steps.prompt: Before the session ends, the facilitator asks: "What would you like from this group?"

options.text: "To learn how to show my child I love them better."
options.then: She nods. "Then come every week. We'll learn it together."

options.text: "Someone to tell me how I can change my child back."
options.then: She answers kindly. "A child can't be changed, and trying only harms them. We can help you."

options.text: "Reassurance that this is just a phase and will pass."
options.then: A parent smiles kindly. "We can't promise that. We can help you stand by them either way."

options.text: "Advice on how to stop the relatives talking about us."
options.then: Several parents nod. "Let's start with how you feel about it."

steps.why: Asking to learn how to show love keeps your focus on your child.

scenarios.relearn: Honest, humble sharing in a support group helps you learn faster and reminds you you're not alone on this journey.

scenarios.hook: Your spouse has been tense for days about how you're raising your child.
scenarios.setup: It is late, and your spouse is pacing the kitchen.

steps.prompt: Your spouse says: "You're too soft. You'll make it worse."

options.text: "I know you're scared too. Acceptance is what protects them."
options.then: Your spouse stops pacing. "Protects them? From what?"

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I'll toughen up on them from now on."
options.then: Your spouse eases, satisfied. "Good. Start tomorrow."

options.text: "You are the one making it worse, shouting at me like this."
options.then: Your spouse's jaw tightens. "So it's all my fault."

options.text: "Let's not fight. I'll go along with whatever you decide."
options.then: Your spouse nods. The decision is theirs, and so is the fear.

steps.why: Naming their fear and pointing to acceptance holds your line without a fight.

steps.prompt: Your spouse says: "My mother says children like this just need a firm hand."

options.text: "I've read what helps. Let's go through it together tonight."
options.then: Your spouse sits down. "Fine. Show me."

options.text: "I just know. A parent can feel these things in their bones."
options.then: Your spouse scoffs. "Feelings aren't proof."

options.text: "Everyone I've asked says the opposite. That's proof enough."
options.then: Your spouse folds their arms. "Who is everyone?"

options.text: "Look it up yourself. I'm tired of explaining everything."
options.then: Your spouse heads for the door, then stops. "No. We're not done."

steps.why: Offering evidence to read together answers the doubt without shame.

steps.prompt: Your spouse says quietly: "I'm scared for them. What if the world is cruel?"

options.text: "So am I. That's why home has to be their safest place."
options.then: Your spouse's shoulders drop. "Yes. Home has to be safe."

options.text: "Then let's teach them to hide it whenever they are outside."
options.then: Your spouse agrees. Your child begins to learn to mask.

options.text: "The world is cruel. They may as well learn that early."
options.then: Your spouse nods grimly. Your child lies awake that night.

options.text: "Then we should protect them by keeping them at home."
options.then: Your spouse relaxes. Your child's world begins to shrink.

steps.why: Making home the safest place is how you answer a frightened spouse.

scenarios.relearn: Naming your spouse's fear and pointing to the evidence holds your line on acceptance without turning it into a fight.

scenarios.hook: You went quiet on your child for weeks while you wrestled with yourself.
scenarios.setup: You find them on the balcony and sit down beside them.

steps.prompt: Your child says: "You stopped talking to me. Why?"

options.text: "I went quiet because of my own struggle, not because of you."
options.then: They look at you for a long moment. "I thought you were angry with me."

options.text: "I was giving you some time to think about what you had done."
options.then: They stare. "What I did? What did I do?"

options.text: "I was busy. You know how hectic things have been at work."
options.then: They look away. "That's what I figured."

options.text: "I just didn't know what to say. It was nothing big at all."
options.then: "Okay," they say. "But it felt like you didn't want to."

steps.why: Saying the silence was your struggle, not their doing, starts the repair.

steps.prompt: Your child says: "I thought I'd done something really wrong."

options.text: "You did nothing wrong. Being you is never a mistake."
options.then: Their eyes fill. They lean into your shoulder.

options.text: "Well, you did surprise us a great deal. That was all."
options.then: They stare. "So I surprised you, and that's why you went quiet."

options.text: "Don't be so dramatic. It is all over now, so let it go."
options.then: They go quiet. "Okay." The question stays.

options.text: "We can talk about it another time. Not today, please."
options.then: They nod. Another time feels a long way off.

steps.why: Telling them plainly that they did nothing wrong is the most important thing they need.

steps.prompt: Your child asks: "Are you going to go quiet again?"

options.text: "I may struggle, but I'll tell you if I need space."
options.then: They nod slowly. "Okay. I can handle that if you tell me."

options.text: "No, never. I will be perfect from now on. I promise."
options.then: They nod, but they know nobody is perfect.

options.text: "Only if you do something again that makes me angry."
options.then: They flinch. Your quiet has become something they can cause.

options.text: "I can't promise anything. We'll just see how it goes."
options.then: They nod slowly. They brace for the next silence.

steps.why: Promising to say so when you need space is honest and stops them guessing.

steps.prompt: Your child says: "Can we do something together this week?"

options.text: "Yes. Pick anything you like. I'm in, and I'm staying."
options.then: A real smile. "Okay. Let's make momos."

options.text: "I'll see if I have time. Work is very busy this week."
options.then: They shrug. "Okay." You both know what that means.

options.text: "Let's talk about your school instead. That's more useful."
options.then: They sigh. It was about being with you, not school.

options.text: "Maybe, once things settle down a bit around here."
options.then: They nod and wait. Things never quite settle.

steps.why: A clear yes, with a promise to stay, shows them the silence is over.

scenarios.relearn: Owning that your silence was your own struggle, not the child's fault, repairs the gap and reopens the door.

scenarios.hook: A neighbour has been eager to ask about your son for weeks.
scenarios.setup: She leans over the gate with a sympathetic look.

steps.prompt: Your neighbour asks: "So is it true about your son?"

options.text: "My son's story is his to tell. He's a great kid and we adore him."
options.then: She blinks. "Oh. Well. Yes, he does seem happy." She lingers at the gate.

options.text: "Honestly, yes. I'm at my wits' end, so let me tell you everything."
options.then: Her eyes light up. She leans closer, already planning who to tell.

options.text: "I don't know what you mean. Excuse me. I have to go inside now."
options.then: She smiles knowingly. "Of course. Just one thing, though."

options.text: "Who told you that? I want the name of everyone who has said it."
options.then: She steps back. "Just what people are saying." You know it is spreading.

steps.why: A calm line that protects his story and shows you are proud of him ends the fishing.

steps.prompt: She says: "I only ask because I care. Everyone is talking, you know."

options.text: "That's kind. If you care, please stop others talking about him."
options.then: She looks a little ashamed. "I'll try."

options.text: "Who is everyone? I want to hear each name from you now."
options.then: She hesitates, then gives two names. You have started a hunt.

options.text: "Let them talk. I don't care what anyone says about us."
options.then: She shrugs. "As you like." She tells others you did not deny it.

options.text: "Please don't repeat any of this to anyone. Not a single word."
options.then: She smiles. "Never." Her tone doesn't quite reassure you.

steps.why: Asking her to stop the talk, kindly, uses her care to protect him.

steps.prompt: Later, your son asks: "Was Aunty talking about me? What did she say?"

options.text: "She was curious. Your story is yours to tell, and I'm proud of you."
options.then: He grins. "Okay, Mama." He leans against you for a moment.

options.text: "No, nothing at all. Don't worry about it, beta. Go and play."
options.then: He nods, but he saw your face when she left.

options.text: "She said awful things about you. Never speak to her again."
options.then: He hides behind you the next time she waves.

options.text: "Grown-ups gossip a lot. Just ignore all of it, beta."
options.then: He shrugs. He still doesn't know what is being said about him.

steps.why: A calm, honest answer that puts his story in his hands keeps him safe and informed.

scenarios.relearn: Protecting your child's privacy while affirming him publicly guards his story and shows you've chosen his side.

scenarios.hook: A friend has been your sounding board for months while you learn to support your child.
scenarios.setup: You meet her for tea to say thank you.

steps.prompt: Your friend smiles: "You look lighter today. What's on your mind?"

options.text: "Thank you for letting me vent. My kid gets the calmer me."
options.then: She beams and reaches for your hand. "I'm so glad."

options.text: "Thanks, but honestly venting to my kid would have been easier."
options.then: Her smile fades. "Easier for you, maybe. Not for them."

options.text: "Nothing much. I don't want to keep burdening you with this."
options.then: She frowns. "You could never burden me." Your thanks goes unsaid.

options.text: "I've decided that I don't need to talk about it any more."
options.then: She nods, a little hurt. "I'm here if that changes."

steps.why: Thanking her says out loud why this habit works for your whole family.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "Do you ever tell your child how you feel?"

options.text: "Only when calm. I say I'm learning, and it's not their fault."
options.then: She nods and stirs her tea. "I should try that with mine."

options.text: "Never. I keep every feeling from them so they don't worry."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "They probably sense it anyway."

options.text: "All the time. It's better that they know every feeling I have."
options.then: She hesitates. "Every feeling? That's heavy for a child."

options.text: "Only when I'm upset, so they understand what they've done."
options.then: She shakes her head. "That teaches them to hide, though."

steps.why: Sharing calmly that you are learning, and it is not their fault, is honest and light.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "What do you do when you feel you'll explode?"

options.text: "Step outside, breathe, and call you or someone I trust."
options.then: She grins. "Call me first. I'll pick up."

options.text: "Wait until I explode, then apologise afterwards to everyone."
options.then: She smiles ruefully. "Explosions still leave marks."

options.text: "Tell my child to leave me alone, whatever the reason."
options.then: She frowns. "They might think it's about them."

options.text: "Take it out on the housework and say nothing at all."
options.then: She laughs. "The kitchen is spotless, and you're still tense."

steps.why: Stepping away and calling someone you trust gives fear a place to go that is not your child.

scenarios.relearn: Thanking your support person reinforces the habit of taking your hard feelings to an adult, so your child gets the calmer you.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two thoughts that put your feelings onto your child.

scene.text: 'I'll talk this through with a counsellor'
'My child should see how much pain this causes me'
'It's my job, not my kid's, to settle my fear'
'If they loved me they'd just stop being this way'
'I can love them today while I'm still learning'

scenarios.why: The caught thoughts make the child responsible for your pain or acceptance.
scenarios.relearn: Watch for thoughts that make your child carry your pain or earn your love; those feelings are yours to work through.
scenarios.source: thoughts that land on the child

scenarios.hook: Spot the two moves that stall your own journey.

scene.text: Reading a little each week to understand
Replaying mistakes to punish yourself nightly
Telling your child 'I'm learning with you'
Demanding you be perfect at this by now
Booking an affirming counsellor

scenarios.why: The caught moves, self-punishment and demanding perfection, freeze you in shame; steady learning and support move you forward.
scenarios.relearn: Self-punishment and demanding instant perfection stall you; steady learning and support move you forward.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that make your child responsible for your comfort.

scene.text: 'My feelings are mine to work through'
'You need to act normal so I feel okay'
'I'll get support so I don't lean on you'
'Reassure me you'll grow out of this'
'You don't have to manage how I feel'

scenarios.why: The caught lines ask the child to perform or reassure for the parent's comfort; a child should never manage a parent's feelings.
scenarios.relearn: Never ask your child to act 'normal' or reassure you; your feelings aren't theirs to manage.
scenarios.source: not their job to comfort you

scenarios.hook: Spot the two beliefs that treat your starting point as a final verdict.

scene.text: 'How I was raised shaped my start, not my limit'
'I felt fear, so I must be a bad parent'
'Feelings can shift as I learn and grow'
'It's too late for me to change'
'Small steps today still make my child safer'

scenarios.why: The caught beliefs treat your start as a fixed verdict; the direction you move is what counts.
scenarios.relearn: Don't treat fear as proof you're bad or change as too late; your starting point isn't your verdict.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two 'shortcuts' that promise relief but harm your child.

scene.text: Finding an affirming counsellor for support
Trying a 'cure' programme to change your child
Joining a parent support group to learn
Outing your child to relatives for advice
Calling Tele-MANAS 14416 for your stress

scenarios.why: The caught shortcuts, a 'cure' and outing the child, harm them.
scenarios.relearn: 'Cures' and outing your child are harmful shortcuts; affirming counsellors and helplines help without endangering them.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two ways a parent makes the child wait until the parent feels ready.

scene.text: Supporting the child now and growing in parallel
Withholding warmth until you've 'come to terms'
Saying 'I love you' before you understand it all
Making the child prove it's not a phase first
Taking one small accepting step today

scenarios.why: The caught moves make the child wait, withholding warmth and demanding proof.
scenarios.relearn: Don't make your child wait for your comfort; support and small steps protect them today, not someday.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two reactions that leak your private fear onto your child.

scene.text: Naming the fear to a counsellor privately
Pulling away coldly when your child is near
Journalling the fear to understand it
Snapping 'look what you've done to this family'
Reminding yourself the fear is yours to carry

scenarios.why: The caught reactions leak your fear onto the child as coldness or blame.
scenarios.relearn: Handle fear privately; cold distance and blame leak it onto your child, while quiet self-work keeps it yours.

pairs.right: An honest repair, not a defence

pairs.right: Lets love lead while understanding grows

pairs.right: Acceptance protects; it doesn't cause it

pairs.left: 'Maybe it's a phase to wait out'
pairs.right: Respect them now, whether or not it shifts

scenarios.hook: Sort: healthy grieving of an imagined future, or grief curdling into rejection?

items.text: Quietly letting go of a picture you'd held
Punishing the child for not being it
Naming the loss to a counsellor
Pulling love back till they 'become normal'
Falling for the real child you have
Treating your grief as the child's fault

scenarios.relearn: Grief is healthy when you let go privately and embrace the real child; it curdles if you punish or blame them.
