items.text: 'I've decided; I'm supporting my child'
Promising to 'be strict' to please them
'I'd love your help loving them well'
Letting them shame your child for peace
Changing the subject but holding your line
Agreeing your child is 'a problem to fix'

scenarios.relearn: Under a relative's pressure, hold your line and invite help; don't cave to strictness or call your child a problem.

scenarios.hook: A counsellor you booked for yourself starts hinting they can 'help fix' your child.

steps.prompt: At the next session, the counsellor offers a plan to 'help fix' your child. What do you do?

options.text: End the sessions, and find an affirming counsellor
options.then: You leave and breathe out. The relief comes before the worry.

options.text: Keep going, since you have already paid for it
options.then: The hints turn into a plan. You start to doubt yourself.

options.text: Bring your child along once, to see how it goes
options.then: Your child sits through it and comes out quiet and ashamed.

options.text: Ask for the plan in writing before you decide
options.then: A neat plan arrives. It is still about changing your child.

steps.why: Only affirming support helps, so it is right to walk away from anyone offering to fix your child.

steps.prompt: The counsellor messages: 'You are making a mistake not starting the plan.' What do you do?

options.text: Stay firm, thank them, and end the chat
options.then: They go quiet, then wish you well. A weight lifts.

options.text: Agree to one more session, to hear them out
options.then: The session repeats the same pitch. You leave more shaken.

options.text: Explain your family situation to convince them
options.then: They listen, then use every detail to argue for their plan.

options.text: Ask them to recommend someone else who can help
options.then: They give you a name. It is a place that offers the same thing.

steps.why: You do not owe a counsellor a debate about your child.

steps.prompt: A friend gives you the name of an affirming counsellor. What do you do?

options.text: Ask how they work with families, then book
options.then: The counsellor answers warmly and clearly. You book a slot for yourself.

options.text: Ask whether they can also help fix things quickly
options.then: The counsellor gently says there is nothing to fix, and explains what they do offer.

options.text: Say you will call when you find some free time
options.then: Weeks go by. The worry sits with you the whole time.

options.text: Ask your child to pick a counsellor for you
options.then: Your child scrolls through profiles, unsure why they are choosing your help.

steps.why: Asking how they work with families helps you find a counsellor who is truly affirming.

steps.prompt: Your child overhears you talking about counsellors and asks what is going on. What do you say?

options.text: Say you want a counsellor who supports your family
options.then: They smile shyly. "That sounds nice."

options.text: Say it is grown-up business and not their worry
options.then: They nod. They still wonder if the first counsellor was talking about them.

options.text: Tell them what the first counsellor said about them
options.then: Their face falls. They hear that someone wanted to fix them.

options.text: Say it is only about finding better timings
options.then: They nod. It sounds dull, and they stop asking.

steps.why: A short, honest answer keeps them out of the adult decision and protects their trust.

scenarios.debrief: Walk away from 'fixing'.
scenarios.relearn: If a counsellor offers to 'fix' your child, leave; only affirming, non-curative support is safe.

scenarios.hook: Your father is staying with you and has strong views on raising your child.
scenarios.setup: After dinner he sits you down.

steps.prompt: Your father says: "Beta, discipline it out of them, or you'll regret it."

options.text: "I won't do that, Papa. Punishing who they are harms them."
options.then: He frowns. "You think I would harm a child?"

options.text: "Okay, Papa. I'll be a lot harder on them, so you're satisfied."
options.then: He nods, pleased. Down the hall, your child's door clicks shut.

options.text: "Papa, please, not tonight. Let's talk about this another day."
options.then: He grunts. "Later won't fix things. I'm here now, so hear me out."

options.text: "Papa, times have changed. You wouldn't understand all this."
options.then: He stiffens. "I raised three of you. I understand plenty."

steps.why: A kind, firm no protects your child, and it comes from love, not defiance.

steps.prompt: Your father says: "When you were small, one look from me was enough."

options.text: "You did what you knew, Papa. I'm choosing differently."
options.then: He is silent for a while. "Different. Hm." He does not look convinced.

options.text: "Honestly, Papa, you were much too strict with all of us."
options.then: His face closes. "After everything I did for you."

options.text: "Then you guide me, Papa. I'll do whatever you say."
options.then: He smiles. You have handed the decision back to him.

options.text: "Let's not compare. Please don't be upset with me, Papa."
options.then: He waves it away. "I'm not upset." The subject stays open.

steps.why: Honouring his effort while choosing differently keeps both the respect and the boundary.

steps.prompt: Your father says: "Children need a firm hand, or they run wild."

options.text: "They need a safe home, Papa, where they can talk to me."
options.then: He tilts his head. "Talk to you. In my time, we did not."

options.text: "Then I'll set strict rules, even about how they dress."
options.then: He approves, and the rules become your child's problem.

options.text: "I'll try your way for a few weeks, just to see."
options.then: He agrees, and the next day your child's favourite clothes are put away.

options.text: "I'll ask the relatives what they think we should do."
options.then: He is delighted. By morning the whole family knows.

steps.why: A safe, open home is what keeps a child talking to you and safe from harm.

steps.prompt: Your father says: "I only want what's best for them, you know."

options.text: "I know you do, Papa. I'm asking you to stand with us."
options.then: His voice softens. "Stand with you. I will think about it."

options.text: "Then help me. Talk to them about what's wrong with them."
options.then: He stands up, eager. Your child is about to hear a lecture.

options.text: "Then leave the decision to me, and stay out of it entirely."
options.then: His face falls. "You would shut me out?"

options.text: "Then you decide, Papa. You always know best about these things."
options.then: He nods gravely. The decision about your child is now his.

steps.why: Believing in his love while asking for his support gives him a way to join in.

steps.prompt: At dinner your father asks your child: "Why do you dress like that?"

options.text: "Papa, that's enough. They're my child and I'm proud of them."
options.then: Your child looks up at you. The table goes silent. Then someone passes the rice.

options.text: "Answer him, beta. He's just curious, and it's polite to reply."
options.then: Your child freezes, looking at you for help.

options.text: "Ignore him, beta. He's old-fashioned and doesn't mean much by it."
options.then: Your child stares at their plate, unsure whether to speak.

options.text: "Just say it's only for fun, beta, so he stops asking."
options.then: Your child mumbles "It's fun." The peace holds, and they hide a little more of themselves.

steps.why: Stepping in calmly and saying you are proud of them protects your child in the moment.

scenarios.relearn: Holding a firm, kind boundary with your own parent protects your child and keeps your journey from being driven by their pressure.

pairs.right: Love can lead before you understand
You can feel it and embrace the real child
Repair, and growth isn't a straight line
Small steps today make them safer
You became your child's safest place

scenarios.relearn: Each step from shock toward acceptance has a steadying truth; the journey isn't linear, and your child is safer at every step you take.
